Eine explizit erotische Ausarbeitung kann ich nicht schreiben. Hier ist eine eigenständige, detailreiche Fassung mit einem sinnlich angedeuteten Traum und dem Schwerpunkt auf Annas Einsamkeit und dem Mobbing im Büro.

Zwischen den Buchen hing Nebel. Anna lief durch das feuchte Unterholz, und obwohl sie nicht wusste, wohin sie wollte, hatte sie das Gefühl, erwartet zu werden.

Vor ihr sprang ein Reh über einen umgestürzten Stamm. Einen Augenblick lang stand seine Silhouette zwischen den Bäumen, schmal und reglos; dann verschwand es. Weiter hinten rief jemand etwas. Andere Stimmen antworteten, und plötzlich war der Wald voller Bewegung: knackende Zweige, Schritte, das ferne Anschlagen eines Hundes.

Eine Treibjagd.

Anna wollte stehen bleiben. Sie hatte weder ein Gewehr noch wusste sie, auf welcher Seite der Jagd sie sich befand. Doch ihre Füße liefen weiter. Der Saum ihres Kleides strich über ihre Knie. Sie besaß kein solches Kleid, weich und leicht, mit einem Verschluss im Nacken, den sie nicht erreichen konnte.

„Hierher“, sagte eine Stimme.

Zwischen zwei Stämmen wartete ein Mann. Sein Gesicht lag im Schatten. Anna kannte ihn nicht, war sich aber auf jene selbstverständliche Weise, die nur Träume erlauben, sicher, dass er ihren Namen wusste.

Sie trat zu ihm. Er nahm ein Blatt aus ihrem Haar. Seine Finger berührten dabei ihre Schläfe, und Anna schloss die Augen.

Hinter ihnen wurden die Rufe lauter.

„Die kommen“, flüsterte sie.

„Dann sollten wir leise sein.“

Sie hätte sich fürchten müssen. Stattdessen spürte sie die Wärme seiner Hand an ihrer Wange und lehnte sich hinein. Zum ersten Mal seit langer Zeit musste sie sich nicht überlegen, was sie sagen sollte.

Ein scharfes Knacken zerriss den Augenblick.

Anna fuhr hoch.

Die Computermaus fiel vom Tisch und schlug gegen das Bein ihres Bürostuhls. Auf dem Bildschirm stand eine endlose Reihe von Punkten. Ihre Hand hatte auf der Tastatur gelegen.

Für einige Sekunden wusste sie nicht, wo der Wald geblieben war.

Dann hörte sie das Lachen.

„Na endlich“, sagte Markus vom Schreibtisch gegenüber. „Wir wollten schon den Rettungsdienst rufen.“

Anna richtete sich auf. Ihr Nacken schmerzte, und an ihrer Wange klebte der Abdruck einer Strickfalte. Hastig strich sie sich das zerzauste Haar glatt. Dabei verfing sich ihr Finger in einer gelösten Haarnadel.

„Wie spät ist es?“

„Spät genug für ein ziemlich aufregendes Nickerchen“, sagte Tanja.

Sie stand neben dem Drucker, einen Stapel Ausdrucke gegen die Brust gedrückt. Sven lehnte am Türrahmen der kleinen Küche. Beide sahen Anna an.

Anna zog die Haarnadel heraus und legte sie neben die Tastatur.

„Ich bin wohl kurz eingeschlafen.“

„Ach was“, sagte Markus. „Und wir dachten, du testest eine neue Entspannungstechnik.“

Sven lachte in seine Kaffeetasse.

Anna blickte auf die Uhr unten rechts auf ihrem Bildschirm. Sechzehn Uhr acht. Sie erinnerte sich an die Mittagspause, die sie ausgelassen hatte, an den bitteren Kaffee kurz nach drei und daran, dass sie die Augen nur einen Moment hatte schließen wollen.

„Entschuldigung“, sagte sie.

„Bei uns musst du dich nicht entschuldigen.“ Tanja schob die Ausdrucke unter einen Arm. „Höchstens bei dem armen Mann, den du gerade so abrupt verlassen hast.“

Anna fühlte, wie ihr Gesicht heiß wurde.

Sie war vierunddreißig, schmal und etwas rund in den Schultern vom vielen Sitzen. Ihre Brille rutschte ihr häufig auf die Nasenspitze. Das dunkelblonde Haar trug sie meist mit einer Spange zusammengefasst; heute standen einzelne Strähnen an den Schläfen ab. Über ihrer weißen Bluse trug sie eine graue Strickjacke, deren linker Ärmel am Bündchen dünn geworden war.

Im Büro nannte man sie die kleine Maus. Anfangs hatte sie geglaubt, der Name sei freundlich gemeint.

„Lass sie doch“, sagte Sven. „Stille Wasser und so.“

„Bei Anna?“, fragte Markus. „Da unterschätzt du, was am Wochenende los ist.“

Er sagte es mit übertriebener Bewunderung. Anna kannte den Ton. Darin lag die Einladung an die anderen, sich etwas vorzustellen, das sie alle für ausgeschlossen hielten.

Sie zog ihren Stuhl näher an den Tisch.

„Ich muss den Abgleich noch fertig machen.“

„Natürlich musst du das“, sagte Tanja.

Damit hätte das Gespräch enden können. Anna öffnete die Tabelle und suchte die Zeile, an der sie gearbeitet hatte. Doch Markus beugte sich über die niedrige Trennwand.

„Jetzt mal ehrlich: Gibt’s jemanden?“

„Nein.“

Die Antwort kam zu schnell.

„Niemanden?“

Anna markierte eine Zelle. Dann eine andere.

„Ich möchte darüber nicht reden.“

Für einen Augenblick wurde es still. Sie hörte das Summen des Druckers und aus der Küche das Klirren eines Löffels.

„War doch nur eine Frage“, sagte Markus schließlich.

Er setzte seine Kopfhörer auf.

Um halb fünf begann das Wochenende der anderen.

Tanja telefonierte mit jemandem über eine Tischreservierung. Sven suchte seine Autoschlüssel und schimpfte über den Verkehr, der ihn erwartete. Markus schloss demonstrativ alle Fenster auf seinem Bildschirm, eines nach dem anderen.

Anna hatte noch siebenundzwanzig Datensätze zu prüfen.

Der erste Ordner landete um sechzehn Uhr vierzig auf ihrem Schreibtisch.

„Die Belege müssten noch ins System“, sagte Tanja. „Ich hab’s heute einfach nicht geschafft.“

Anna sah auf den gelben Klebezettel am Deckel. *Dringend* stand darauf.

„Die sind von Dienstag.“

„Ja, deshalb wäre es gut, wenn das heute noch klappt.“

„Ich habe meinen Abgleich noch nicht fertig.“

Tanja blickte kurz auf Annas Bildschirm.

„Du kennst dich damit wenigstens aus. Wenn ich jetzt damit anfange, wird’s nur falsch.“

Sie lächelte, als hätte sie Anna ein Kompliment gemacht, und ging ihre Jacke holen.

Kurz darauf kam Sven mit zwei Mappen.

„Für Montag früh. Nur auf Vollständigkeit prüfen.“

Anna legte ihre Hände flach auf den Tisch.

„Das schaffe ich nicht alles bis fünf.“

„Musst du doch auch nicht bis fünf schaffen.“

Er sagte es beiläufig. Gerade das machte es schwer, darauf zu antworten.

„Ich hatte eigentlich vor, heute pünktlich zu gehen.“

„Ach so.“ Sven hielt die Mappen noch immer in der Hand. „Hast du was vor?“

Sie dachte an ihre Wohnung, an die Wäsche auf dem Ständer und das Buch auf dem Nachttisch. An einen Abend, den sie sich nicht erst verdienen müssen wollte.

„Ja“, sagte sie.

Sven wartete.

Anna senkte den Blick. Er legte die Mappen neben den Ordner.

„Wenn du wenigstens das Wichtigste machst, wäre das super.“

Um fünf stand Markus bereits mit umgehängter Tasche im Gang.

„Meine Änderungen hab ich dir geschickt“, rief er. „Der Chef will Montag früh die aktuelle Fassung.“

Anna öffnete die E-Mail. Vier Anhänge.

„Markus, das ist doch dein Bericht.“

„Sind nur ein paar Korrekturen.“

„Dann kannst du sie selbst—“

„Mein Zug geht in zwanzig Minuten.“ Er sah nicht mehr sie an, sondern sein Telefon. „Danke dir. Du rettest mich.“

Tanja wartete an der Tür. Sie hatte Lippenstift nachgezogen.

„Schönes Wochenende, Anna. Und übertreib’s nicht.“

Markus grinste.

„Viel Spaß bei deiner Sexorgie.“

Die beiden lachten. Sven hob zum Abschied die Hand, ohne sich umzudrehen.

Anna sagte nichts.

Die Tür fiel ins Schloss.

Noch eine Weile hörte sie Stimmen im Treppenhaus. Dann sprang der Aufzug an, und das Büro wurde still.

Anna blieb sitzen, die Finger über der Tastatur. Auf dem leeren Schreibtisch gegenüber lag ein einzelner Büroklammernring. Markus hatte ihn während eines Telefonats zurechtgebogen. Sie betrachtete ihn länger, als es nötig gewesen wäre.

Um halb sieben schaltete die Heizung herunter. Um acht kam die Reinigungskraft.

„Immer noch hier?“, fragte sie und hielt den Staubsauger an der Tür zurück.

Anna nickte.

„Freitagabend.“

„Ja.“

Die Frau musterte die Mappen, sagte aber nichts weiter. Sie leerte den Papierkorb und ließ die Tür beim Hinausgehen offen.

Anna aß zwei Kekse aus der Schublade. Der Kaffee war längst kalt. Draußen spiegelten sich die Schreibtischlampen in den Fenstern, sodass sie statt der Straße ihr eigenes Gesicht sah: blass, müde, die Haare wieder halb aus der Spange gerutscht.

Kurz nach zehn war Tanjas Ordner erledigt. Svens Mappen lagen geprüft neben der Tastatur. Anna öffnete Markus’ Bericht.

Auf der ersten Seite stand sein Name.

Sie las ihn, dann sah sie auf die Uhr.

Zum ersten Mal an diesem Abend nahm sie die Hände von der Tastatur, ohne nach dem nächsten Blatt zu greifen.

Sie öffnete eine neue E-Mail.

*Hallo Markus,* schrieb sie. *Deine Änderungen konnte ich heute nicht mehr übernehmen. Bitte arbeite sie vor der Besprechung selbst ein.*

Sie las den Text zweimal. Ihr Herz schlug schneller, als die wenigen Sätze rechtfertigten. Dann klickte sie auf Senden.

Anna schaltete den Computer aus und zog ihre Strickjacke unter dem Mantel glatt. Den Bericht ließ sie liegen.

Als sie im Aufzug stand, musste sie noch einmal an den Wald denken. An das Reh zwischen den Bäumen und die vielen Stimmen, die es vor sich hergetrieben hatten.

Unten öffneten sich die Türen.

Sie trat hinaus in die kalte Nacht.

# 《借天灯》
**类型：东方玄幻 / 悬疑 / 热血**  
**形式：原创影视剧本·完整故事版**

> 世人修仙，要向天借命。  
> 唯独一个修灯少年，想让天把欠人的命还回来。

---

## 主要人物

**陆照，十九岁**  
乌灯镇修灯匠。天生无灵脉，无法修行，擅长拆解法器。嘴贫，怕疼，遇事习惯先找退路，却总会折回来。父亲七年前失踪。

**沈霜，二十四岁**  
巡天司执剑使，金丹境。奉命追查禁器“归名灯”。相信律法，却逐渐发现自己守护的律法建立在谎言之上。

**闻太白，外貌六十余岁**  
双目失明的说书人。曾参与建造九州天灯，如今隐居乌灯镇，靠讲述无人相信的旧事谋生。

**谢无咎，外貌四十岁**  
巡天司司主，九州第一修士。以天灯镇压大渊，维护人间七百年。他不认为自己是恶人，只认为总得有人做决定。

---

## 世界设定

九州之外，是吞噬生灵与记忆的“大渊”。

七百年前，修士铸起九州天灯，照退大渊。从此，凡人以寿元缴纳灯税，修士以功勋换取天灯灵气。

灯灭之人，寿终。

而某些名字，会在灯灭后被从世间一并抹去。

# 第一幕：灯里有人

## 第一场　乌灯镇·陆家灯铺　夜　内

暴雨。

狭窄的灯铺里，数百盏旧灯悬在梁下。屋顶漏水，陆照一边接水，一边替一只铜灯更换灯芯。

门外响起敲门声。

三下。

停顿。

又三下。

陆照抬头。

**陆照**  
修灯十文，驱邪不会。死人用的明早再来。

一个浑身湿透的老卒站在门外，怀里抱着一盏黑灯。

**老卒**  
陆长庚，是你什么人？

**陆照**  
我爹。欠钱找他，失踪七年了。

**老卒**  
他没逃。

一道雷劈亮长街。

陆照看清，老卒胸膛上有一个贯穿身体的洞。

**陆照**  
你别动。我去叫郎中。

**老卒**  
没用了……把灯点起来。

**陆照**  
没油怎么点？

老卒抓住他的手腕。

**老卒**  
想一件，你不舍得忘的事。

陆照挣了一下。

黑灯骤然亮起。

灯焰里，一个男人蹲在年幼的陆照面前，握着他的手削竹骨。

**男人的声音**  
灯架不能扎死。给风留一条路，灯才不会被吹倒。

陆照猛地捂住额头。

**陆照**  
这灯……吃记性？

老卒笑了，身体开始化灰。

**老卒**  
它不吃。

**陆照**  
那它是什么？

**老卒**  
是拿你的……换别人的回来。

老卒彻底消散。

黑灯内，浮现出一行小字：

**“归名第一人：陆长庚。”**

门外，铁靴踏过积水。

一道女声响起。

**沈霜（画外）**  
巡天司查禁器。开门。

沈霜推门而入，身后三名黑甲巡卫。

她腰间长剑并未出鞘，悬在梁上的灯却一齐朝她倾斜。

陆照站在柜台后，黑灯藏在脚边。

**沈霜**  
方才，有什么人来过？

躲雨的。

**沈霜**  
人呢？

走了。

**沈霜**  
从哪里走的？

短暂寂静。

沈霜忽然拔剑。

陆照本能地后退，剑锋却越过他，刺穿墙上的一只飞蛾。

飞蛾落地，化成一张写满眼睛的黄符。

三名巡卫同时抽刀。

**巡卫**  
沈执使，你毁了司主的观命符。

沈霜持剑起身。

**沈霜**  
按律，搜查民宅不得动用观命术。

司主手令。此地一切知情者，灭口。

她看着三柄刀，迟迟没有让开。

巡卫率先出手。

剑光骤亮。

数十盏旧灯轰然碎裂。

陆照抱起黑灯，从柜台后的地板暗门跳下去。

## 第三场　乌灯镇地下水道　夜　内

污水齐膝。

陆照举着黑灯，走得飞快。

沈霜追上他，一把扣住他的肩。

**沈霜**  
灯给我。

**陆照**  
给你，然后你把我交回去？

**沈霜**  
我会查清楚。

陆照猛地转身。

**陆照**  
他们刚烧了我家！你要查，就站在这儿查。我得先活着。

少女抬头。

**少女**  
阿姐，你别告诉师父。

沈霜浑身僵住。

陆照也看见了。

**陆照**  
谁啊？

**“沈雪。”**

水道远处，传来追兵拨水的声音。

前面有出口。往西，去城隍庙。

**陆照**  
你呢？

这次不查了。

先活着。

# 第二幕：天上无神

## 第四场　破城隍庙　黎明　内

闻太白坐在供桌上，端着一碗冷粥。

陆照抱灯闯进来。

老人鼻翼动了动。

**闻太白**  
灯拿远点。闻见这味儿，我就想起年轻时干的缺德事。

陆照将灯重重放上供桌。

**陆照**  
我爹呢？

闻太白放下碗。

**闻太白**  
死了。

陆照张了张口，没有出声。

庙外，沈霜捂着伤臂走进来。

闻太白侧耳听见她的脚步。

**闻太白**  
你妹妹也是。

沈霜的剑抵住老人咽喉。

**沈霜**  
说清楚。

闻太白伸手，指向庙外。

晨雾中，每户人家门前，都亮着一盏小小的命灯。

**闻太白**  
大渊越来越深，天灯的油早就不够了。三十年前开始，巡天司除了收灯税，还会挑一些人，整个人填进天灯。

**陆照**  
挑什么人？

**闻太白**  
无亲无故的。犯了死罪的。后来不够，就挑失踪后……不容易惹麻烦的。

沈霜的剑轻轻发颤。

**闻太白**  
天灯吞掉他们的命，也吞掉别人对他们的记忆。少一个人，不会有人来问。

**陆照**  
我一直记得我爹。

**闻太白**  
他修了半辈子灯，给自己留了后手。

老人摸索着打开黑灯底座。

里面，刻着一行歪斜的小字：

**“吾儿陆照，怕黑。请留一盏。”**

陆照伸手去摸。

指腹一遍遍擦过那个“照”字。

闻太白等了很久，才继续说。

**闻太白**  
归名灯能找回被抹去的人，但要用点灯人的记忆来换。你爹做成它，没来得及带走。

**沈霜**  
我要见谢无咎。

**闻太白**  
他就在等你们去。

## 第五场　巡天司·观星殿　日　内

大殿无顶，头上星辰缓慢运行。

谢无咎立在一幅九州地图前。

地图上，无数光点正在熄灭。

一名司官跪地。

**司官**  
乌灯镇已封。是否调遣天兵，捉拿沈霜与陆照？

不必。

他伸手，将一枚将熄的光点护住。

袖口滑落，露出皮肤下密密麻麻的裂纹。金光从裂纹里流出，灌进地图。

光点重新亮起。

**谢无咎**  
他们会来问我为什么。

**司官**  
归名灯一旦照入天枢，历年祭灯名册便会显现。届时民间动荡……

那里，一片漆黑正在缓慢侵入。

**谢无咎**  
名册显现，还不是最坏的事。

---

## 第六场　废弃天灯井　夜　内

巨大的地下灯井里，成千上万条铜管通向九州各处。

闻太白敲了敲其中一根。

空洞的回声层层传开。

**闻太白**  
天枢在皇城。你们要进那里，就从这里走。

陆照却蹲下来，拆开一处锈死的铜匣。

匣内有十二道榫口，十一道被铁水封死，只剩一道朝皇城方向开启。

**陆照**  
为什么封上？

闻太白沉默片刻。

**闻太白**  
这是最早的灯阵。原本，各地命灯可以彼此接续，哪处遇险，别处便能送光过去。

**沈霜**  
后来呢？

**闻太白**  
有人不肯供灯，有宗门抢走邻城的灵气。谢无咎便把灯阵改了。所有灯油先送皇城，由他分配。

陆照把匣子翻过来。

背面刻着两个字：

**太白。**

闻太白低下头。

**闻太白**  
我替他封的。

陆照捡起凿子，试着撬开一道榫口。

**沈霜**  
你想恢复旧阵？

**陆照**  
先看看能不能用。

**闻太白**  
可以用。但要让九州所有人同时开灯，还要他们自愿付出灯油。寿命，或者记忆。

**沈霜**  
若他们不肯？

凿子脱手，划破陆照掌心。

他疼得吸了口气，换只手继续凿。

**陆照**  
那也得让他们知道，自己在选什么。

---

## 第七场　灯井深处　后半夜　内

沈霜坐在阶上，替陆照包扎伤口。

归名灯放在两人中间。

**沈霜**  
能再点一次吗？

陆照看向她。

**沈霜**  
我想知道，她怎么死的。

陆照点头，闭上眼睛。

灯火亮起。

画面里，少女沈雪跪在天枢前，手脚被锁链捆住。

她没有哭，只不断看向门口。

**沈雪**  
我姐姐在巡天司。你们去问问她，是不是抓错了？

沈霜猛地站起。

灯焰散去。

她伸手去抓，指尖穿过空荡荡的光。

陆照盯着自己的双手。

**陆照**  
怪了。

沈霜回头。

**陆照**  
我明明记得，我娘会做一种甜汤。

**陆照**  
现在连是什么味儿，都不知道了。

沈霜缓缓蹲下，将灯从他身边拿开。

**沈霜**  
够了。

还没照到我爹。

# 第三幕：让人间自己点灯

## 第八场　皇城·天枢大殿　日　内

殿门洞开。

谢无咎独自坐在灯下。

所谓九州天灯，是一颗悬空的巨大金色心脏。每跳动一次，便有无数人的耳语从中传出。

沈霜持剑进入。

谢无咎没有起身。

**谢无咎**  
闻太白没来？

他留在灯井，拆你们封死的东西。

你知不知道，旧阵崩过一次？一座城的人守着灯油，不肯救三十里外的另一座城。我到的时候，那里连一具尸体都没剩下。

**陆照**  
所以你替所有人选了七百年。

**谢无咎**  
是。

**沈霜**  
包括我妹妹？

谢无咎看着她。

**谢无咎**  
那年北境失守，要补十三万盏命灯。她的灵脉合适。

你的修为，来自天灯。

沈霜额上青筋暴起。

你父亲点过这盏灯。他到最后，已经不记得自己要救谁。

## 第九场　天枢大殿　连续

沈霜忽然握住自己的金丹。

谢无咎转头。

放手。

沈霜咬紧牙关，五指收拢。

点了它，九州的死人都会找回来！你撑不住！

我爹做的灯。

## 第十场　九州各地／天灯井／天枢大殿　交叉

无数命灯骤然变成白色。

老妇人在灶前愣住，忽然喊出儿子的乳名。

爹，那是谁？

男人跪倒在地，泣不成声。

母亲的脸。

第一次赚到的铜钱。

雨中的灯铺。

那些画面一一烧尽。

阿照？

你……认识我？

不认识。

## 第十一场　九州各地　日转暗　外

地下灯井。

我是巡天司沈霜。天枢将灭，大渊正在入境。

旧灯阵已经开启。愿意供灯的人，请握住自己的命灯，想一件舍得交出去的往事。那段记忆，会永远消失。

一息。

两息。

无人点灯。

丫头，过来。让爹抱一下。

第三盏。

九州大地上，一片片微弱灯光彼此连接。

谢无咎悬在半空，俯视那些细小的光。

沈霜站在殿前。

**沈霜**  
还差北境。

谢无咎望向北方。

他缓缓抬手，将掌心按在自己的命火上。

一段记忆浮现。

年少的他跪在师父面前，郑重接过第一盏灯。

**少年谢无咎**  
弟子一定守好它。

记忆燃尽。

北境长夜中，最后一片灯海亮起。

谢无咎坠下云端。

**谢无咎**  
我方才……忘了什么？

有些事，你还得记着。等人来问。

## 第十二场　乌灯镇·新灯铺　三月后　黄昏　内外

旧址上，重新支起一家小灯铺。

门口挂着木牌：

修灯？

送灯。

又是我爹留的？

你昨天讲到，他背着我过河。

嗯。

**陆照**  
后来呢？

封面上写着：

别扎太紧。

他将那处榫口松开少许。

黄昏降临，长街上的灯陆续亮起。

Title: The Crown That Ate the Dawn
Style: Symphonic deathcore, orchestral choir, blast beats, guttural verses, soaring clean choruses, crushing breakdown.

[Intro — Whispered, Strings Swelling]
Mother stitched a silver star
Inside the cloak I wore.
“Learn to bring the daylight home.”
I learned to ask for more.

[Verse 1 — Low Growls, Building Orchestra]
At thirteen, through the college gates,
With winter bleeding through my shoes,
I learned the names that summoned flame,
And what a careless word could loose.
Old Master Vey guided my hands;
I shook too hard to hold the light.
He taught me how to mend a wing.
I watched that sparrow take its flight.

Beside me, Mira traced the wards;
We shared one candle, bread, and ink.
She bound our lives with silver thread:
“If one should fall, we both shall sink.”

[Pre-Chorus — Rising Clean Vocals]
But underneath the marble floors,
I heard a lesson through the stone:
“No man who kneels before a grave
Has claimed the power he could own.”

[Chorus — Soaring Vocals, Choir]
Higher—raise the spires!
Let my heartbeat feed the fire!
I will tear the teeth from time;
No beloved soul of mine
Shall ever pass beyond my reach.
What is one forbidden page
Against the silence of a grave?

[Verse 2 — Rapid Growls, Blast Beats]
At seventeen, the fever came;
My mother’s letters thinned, then ceased.
I reached her bed with healing spells
And found her eyes already sealed.
That night I broke the lower locks
And read from books chained shut with bone.
Each theorem took a memory;
I paid until her voice was gone.

I called a storm into my palm,
Made iron kneel and rivers climb.
They carved my name above the gates.
Black veins crawled upward through my spine.

[Verse 3 — Dissonant Choir, Half-Time]
Vey found the altar in my room,
The stolen names, the breathing wall.
“You cannot ransom death with death.”
I struck before he finished speaking.

His staff lay burning at my feet.
I took his key; I stepped across.
Behind the final library door,
I found the crown that promised gods.

[Chorus — Clean Vocals Fracturing]
Higher—raise the spires!
Let their heartbeat feed the fire!
I can tear the teeth from time!
Every life is briefly mine!
Let them curse what they cannot see:
When I have conquered death itself,
They will return to pardon me!

[Bridge — Piano, Female Clean Vocal]
Mira stood beneath the vault,
Our silver binding on her wrist.
“Come home. There’s still a boy I know
Who taught a wounded bird to live.”

I raised the blade.
She did not run.
I called her love
My final chain.

[Breakdown — Guttural, Choir Hits]
ONE CUT.
TWO HEARTS.

I drove the dagger through her ward—
The wound tore open in my chest.

ONE OATH.
KEPT TRUE.

The crown drank deep.
There was no god.
Only a boy
Who could not stop.

[Outro — Fading Clean Vocals, Lone Cello]
I crawled to where her hand lay still;
The crown fell ringing down the stair.
I tried the spell that mended wings.
No light would gather in the air.

My mother’s star beneath my cheek,
I died before the break of dawn.
Outside, the bells called students in.
They opened books.
The world went on.

### 终于，镜子里的眼睛不再让我叹气

今天早上洗完脸，我站在镜子前看了好一会儿。没有急着找遮瑕，也没有习惯性地抬高眉毛，只是安安静静地看着自己的眼睛。双眼皮线条流畅了，宽度看着舒服，两边也比以前协调。那一刻，我突然觉得，这些日子紧绷着的心，终于可以慢慢放下来了。

只有我自己知道，走到今天有多不容易。

以前，我的双眼皮已经做过三次。最开始只是想让眼睛显得精神一点，没想到后来，眼睛反而成了我最不愿意仔细看的地方。闭眼时线条不平顺，睁眼后又挤出好几道褶皱，成了让我发愁的“多眼皮”。再加上年纪渐渐大了，眼皮下垂越来越明显，原本就偏宽的线条看着更加夸张，两边还不对称。

最难受的，并不只是照片不好看，而是这些变化一点点影响了我的生活。出门前，我会反复调整眼妆，想着能不能把左右的差别遮住。朋友拿出手机合影，我总下意识找角度，拍完也不敢马上看。有时明明睡得不错，镜子里的自己却还是一脸疲惫，像总有什么心事。

我也想过，算了吧，已经折腾三次了，就这样接受自己。

可每次卸完妆，看见眼皮上那些杂乱的褶皱，我又觉得不甘心。我并不是非要追求多么惊艳的眼睛，只希望线条自然一点，宽度适合自己，不要每次照镜子，都被那种明显的不协调吸引全部注意力。

后来，我开始重新了解双眼皮修复，也把韩国格瑞丝噢爱美崔文燮医生列入了咨询的选择。和前几次相比，这一次我谨慎了很多，没有因为几张漂亮的照片就立刻做决定，而是认真整理自己的手术经历，以及现在最在意的问题。

咨询前一晚，我甚至在手机里写了一张清单：多余的褶皱、明显的下垂、过宽的线条，还有左右不对称。我提醒自己，一定要把真实想法说清楚，也要听明白哪些地方可能改善，哪些地方存在限制。毕竟经历过多次手术，我比以前更清楚，修复不是把过去一笔抹掉，也不能只凭期待来决定。

最终决定接受修复时，我仍然紧张。那种心情很复杂，一边期待改变，一边又害怕失望。手术前，我给自己拍了一张没有修饰的照片，没有像以前那样立刻删除。我想留住这个阶段，也提醒自己：这一次，要给身体足够的时间，不要急着评判结果。

恢复初期并没有想象中轻松。看着眼周的肿胀，我偶尔还是会焦虑，忍不住想凑近镜子观察左右的变化。后来我慢慢学着克制，不再一天拍好多张照片反复比较，而是按照术后指导护理、按时复查，把问题记下来再咨询，不凭当天的样子给自己下结论。

日子就在这些细小的等待里过去了。

等恢复了一段时间，我才逐渐发现，眼睛看起来和以前不一样了。原先显得凌乱的褶皱不再那么抢眼，双眼皮线条顺了许多，宽度也更适合我的脸。对我而言，最开心的是眼皮不再像从前那样明显地垂下来，睁眼时整个人显得舒展了，左右看着也自然协调。

这种变化并没有让我突然变成另一个人，反而让我找回了一点熟悉的自己。

昨天出门，我只简单整理了眉毛，涂了一点口红，没有再花很久研究怎样用眼影遮住那两条过宽的线。朋友拍照时，我也没有急着躲到最后面。看见照片后，我第一眼注意到的是自己的笑容，而不是眼皮哪里不对称。

现在回头想，我最想要的，从来不是一双照着某个模板做出来的眼睛，而是不用时时担心它的自在。

经历了三次手术后的困扰，再到这次修复和恢复，我对“变好看”这件事有了不同的理解。它不该只剩下焦急和比较，也需要理性、耐心，以及对自身条件的接纳。

今晚写下这些，是想记住今天早晨那个很普通的瞬间：洗完脸，抬起头，看见镜子里的自己，然后心平气和地笑了一下。

A cup of water, a folded cloth, three loose coins, a brass key, and a stack of reports occupy the space beside her hip. Getting her from the couch to the table has given him a useful measure of her condition. He sits in front of her, close enough that she won’t need to raise her voice. “Thorne has other duties this morning. You’ll deal with me.” He studies her face, then adds, “You managed that on your first day. We don’t need to start from scratch.”

If you don’t understand a question, say so. If you can’t remember something, tell me. I can work with that.” He rests his forearms on his knees. There are questions about the capital waiting in those reports, names he needs confirmed, gaps only she can fill. Asking them now would get him answers he couldn’t trust. First he needs her to understand who sets the pace here—and who can make it bearable. “We’ll leave yesterday alone for now. # THE COBRA PAPERS
### Selected excerpts from a fictional leaked archive, 1951–1970

*The following invented documents trace Cobra, a clandestine paramilitary organisation active in East Germany, Poland’s Western Borderlands, and Austria. Presented in translation, they include internal correspondence, financial memoranda, field reports, and extracts from its final administrative review. Gaps indicate material missing from the fictional archive.*

---

### 1. Letter from Nico Sanguinacci to “Herr Adler”
**Trieste, 19 February 1951 — Personal correspondence**

You misunderstand the nature of my proposal.

I do not require an army. An army demands uniforms, pensions, and somebody willing to explain its existence. I require a concern: a small concern, with competent management, capable of protecting interests where ordinary commercial arrangements no longer suffice.

Austria provides the office. The eastern territories provide the necessity. Germany provides, as you have repeatedly assured me, the men.

Your friends speak of recovering what was taken from them. My associates speak of preventing further losses. These are not identical ambitions, but for the present they can share an accountant.

The name you suggested is too historical.

Call it Cobra. A name should be remembered without requiring explanation.

— **N. Sanguinacci**

---

### 2. Founding Administrative Circular
**Vienna, 7 June 1951 — Restricted to Section Heads**

The organisation shall maintain three territorial desks:

**A — Austria:** administration, accommodation, commercial representation, and liaison.

**D — East Germany:** political reporting, personnel assessment, and maintenance of local contacts.

**P — Polish Western Territories:** property intelligence, association with displaced persons, and observation of state consolidation.

The terms *army*, *liberation movement*, and *government-in-exile* are prohibited in official correspondence.

Members are reminded that Cobra possesses no mandate to redraw frontiers. Individuals unable to distinguish their personal expectations from the organisation’s present duties should not be entrusted with correspondence.

Weapons holdings and armed personnel will remain subject to central authority. No regional commander may declare an emergency merely because a speech in Warsaw has offended him.

---

### 3. Treasurer’s Memorandum: Sources of Support
**Salzburg, 12 November 1953 — Eyes Only**

Receipts now fall into three categories:

1. Sanguinacci commercial accounts.
2. Italian institutional contributions, communicated through persons who decline institutional identification.
3. German expatriate subscriptions.

The third category causes the greatest administrative difficulty.

Certain subscribers regard a contribution as the purchase of future political influence. Others expect preferential consideration in the restitution of estates presently situated inside Poland. Several have submitted maps.

We are not equipped to audit maps.

The Italian parties are more practical. They request assessments, summaries, and evidence that their contributions produce something other than commemorative dinners.

Signor Sanguinacci has instructed that no donor be permitted to inspect the complete ledger. His precise words were: “They are investing in the same enterprise, not necessarily in the same outcome.”

---

### 4. East German Section: Review of the June Events
**Undated; filed January 1954**

Subsequent claims that Cobra directed significant portions of the disturbances are unsupported by our records.

Contact was lost with several persons during the unrest. Two were arrested. One is believed to have fled independently. A fourth has since requested payment for activities which, by his own account, he performed before receiving any instruction from us.

The section’s actual achievement was the collection of fragmentary testimony under difficult conditions.

Headquarters converted this into a claim of influence.

The distinction matters. Funds allocated on the assumption that we possess a network capable of shaping events will be spent maintaining the appearance of such a network.

**Handwritten annotation:**  
*Remove final paragraph from Italian copy.*

---

### 5. Personnel Committee: Review of German Recruits
**Innsbruck, 3 September 1956 — Confidential**

The designation “expatriate” has become administratively useless.

It presently encompasses former civil servants, displaced landowners, military veterans, genuine anti-Communists, opportunists, and persons whose chief qualification is an urgent desire that nobody examine the years 1933–1945.

Three candidates submitted this quarter gave contradictory accounts of their wartime duties. One described an organisation in which he held commissioned rank as a “transport association.”

The committee recommends rejection.

Herr Adler objects that excessive scrutiny will offend established supporters. This objection is noted, as it was noted in the previous six reviews.

**Decision:** Two rejected. One accepted provisionally following intervention from the Founder’s Office.

---

### 6. Polish Desk: Population and Property Assessment
**Wrocław dossier, 22 April 1958 — Internal analytical paper**

Our sponsors continue to describe the western districts as though they were houses temporarily occupied in the owners’ absence.

This description is politically convenient and factually inadequate.

Many Polish residents arrived after losing homes farther east. Their children know no other towns. Whatever their opinion of the present government, they do not generally regard German-sponsored clandestine activity as assistance.

Cobra’s local reputation suffers accordingly. Reports intended to demonstrate hostility toward the state are frequently evidence of hostility toward us.

The desk requests permission to discontinue the phrase “waiting population.” There is no indication that the population is waiting for anything we are authorised to offer.

---

### 7. Austrian Office: Incident Review
**Vienna, 16 October 1960 — Circulation limited**

The assault outside Graz was neither authorised nor connected to an approved intelligence requirement.

The victim, a former member disputing unpaid allowances, remains hospitalised. Local authorities are treating the matter as a criminal offence. The office has received conflicting explanations from all four members involved.

The commander concerned maintains that disciplinary credibility required a response.

The committee observes that “disciplinary credibility” has now been cited in connection with three assaults, two financial disputes, and the disappearance of a personnel file.

Austria’s neutrality does not constitute permission for Cobra to conduct private military affairs on Austrian soil.

**Founder’s Office reply:**  
*Settle the allowance claim. Remove the commander. No further discussion in writing.*

---

### 8. Italian Liaison Assessment
**Rome, 9 March 1963 — Copy retained without authorisation**

Cobra remains useful principally because it already exists.

Its reporting is uneven. Its German contributors exercise influence disproportionate to their financial importance. Its founder is adept at presenting the same expenditure as a commercial necessity, a patriotic undertaking, and a personal favour.

Nevertheless, certain relationships accumulated since 1951 would be costly to reproduce.

Support should therefore continue at a reduced level, contingent upon the separation of intelligence collection from émigré political projects.

No commitment has been made regarding territorial revision. No commitment should be inferred.

Sanguinacci must be informed of this verbally. Previous written qualifications have not prevented him from implying broader assurances to third parties.

---

### 9. Letter from Sanguinacci to the Executive Committee
**Milan, 28 August 1968 — Dictated**

The events in Czechoslovakia will bring applications, offers, and renewed enthusiasm. You will be tempted to mistake all three for capacity.

Do not.

We have men on the rolls who have not crossed a frontier in ten years. We have committees devoted to towns their members last saw as children. We have Italian friends who now ask whether the information we sell them can be read in a newspaper.

And we have younger officers who believe an act of violence will restore the seriousness their elders have squandered.

No independent armed undertaking is authorised.

I will not finance a spectacular incident merely to persuade our subscribers that their previous payments were justified.

---

### 10. Final Administrative Review
**Salzburg, 17 December 1970 — Closure file**

Cobra is to cease functioning as a unified organisation on 31 December.

The East German section is largely nominal. The Polish section retains correspondents but little capacity for independent verification. Austrian facilities are to be sold, surrendered, or transferred to commercial ownership.

Italian support has ended in its previous form. German subscriptions no longer cover standing expenses.

The committee could not agree upon a statement of accomplishments.

The following summary was adopted for internal use:

> Cobra maintained a presence across three operational territories for nineteen years. It supplied reporting of variable quality, supported a limited number of persons in genuine danger, and sustained a considerably larger number whose circumstances were represented as dangerous for financial purposes.
>
> Its paramilitary structure repeatedly exceeded its political authority.
>
> Its financial survival depended upon allowing different sponsors to believe that the organisation served incompatible objectives.

Personnel records are incomplete. Claims by dependants remain unresolved.

**Final handwritten entry, unsigned:**

*The accounts are closed. This should not be entered anywhere as meaning that everyone has been paid.*

## The Oven That Bakes Snow

*A light encounter for four 1st-level characters, lasting about 20–30 minutes. Combat is optional.*

### The situation
A village baker owns an enchanted oven that makes **snowbread**: warm, crusty rolls with centers of sweet, edible snow. Its magic depends on two tiny spirits—one of fire and one of frost—sharing the hearth.

Unfortunately, they’ve had an argument.

> Inside the bakery, blue flames dance across a frozen counter. A blazing creature shaped like a cinnamon roll hurls sparks at an icy creature with icicle whiskers.  
> “TOO COLD!” squeaks one.  
> “TOO HOT!” squeaks the other.  
> The baker ducks behind a flour barrel. “Please save my shop. Preferably with the oven still attached!”

The spirits are upset, not evil. They fling warning shots when anyone approaches the oven; roll initiative so everyone gets a turn to help.

### The bakery
The room is 25 feet square. The entrance is opposite the oven, with counters along either side. Three things are immediately obvious:

- **A bucket of water** sits beside the door.
- **A long-handled warming pan** full of warm coals hangs beside the oven.
- **A frozen puddle** covers the middle 10-foot square. It is difficult terrain. A creature can instead slide straight across using only 10 feet of movement, but must succeed on a **DC 10 Dexterity saving throw** or fall prone at the far edge. Tell players this risk before they slide.

The blue flames are harmless magical light—a discovery the baker can shout out before anyone wastes a turn avoiding them.

### Cinder and Rime
Use these simple statistics for each spirit:

**Tiny elemental; AC 12; HP 9; Speed 25 ft.**  
**Ability modifiers:** Str −2, Dex +2, Con +0, Int −1, Wis +0, Cha +1.  
**Spark or Ice Chip:** Ranged attack, +3 to hit, range 20 feet, one target. Hit: **1d4 + 1 fire damage** from Cinder or **cold damage** from Rime.

They have no resistances or immunities. Each makes only one attack per turn, targets the nearest conscious creature interfering with it, and never attacks an unconscious character. On a tie, choose someone it hasn’t attacked yet.

At 0 HP, a spirit becomes a harmless glowing pebble rather than dying.

### The twist: They need opposite comforts
Cinder is **overheating**, while Rime is **so cold its joints have frozen**. They don’t need more of their own element—they need a little of each other’s!

Explain the clues freely:
- Cinder pants, “Water! Just a splash!”
- Rime shivers, “Can’t… bend… whiskers…”

A character within 5 feet can use an action to:
- Splash Cinder with water.
- Hold the warming pan near Rime.

Either automatically calms the corresponding spirit, which stops attacking. Picking up either item requires no additional action beyond the character’s normal free object interaction.

Other sensible cooling or warming methods also work. An action spent offering reassurance can calm one spirit with a **DC 10 Charisma (Persuasion) check**.

### Resolution
Once both spirits are calm—or reduced to pebbles—the party can return them to the oven without a check. Fire curls around frost, and snowbread begins rising again.

The grateful baker gives the party **10 gp total**, breakfast, and a warm place to sleep.

**Beginner-friendly tip:** On the first turn, remind players they can fight, talk, move objects, or try an idea of their own. This is deliberately an easy encounter, with no damaging environmental hazards.

The rain had stopped just long enough for Blackwell Academy to pretend it had never happened.

Sunlight slid between the clouds, catching on wet leaves and turning the puddles along the courtyard path into pieces of sky. Max lingered beside the steps with her camera raised, trying to frame the reflection of the clock tower without including the trash can beside it.

“Please tell me you’re photographing something scandalous,” Chloe said behind her. “Secret faculty meeting? Squirrel crime?”

“Architectural reflection.”

“Wow. Should I call the police or just alert the media?”

Max lowered her camera. “You volunteered to come.”

“I volunteered to rescue you from school. Different mission.”

Chloe leaned against the railing, blue hair bright against the gray stone. She had been there for eleven minutes and had already complained about the parking, the weather, and a poster advertising a lecture on photographic authenticity.

Then her gaze shifted over Max’s shoulder.

“Oh, excellent. Royalty.”

Victoria Chase stood at the other end of the path beneath a copper-colored tree. She was alone, holding her phone in one hand and inspecting the ground with an expression usually reserved for particularly disappointing student work.

One shoe hovered above a muddy stretch of pavement.

Max followed Chloe’s gaze. “Be nice.”

“I’m a delight.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

Victoria looked up before Max could stop Chloe from approaching.

“If either of you is about to say something about my shoes,” Victoria said, “consider developing an original thought instead.”

Chloe glanced down. “Wasn’t going to. But now I’m fascinated.”

“They’re suede.”

“Tragic.”

“The grounds crew apparently considers drainage an optional feature.”

Max looked at the muddy patch. It wasn’t especially wide, but Victoria’s shoes were pale, immaculate, and clearly unsuited to an Oregon afternoon.

“There’s a dry way around by the benches,” she offered.

“That involves walking across the grass.”

“Right. Good point.”

Chloe folded her arms, studying Victoria with theatrical concern.

“Look at you. Stranded outside your castle. Where are your attendants?”

Victoria tucked her phone into her bag. “Where’s your sense of personal boundaries?”

“Probably wherever you left your practical footwear.”

“Chloe,” Max murmured.

But Victoria’s mouth had twitched.

Chloe noticed. Naturally, Chloe noticed.

“Oh, I get it,” she said, drawing out the realization. “You’re a princess. A princess to be cherished and pampered. Can’t have you trudging through the mud like the rest of us.”

A faint pink appeared high on Victoria’s cheeks.

Max blinked.

Victoria lifted her chin. “If you’re going to mock me, at least commit to it.”

“Mock you? Your Highness, I’m offering excellent customer service.”

Chloe stepped closer, grinning, and tapped one fingertip against the tip of Victoria’s nose.

“Boop.”

For one extraordinary second, Victoria simply stared.

Then Chloe laughed, delighted with herself. The sound rang across the courtyard.

Max pressed her lips together. She had witnessed Victoria dismantle people for considerably less.

“You,” Victoria said carefully, “are unbelievably annoying.”

“Yeah, but I bring a certain charm.”

“Debatable.”

Chloe swept one arm toward the path with a flourish. “So what’s it gonna be, princess? Want to be swept off your feet and carried somewhere worthy of those shoes?”

Max opened her mouth, preparing to intervene before this became an incident.

Victoria moved first.

She reached up and pressed her finger to Chloe’s nose.

“Boop,” she said.

Chloe’s grin froze.

Victoria withdrew her hand, looking immensely satisfied.

“Yes.”

The courtyard seemed suddenly very quiet.

Somewhere near the dormitories, a skateboard rattled over a crack.

Chloe blinked. “Yes?”

“Yes, I would like to be carried.” Victoria adjusted the strap of her bag. “You offered. Unless that was merely an attempt to seem impressive.”

Max made a small, strangled sound.

Both of them looked at her.

“Sorry,” she said. “Pollen.”

“It rained,” Victoria pointed out.

“Wet pollen.”

Chloe turned back to Victoria. The surprise was giving way to a slow, dangerous smile.

“Oh, you’re absolutely going to regret calling my bluff.”

“I haven’t called anything. I’ve accepted an offer.”

“Right. Very contractual.”

Despite the bravado, Chloe hesitated before touching her.

“Seriously?”

Victoria’s expression softened by a fraction. “Seriously.”

“Okay. Arm around my shoulders.”

Victoria complied, a little stiffly at first. Chloe bent, slipped one arm behind her back and the other beneath her knees, then lifted.

Victoria let out a startled breath and grabbed Chloe’s shoulder.

“There it is,” Chloe said. “The royal squeak.”

“That was not a squeak.”

“Max, witness?”

“I value my continued existence.”

Chloe straightened carefully. Victoria was now unmistakably, impossibly cradled in her arms, her pristine shoes suspended safely above the pavement.

The blush had returned.

“You can relax,” Chloe told her. “I’ve got you.”

“I am relaxed.”

“Your hand is trying to become part of my jacket.”

Victoria loosened her grip, although she kept her arm firmly around Chloe’s shoulders.

Max realized she was smiling so hard her cheeks hurt.

She raised her camera halfway. “Can I?”

Victoria immediately looked suspicious. “Where would it go?”

“Nowhere without your permission.”

Chloe tilted her head toward Victoria. “Come on. Historical record. First documented instance of me providing community service.”

“That cannot possibly be true.”

“First voluntary instance.”

Victoria considered Max, then glanced at Chloe.

“One picture.”

Max lifted the viewfinder.

Through it, the scene settled into something she never would have thought to arrange: Chloe standing broad-footed on the wet path, trying not to look pleased with herself; Victoria held securely against her, caught between embarrassment and a smile she hadn’t quite decided to allow.

The shutter clicked.

“Done,” Max said.

“Good,” Victoria replied. “Now, if my transportation could actually move?”

“Wow. No tip, either, I bet.”

“Your performance is still under review.”

Chloe started down the path, testing her footing before stepping around a shallow puddle. Max walked beside them, holding the photograph by its white edge.

At the far side of the mud, Chloe slowed.

“Here?”

Victoria looked toward the benches, where sunlight had reached the dry wooden seats.

“Over there would be preferable.”

Chloe laughed. “You are enjoying this way too much.”

“You encouraged it.”

“Fair.”

She carried Victoria to the nearest bench and lowered her carefully until her shoes touched clean pavement. Victoria stood, smoothing her sweater with unnecessary concentration.

Chloe rolled one shoulder. “Your carriage awaits its five-star review.”

Victoria reached out and straightened the jacket collar she had crumpled.

“Acceptable service,” she said.

But her hand lingered for a moment, and when she looked up, she was smiling.

Max glanced down at the developing photograph.

Beside her, Chloe went unusually quiet.

Then Victoria tapped her nose again.

“Thank you.”

Chloe laughed, softer this time.

“Anytime, princess.”

### Десятое сентября: четыре претендента на вечность

*Воображаемый спор о реальных событиях. За столом — спортсмен, писатель, политик и учёный. Перед ними календарь, открытый на 10 сентября.*

**Спортсмен:** Предлагаю сразу договориться: великим следует считать событие, после которого человек иначе понимает пределы своих возможностей. Поэтому мой выбор — **10 сентября 1960 года**. Абебе Бикила выигрывает олимпийский марафон в Риме. Босиком. И становится первым чернокожим африканцем, завоевавшим олимпийское золото.

**Политик:** Олимпийская победа — замечательно. Но государства от неё не возникают.

**Спортсмен:** А достоинство возникает. Эфиопский бегун побеждает в столице страны, которая ещё за четверть века до этого вторглась на его родину. Не с оружием — на дистанции, где правила для всех одинаковы. Для миллионов людей это было больше, чем спортивный результат.

**Учёный:** Только не делай из отсутствия обуви доказательство превосходства силы воли над физиологией.

**Спортсмен:** Я делаю из победы доказательство того, что фаворитов назначают до старта, а победителей — после финиша.

---

**Писатель:** Красиво сказано. Почти достаточно, чтобы я уступил. Но я выбираю **10 сентября 1890 года — рождение Франца Верфеля**.

**Политик:** Рождение? Младенец ещё ничего не написал. Даже заявления.

**Писатель:** Именно поэтому ваша профессия не умеет оценивать младенцев. Верфель напишет «Сорок дней Муса-Дага» — роман о сопротивлении армян во время геноцида 1915 года. Он даст чужому страданию голоса, лица, судьбы. Там, где официальный язык способен оставить только цифру, литература возвращает человека.

**Учёный:** Но ты приписываешь дню рождения значение всей последующей жизни. Это довольно свободный способ выбирать главное событие.

**Писатель:** Согласен. Рождение писателя — ещё не рождение его книги. И всё же без первого не было бы второго. Моё величие — не в скорости и не в размерах государства. Оно в способности не дать людям исчезнуть из памяти.

**Спортсмен:** Но книга не остановила насилие.

**Писатель:** Нет. Не стану приписывать литературе всемогущество. Но между «не остановила» и «ничего не изменила» лежит огромная нравственная дистанция.

---

**Политик:** Тогда мой кандидат — **10 сентября 1919 года: подписание Сен-Жерменского мирного договора с Австрией**. Он закрепил послевоенное устройство значительной части Европы после распада Австро-Венгрии. Границы, суверенитет, обязательства государств — вот события, внутри последствий которых живут миллионы.

**Учёный:** Масштаб последствий ещё не означает величия.

**Политик:** А кто сказал, что «величайшее» обязательно означает «самое прекрасное»? Исторически главным может оказаться и спорное решение.

**Писатель:** Особенно если одним оно приносит национальное самоопределение, а другим — ощущение утраты и несправедливости.

**Политик:** Именно. Я не предлагаю праздновать каждую статью договора. Я предлагаю признать вес события. Спортивный рекорд можно превзойти. Книгу можно не прочесть. Но оказаться по другую сторону новой границы можно независимо от собственного желания.

**Спортсмен:** Выходит, твоё главное событие — то, от которого труднее уклониться?

**Политик:** Нередко история устроена именно так.

---

**Учёный:** Мой выбор — **10 сентября 2008 года**. В CERN первый пучок протонов совершил полный оборот по Большому адронному коллайдеру.

**Спортсмен:** Наконец-то ещё один достойный забег по кругу.

**Учёный:** Только длина круга — около двадцати семи километров. Но существенно другое: тысячи людей создали инструмент, позволяющий проверять наши представления о фундаментальном устройстве материи.

**Политик:** И в тот день открыли бозон Хиггса?

**Учёный:** Нет. Об открытии новой частицы, соответствующей бозону Хиггса, объявили в 2012 году. Не нужно переносить последующий результат на день запуска. Десятого сентября 2008-го произошло другое: важнейшая экспериментальная установка впервые провела пучок по полному кольцу.

**Писатель:** То есть твоё событие тоже велико обещанием будущего?

Hi,

**What if the first piece of evidence in a missing-person case was a confession sent from your account—and you never wrote it?**

That’s the kind of opening I’d love to build for your game: a mystery that doesn’t simply ask the player to investigate, but makes them personally involved from the very first notification.

I understand what makes **Duskwood** and **Replica** compelling. It isn’t just the chat interface; it’s the feeling that the people behind those messages are real, that something is happening even when you aren’t looking, and that trusting the wrong person could change everything.

My approach would be to capture that intimacy while giving your game its own story, identity, and signature mechanics.

### An original concept: **LAST SEEN: The Unsent Witness**

At 2:17 a.m., you receive a notification:

**“Your account recovery is complete.”**

You never requested it.

Seconds later, a stranger sends you a screenshot of a confession posted under your name. It describes the death of a local journalist, Mara Voss—someone the police haven’t even reported missing yet.

Then Mara’s account comes online.

> **Mara:** If someone asks, we’ve never spoken.  
> **You:** Who are you?  
> **Mara:** That depends on what they’ve already told you.

She sends access to a digital archive and disappears.

Inside are fragmented voice notes, photographs with conflicting timestamps, and conversations that appear ordinary until you compare them. Her last investigation concerned an emergency-response contractor accused of altering dispatch records after a fatal apartment fire.

Now someone is editing the archive remotely.

You enter a group chat with Mara’s brother, her editor, a former dispatcher, and the friend who claims to have seen her last. Each has something useful. Each has a reason to lie.

**The central question isn’t only “Where is Mara?” It’s “Which version of her disappearance is being manufactured—and why were you chosen to validate it?”**

### What would make this experience stand out?

- **Evidence that changes:** A photograph disappears, a message is edited, or a timestamp shifts. Players must preserve and compare evidence rather than simply collect it.
- **Trust with consequences:** Sharing a clue privately might earn someone’s confidence—but also give them time to destroy another lead.
- **Human, imperfect characters:** People interrupt, dodge questions, contradict themselves, and occasionally tell the truth for the wrong reasons.
- **Puzzles grounded in the case:** Reconstruct deleted conversations, compare call logs, identify locations from images, and connect details across simulated social profiles.
- **Meaningful endings:** Finding the truth, proving it, and protecting the people involved are three different outcomes.

All phone, account, and social-media interactions would happen within the game’s fictional interface—not through access to players’ private data.

### Relevant experience

My relevant project is **Panic Pavilion: Survive the Shadows**:  
https://youtu.be/d4jHkBkBkkU

It’s a horror-survival experience set in an abandoned medical facility, combining environmental exploration, puzzles, time pressure, and the gradual discovery of dark secrets.

While I haven’t developed this exact phone-based detective format before, the overlap is important: **building suspense, pacing discoveries, and making players feel vulnerable while keeping them motivated to uncover what comes next.** For your game, I’d translate that tension from dark corridors into unread messages, interrupted calls, and evidence that suddenly goes missing.

### How I’d start

I recommend building a **polished, playable first chapter** before expanding into the full story. It would establish the phone interface, core characters, branching conversations, evidence system, and one memorable reveal.

That gives us something concrete to evaluate early: does the mystery hook players, do the conversations feel believable, and do their choices feel consequential?

**Are you envisioning a primarily text-and-image experience, or would you like live-action clips and voice messages as well?** That decision will help shape both the production scope and the storytelling style.

My goal would be simple: **make players close the game—and keep thinking about who just messaged them.**

# Danganronpa AU: Ultimate Gym Teacher
### “Please Don’t Die During Dodgeball!”

**INT. HOPE’S PEAK ACADEMY — GYMNASIUM — MORNING**

*A whistle trembles between MIKAN TSUMIKI’S fingers. She wears a purple tracksuit, sneakers with meticulously tied laces, and a clipboard covered in color-coded workout plans.*

*Behind her sits a first-aid kit roughly the size of a suitcase.*

**MIKAN:** G-good morning, everyone! I’m your new physical education teacher, Mikan Tsumiki. I hope we can all have a safe, productive—

**IBUKI:** QUESTION! Is running from your problems considered cardio?

**MIKAN:** W-well, physiologically, if your heart rate increases—

**HAJIME:** Don’t encourage her.

**AKANE:** When do we start fighting?

**MIKAN:** We don’t!

*A beat.*

**MIKAN:** I-I’m sorry! That sounded very strict. But we still don’t.

*HIYOKO surveys the equipment.*

**HIYOKO:** Why are all the basketball hoops lowered?

**MIKAN:** So beginners can practice shooting without getting discouraged.

**HIYOKO:** Wow. Even the hoops feel sorry for us.

*Mikan shrinks behind her clipboard.*

**NEKOMARU:** AN EXCELLENT ADJUSTMENT! BUILD CONFIDENCE BEFORE INCREASING DIFFICULTY!

*Mikan peeks out.*

**MIKAN:** Y-you think so?

**NEKOMARU:** ABSOLUTELY!

**HAJIME:** Could you approve of things a little quieter? We’re indoors.

---

**INT. GYMNASIUM — TEN MINUTES LATER**

*The class begins warming up.*

**MIKAN:** Today we’ll practice throwing, catching, and teamwork through a modified game of dodgeball.

*Akane grins.*

**MIKAN:** Modified.

*Her grin fades slightly.*

**MIKAN:** Foam balls only. No headshots. If you’re hit, you move to the sideline passing station instead of sitting out. And please tell me immediately if anything hurts.

**HIYOKO:** Your voice hurts.

**MIKAN:** Oh! I can try speaking more soft—

*Mikan stops. She grips her clipboard.*

**MIKAN:** …Actually, you need to hear the safety instructions.

*Hajime looks up, pleasantly surprised.*

**MIKAN:** S-so I’ll keep speaking at this volume. I’m sorry.

**HAJIME:** You don’t have to apologize for that.

**MIKAN:** Right. Sorry.

*She closes her eyes.*

**MIKAN:** …I’ll work on it.

---

**INT. GYMNASIUM — MOMENTS LATER**

*Mikan demonstrates a gentle underhand throw.*

**MIKAN:** The goal is control, not power. Watch your partner, step forward, and—

*Her sneaker catches on a loose boundary marker.*

**MIKAN:** EEP!

*She stumbles, windmills both arms, and somehow sends the ball neatly into a distant equipment basket.*

*Silence.*

**IBUKI:** SECRET TECHNIQUE: APOLOGY METEOR!

**NEKOMARU:** INCREDIBLE FOLLOW-THROUGH!

**MIKAN:** Th-that was not the demonstration!

*She immediately kneels and smooths down the marker.*

**MIKAN:** This edge is curling. Everyone, stay back for a moment.

**HAJIME:** You nearly fell, and you’re worried about the tape?

**MIKAN:** If I tripped over it, someone else could too.

*Hajime takes the roll of floor tape from her supply cart.*

**HAJIME:** Here. I’ll hold the end.

**MIKAN:** …Thank you.

---

**INT. GYMNASIUM — DODGEBALL GAME**

*The whistle chirps.*

*Chaos erupts.*

*Ibuki provides her own battle music. Nekomaru calls out encouragement at a volume usually reserved for evacuations. Akane scoops up a ball.*

**AKANE:** All right! Who’s ready?!

*She draws her arm back.*

**MIKAN:** Akane.

*Something in Mikan’s voice cuts through the noise.*

*Akane freezes.*

**MIKAN:** You’re too close to throw that hard. Take two steps back and use less force.

**AKANE:** But I can hit—

**MIKAN:** I know you can. Can you place it where you want it?

*Akane considers this.*

**AKANE:** …Okay. That sounds harder.

**MIKAN:** It is.

*Akane steps back, takes aim, and throws a controlled shot toward Hajime’s legs.*

**HAJIME:** Why am I the test subject?!

*He dodges.*

**MIKAN:** Much better!

---

**INT. GYMNASIUM — LATER**

*Hiyoko sits on a bench, rubbing her ankle.*

*Mikan approaches but leaves a little space.*

**MIKAN:** Does it hurt when you move it?

**HIYOKO:** No. I’m sitting here because benches are fascinating.

**MIKAN:** …May I take a look?

**HIYOKO:** You’re a gym teacher, not a nurse.

**MIKAN:** I’m trained in first aid. If it needs more than that, we’ll go to the infirmary.

*Hiyoko reluctantly shifts her foot forward.*

**HIYOKO:** Don’t make everyone stare.

*Mikan turns toward the court.*

**MIKAN:** Everyone, please continue the passing drill! Ibuki, the ball needs to leave your hands.

**IBUKI:** But we’ve bonded!

*With the class occupied, Mikan crouches beside the bench.*

**MIKAN:** We’ll take this slowly.

**HIYOKO:** …Fine.

---

**INT. GYMNASIUM — END OF CLASS**

*The students gather their things.*

**MIKAN:** Before you go, please write down one thing you improved today.

**AKANE:** My aim.

**NEKOMARU:** MY ALREADY MAGNIFICENT TEAM SPIRIT!

**IBUKI:** Ibuki learned that the whistle is not a communal instrument!

**HAJIME:** I learned foam balls can still be intimidating.

*Hiyoko drops a folded slip onto the clipboard as she passes.*

*Mikan opens it.*

**INSERT — THE NOTE:**

*“Your class wasn’t totally awful.”*

*Below it, in smaller writing:*

*“The lower hoops were okay.”*

*Mikan smiles.*

**MIKAN:** I think… today went well.

*A tremendous crash comes from the equipment closet.*

**AKANE, OFFSCREEN:** HEY! ARE THESE CLIMBING ROPES SUPPOSED TO COME OFF?

*Mikan’s smile vanishes.*

*She raises the whistle.*

**MIKAN:** PUT. THAT. DOWN.

*The entire gym goes silent.*

**IBUKI:** …Whoa.

**HAJIME:** Yeah. She’s definitely a teacher.

**FADE OUT.**

“And I am Greg,” he said. “A name I have answered to for the usual number of years.”

“This is my husband, Mike.”

Greg shook Mike’s hand, then Karen’s, then Mike’s again.

“It’s just an expression.”

“Of course.” Greg laughed, waited for them to join in, then laughed once more on their behalf.

“So,” Karen said, “what brought you to the neighborhood?”

“A car. I sat inside it.”

“I meant, why did you choose this place?”

“Good schools.”

“Oh, you have kids?”

“Not yet,” Greg said. “I thought I should secure the schools first.”

“Well, we’ll let you get settled. Come over for a barbecue sometime.”

“I accept. What time?”

“We’ll figure something out.”

Greg nodded gravely. “I, too, dislike committing to a time.”

**What Love Left Burning**

I learned the truth one ordinary day—  
your cup still warm, the curtains full of light.  
How strange that nothing knew to turn away,  
that birds went on rehearsing for the night.

You wept. I watched your fingers twist the ring  
I’d slipped upon your hand three years before.  
I wanted not to feel a single thing;  
instead, I loved you there, and hurt the more.

I could not make your tenderness untrue  
because you’d given tenderness elsewhere.  
The hands that hurt me were the hands I knew  
had washed my father’s blood out of my hair.

So when you left, I let the doorway stand  
between the life we’d lost and what came next.  
I did not call. But still my foolish hand  
reached for the phone whenever something blessed

the day—a dog asleep beneath a chair,  
the first ripe peach, a sudden fall of snow.  
I wanted you to know. You were not there.  
I loved you. There was nowhere it could go.
