# Chapter One  
## a messy plaster cast

The first thing Tessa said when the nurse brought out the scissors was, “Those jeans cost forty-six dollars.”

The nurse stopped at the foot of the hospital trolley. She had silver-rimmed glasses, a dark braid pinned around her head, and the patient expression of a woman who had already heard every possible objection to scissors.

“Then I’ll try to make forty-six dollars’ worth of cuts.”

On the chair beside the trolley, Nora laughed into Tessa’s ski jacket.

“You’re supposed to be on my side,” Tessa told her.

“I was on your side. I was on the easy slope. You waved at me on your way past.”

“It was an encouraging wave.”

“It involved one finger.”

“An exceptionally encouraging finger.”

The nurse glanced at the chart hooked over the end of the trolley. “Tessa Bell. Twenty-seven.”

“Until this morning. I’ve aged considerably.”

“I’m Ruth.” She set the scissors down. “And before we do anything to your jeans, we’re going to get your pain under better control.”

For the first time since the mountain, Tessa had no joke ready.

Her right leg lay supported in a temporary splint. Below the knee, something deep inside it seemed to pulse independently of the rest of her body. She had managed the ride down the slope, the ambulance, and the X-rays by concentrating on small, irritating details: a crooked ceiling tile, the squeak of a wheel, Nora saying *almost there* when she could not possibly know.

Now that nobody was moving her, she was beginning to shake.

Ruth noticed. She drew a blanket over Tessa’s shoulders without commenting.

That was somehow worse than being fussed over.

“Thank you,” Tessa said, studying the blanket.

Outside the curtained bay, a telephone rang. Somewhere farther away, a radio was playing Whitney Houston through a haze of static.

It was February 1987. Tessa had bought the jeans three weeks earlier, had seven dollars in her purse, and had been absolutely certain that she knew how to ski.

***

Dr. Elaine Mercer arrived carrying the X-rays and wearing running shoes beneath her white coat.

Tessa liked her immediately. Anybody sensible enough to wear comfortable shoes at work might also be sensible enough to send a person home with aspirin and an encouraging speech.

Dr. Mercer put the films against the light box.

Unfortunately, the bones did not appear interested in encouragement.

“You’ve broken your tibia,” she said, pointing. “Here. And your fibula here.”

Nora leaned forward. Tessa leaned back.

“That seems excessive,” Tessa said. “I only fell once.”

“The good news is that the alignment is acceptable. We don’t need to operate today.”

“See?” Tessa said to Nora. “An efficient accident.”

“The less welcome news is that you’ll need a long-leg cast. From your foot to high on your thigh.”

“How high?”

Dr. Mercer indicated the upper part of her own leg.

Tessa stared at her. “That’s practically up to my bottom.”

“It needs to control movement at the knee as well as protect the fracture.”

“My knee wasn’t even involved. It was an innocent bystander.”

“It will have plenty of time to resent the arrangement.”

Nora made a noise that she disguised, poorly, as a cough.

Dr. Mercer explained the plan: pain relief, removal of the splint, another examination, then a padded plaster cast. Because the injury was fresh and swelling was expected, they would split the cast afterward to give the leg room. There would be more X-rays, crutches, and an early follow-up appointment.

Tessa listened carefully until the doctor said, “You won’t be putting weight on it.”

“For how long?”

“We’ll decide as it heals. Think in weeks, not days.”

Tessa looked at Nora.

Nora’s smile had disappeared.

Tessa wished she had kept looking at the X-rays.

***

The medicine softened the sharpest edges of the pain. It did not turn removing her jeans into a reasonable activity.

“I can do the button,” Tessa said when Ruth reached toward her waistband.

“All right.”

“And the zip.”

“All right.”

These small victories achieved, Tessa discovered that taking off snug jeans while keeping one leg perfectly still was a problem for which enthusiasm offered no solution.

She tugged at the denim over her left hip.

Her right leg answered.

She stopped so suddenly that Nora stood up.

“Don’t,” Tessa said.

Nora froze. “Don’t what?”

“Make that face.”

“What face?”

“The one where you’re about to be helpful.”

For a moment, nobody spoke.

Then Ruth picked up the scissors again.

“We can cut along the seam on the injured side. Much less movement.”

Tessa looked down at the jeans. They had faded just right at the knees. She had worn them dancing the previous Saturday and to breakfast with Nora the morning after, with yesterday’s eyeliner still under one eye.

It was ridiculous to feel betrayed by a pair of trousers.

“Go on, then,” she said. “But I want it recorded that they died doing something adventurous.”

Ruth cut the denim slowly, keeping the lower blade away from Tessa’s skin. With Nora supporting her shoulders and Ruth guiding the fabric clear of the splint, they eased the ruined jeans off.

Tessa was left in her sweater and pale blue cotton panties.

She tugged the sweater down.

Ruth immediately spread a sheet over her lap. “We’ll keep you covered as much as we can.”

“Good. I hadn’t planned to make my hospital debut in these.”

“They’re perfectly nice,” Nora said.

“That is exactly the devastating review every woman hopes for.”

Getting onto the casting table required more hands than Tessa wanted to admit. Ruth called in another nurse, a compact woman named Anita, and between them they arranged the trolley beside it.

“Let us do the moving,” Anita said.

“I can lift myself.”

“You can help with your arms when I tell you. We’ll support your leg.”

Tessa opened her mouth, caught Ruth watching her, and closed it again.

The transfer was brief and unpleasant. She gripped Nora’s hand hard enough to leave four pale marks.

Once she was settled, she let go at once.

“Sorry.”

Nora flexed her fingers. “I’ll send you an invoice.”

***

The casting room had pale green walls, a high window, and a calendar showing a kitten asleep in a teacup. On the counter stood a basin of water beside several wrapped rolls of plaster bandage.

Tessa regarded the supplies.

“I expected something more technological.”

“We keep the space-age equipment for people who follow the trail signs,” Nora said.

“I followed a trail sign.”

“You followed it past a rope.”

“It was a very low rope.”

Dr. Mercer examined the leg again while Ruth supported it. She checked Tessa’s toes and asked about sensation. Without the temporary splint, the injury felt horribly vulnerable; Tessa fixed her eyes on the kitten and tried not to move.

“Tell us if anything becomes too painful,” the doctor said.

“I’ve been told I’m very brave.”

“By whom?”

“Women who wanted me to climb ladders.”

Dr. Mercer smiled, but her hands remained steady and precise.

A soft stockinette went on first, then layers of padding. Ruth kept the sheet arranged over Tessa’s lap while they worked higher along her thigh. Tessa watched the padding swallow the shape of her leg.

At first, she had imagined a cast as something applied to an injury.

This looked more like a construction project.

Anita dipped the first plaster roll into the basin. Bubbles rose through the water. When she lifted it out, cloudy droplets spattered the floor.

“Oh,” Tessa said. “We’re doing arts and crafts.”

“The materials are less forgiving than they look,” Anita replied.

The wet plaster felt cool through the padding. Dr. Mercer and Ruth supported and positioned her leg while Anita passed fresh rolls. White bands overlapped around her foot and ankle, then climbed her calf.

Nora watched with fascinated concentration.

“You’re enjoying this,” Tessa accused.

“I enjoy watching other women work while you’re quiet.”

“I’m injured, Nora. Be generous.”

“I drove forty miles behind your ambulance with one of your skis rattling against my ear.”

“That’s the generous part. Now try sympathetic.”

The plaster spread over her knee and up her thigh. Its weight became unmistakable. Ruth adjusted the covering as they finished the upper edge, which sat disconcertingly close beneath her bottom.

Tessa lifted her head to look.

“That is an enormous amount of leg.”

“It was an enormous amount before,” Nora said. “You simply weren’t paying attention.”

Anita smoothed another layer into place. A fleck of plaster landed on Tessa’s sweater.

Then another.

“Excuse me,” Tessa said. “The patient is being decorated.”

Ruth glanced at the white spots. “We’ll clean those off.”

“Could you do a little on the other side? Make it look deliberate?”

Nora laughed, and Tessa smiled back. Then Dr. Mercer shifted her hands, carefully maintaining the position of the leg, and pain flashed through the softened fog of the medicine.

Tessa sucked in a breath.

Everyone stopped.

“Where?” Dr. Mercer asked.

“The break. It’s—”

She had meant to say *fine*.

The word was already waiting. She used it at work when she had too much to do, on the telephone with her mother, and whenever Nora asked whether she could manage the rent alone.

This time she could not get it out.

“It hurts,” she said.

Dr. Mercer nodded. “All right. We’ll pause.”

Nobody sighed. Nobody told her she should have expected it.

Nora offered her hand again.

After a moment, Tessa took it.

***

The cast grew warm as it set.

Tessa lay back against the pillow and watched Anita wipe plaster from the floor. There was white residue on the basin, on Ruth’s apron, and along the side of one of Dr. Mercer’s shoes.

“A messy plaster cast,” Tessa murmured.

“Messy room,” Ruth corrected. “Very respectable cast.”

It was smooth and white and much larger than Tessa had expected. Her toes stuck out at the end, looking absurdly casual.

Once the plaster was firm enough, Dr. Mercer split it to accommodate swelling. She explained the next steps again, including what pain, numbness, or changes in the toes should prompt an urgent call.

This time Tessa asked questions.

She asked about sleeping. About stairs. About bathing without getting the cast wet.

At the mention of stairs, Nora lowered the bundle of ruined jeans she had been folding.

“Tess.”

“No.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’ve got your spare-bedroom voice.”

“You live on the third floor.”

“There’s a railing.”

“And your bathroom has that little step.”

“It’s not a little step. It’s a charming architectural defect.”

“My place is on the ground floor.”

Tessa stared at the ceiling.

She could picture Nora’s flat: the wide sofa, the kitchen close enough to shout into, the spare room currently full of laundry. She could also picture herself occupying it, needing tea brought over and shopping fetched and doors held open.

Nora waited.

Ruth busied herself at the counter, granting them the privacy of not appearing to listen.

“I don’t want to move in and become your job,” Tessa said at last.

“You’d be a terrible job. No pension.”

“Nora.”

“You can stay tonight. We don’t have to settle the rest of your life before supper.”

That was small enough to consider.

Tessa picked a dried speck of plaster from her sweater. “I may need help getting into the car.”

“Yes.”

“And out.”

“Probably.”

She looked at her friend. “Would you help me?”

Nora’s answer came without ceremony.

“Of course.”

Tessa nodded, as if they had merely agreed on where to eat.

Then she looked toward the counter.

“Ruth?”

The nurse turned.

“Please tell me you’ve got something I can wear home. Because unless those scissors have a reverse setting, I appear to have a problem.”

Nora held up the jeans. One side hung open from waist to ankle.

Ruth considered them.

“I can find you a gown.”

“Backless?”

“I’m afraid so.”

Tessa sighed and settled against the pillow.

“Fine. But Nora walks behind me. I’ve already given this hospital quite enough to talk about.”

The strongest thing connecting these ingredients, to me, is **the tension between wonder and the business of making wonder accessible**. Someone has to clean the bathrooms at the edge of the impossible. Someone sells postcards of a creature who actually lives down the road. Something magnificent can survive for millennia while the motel named after it goes bankrupt.

Oaks fits particularly well into that tension: he can be comfortable with the extraordinary without being immune to it. His steadiness needn’t mean he knows all the answers—only that, when confronted with something inexplicable, he still thinks they should check the spare tire.

Here are three directions, each making different choices about the world and his origins.

## 1. The Last Season at Monument Basin
*An uncanny park mystery about the difference between protecting a place and preserving what people want it to be.*

### The setting

Monument Basin National Park lies in a parallel world populated by mythical creatures. Its employees are salaried, its vehicles run on gasoline, and its visitor center has been waiting eleven years for a new roof.

The park’s heyday was the era of family motoring holidays. Now the interstate bypasses its gateway town, its most famous overlook has been closed after a rockfall, and its monumental stone formations no longer quite resemble the photographs on the postcards.

That last problem is more serious than anyone admits.

### The newcomers

**Mara, twenty-one**, is a human who takes a wrong turn while driving to a seasonal hospitality job. By the time she realizes that the antlers on the gas-station attendant are real, the road behind her no longer leads home.

Humans are known in this world, but chiefly from dubious expedition accounts. The park superintendent offers Mara temporary accommodation and a maintenance job while someone investigates her arrival. This is partly kindness and partly a practical response to finding an undocumented person sleeping in a car.

**Oaks, twenty-four**, is a junior ranger assigned to supervise her. He is a natural-born jackalope, not an artificial one. He is strict about food storage, restricted areas, and documenting mileage. He is not particularly impressed by her humanity.

He’s also local. He knows which closed businesses still have working pay phones, whose grandmother has keys to the abandoned lodge, and which park stories you should never repeat over a radio after dark.

### The story

Mara initially treats the park as an obstacle between her and home. But while working with Oaks, she discovers that the landscape’s discrepancies follow a pattern. Trails lengthen overnight. A stone arch appears in an employee’s childhood photograph but not in any official survey. Tourists report seeing a lit motel in a basin where there has never been a road.

The park has an older cycle: once every few generations, its formations move. Not through erosion. They get up.

The first park administrators knew this. Their successors installed buried restraints that kept the formations in place, preserving the famous views and allowing roads and buildings to become permanent. Now those restraints are failing. The disturbances that brought Mara across are an early symptom.

The dilemma isn’t simply “nature versus a wicked developer.” Letting the landscape move could destroy the gateway town. Keeping it fixed could kill whatever Monument Basin actually is.

Oaks’s parent runs a struggling business there. His commitment to procedure is partly a commitment to keeping an already precarious community intact.

### The climax and landing

Mara and Oaks discover an old migration corridor beneath the abandoned tourist district. Opening it would spare the inhabited town—but require deliberately sacrificing the historic lodge, the original highway, and the postcard view everyone has spent decades trying to save.

During the evacuation, Oaks must enforce a closure he knows will end his family’s business. Mara must stop thinking like a visitor who can eventually escape the consequences.

They succeed, but the park is genuinely changed. It doesn’t regain its golden age. It becomes a different, less marketable, more living place.

Mara receives an opportunity to return home during the migration. Whether she takes it can remain an ending choice; the emotional resolution is that she now understands what staying would mean.

**Why Oaks matters:** He isn’t a keeper of ancient wisdom. He’s a young employee who has confused reliability with maintaining the status quo, and who eventually learns that being dependable can mean helping people survive a necessary upheaval.

---

## 2. Genuine Wonders, Exit 131
*A roadside mystery with an artificial Oaks, petty fraud, and a surprisingly intimate question: who owns a miracle?*

### The setting

In our world, on an increasingly empty stretch of southwestern highway, stands **Bellweather’s Genuine Wonders**:

- a trading post;
- a twelve-room motel, eight rooms habitable;
- a “museum of natural impossibilities”;
- a shuttered miniature railroad;
- and an enormous fiberglass jackalope visible from the road.

Most of its wonders are fake. A few are not.

The supernatural is geographically limited and poorly understood. There is no hidden magical civilization with its own bureaucracy—just things that have happened here and people trying to live around them.

### The newcomers

**Kit, twenty-three**, arrives to inventory the property after inheriting it from an estranged great-aunt. Kit needs money, knows nothing about running a motel, and intends to sell.

**Oaks, apparently twenty-five**, has been managing the place. He wears an employee polo, charges guests for late checkout, and will describe a bathtub as “recently restored” if he has recently unclogged it.

He introduces himself to Kit after closing, when there are no guests around to see him. Publicly, he is supposed to be the attraction’s very convincing mascot.

Privately, he is the original jackalope exhibit, brought to life twenty-five years earlier. His original label read **HOAXEY: THE WEST’S MOST UNBELIEVABLE CRITTER!** He considers the shortened name an improvement.

His creator, Kit’s great-aunt’s former business partner, is still alive but refuses to set foot on the property.

### The story

Kit finds an apparently straightforward buyer: a collector who wants the exhibits and will pay enough to settle the estate’s debts. Oaks obstructs the sale through missing keys, inconsistent inventories, and extremely literal readings of the will.

Kit assumes he fears unemployment. Then a moth-eaten “mermaid” disappears from its case, leaving wet footprints through a locked room.

Years ago, Oaks’s creator discovered that a spring beneath the property could give an assembled specimen life. The process wasn’t repeatable on demand, and it produced beings rather than obedient attractions. After Oaks, the partners stopped experimenting—but they had already sold several apparent failures.

The collector has traced those sales. He believes Bellweather’s contains a reproducible process worth far more than a roadside museum.

Oaks knew about the spring. He did not know that some of the sold exhibits had eventually awakened.

Kit and Oaks begin visiting closed attractions, estate warehouses, and storage units to find them before the collector does. This supplies a road-story middle full of faded dinosaur parks, bankrupt curiosity museums, and people who have spent decades quietly looking after something they cannot explain.

### The central complication

Oaks has secretly been buying back old exhibits with motel revenue. Some of the business’s financial trouble is his fault. He has also concealed letters from Kit’s aunt because he assumed any heir would sell him along with the furniture.

Kit’s anger is justified. So is his fear.

Meanwhile, his creator views him with affection but still calls him her finest work. Oaks has never quite found a way to explain why that bothers him.

### The climax and landing

The collector acquires a legitimate interest in the property through its debts. The final struggle is therefore partly a break-in and partly an ugly negotiation: Kit cannot solve everything by declaring the place hers.

They remove the living exhibits and destroy the apparatus that made the spring usable. To clear the remaining debts, Kit sells the valuable highway frontage—including the fiberglass jackalope.

The motel survives on a smaller scale. Oaks becomes a co-owner rather than an inherited employee. He remains a questionable salesman, but now there are explicit limits on what he can sell and whose secrets he can use.

**Why Oaks matters:** He is both a person and the product around which the business was built. His arc isn’t becoming “more human”; it’s acquiring the right to be ordinary, flawed, and self-directed.

---

## 3. The Road That Used to Go Somewhere
*A melancholy, sometimes funny road story in which the roadside attractions are signs of a vanished natural phenomenon.*

### The setting

An entirely mythical parallel world, with no human protagonist and no necessary portal.

Its western interior used to be crossed by enormous migrating creatures called **wayfarers**: slow-moving, mountain-sized animals that passed once every seven years. Towns built viewing platforms. Motels offered wake-up calls when one approached. Gas stations sold collectible glasses. Children climbed fiberglass replicas.

The wayfarers stopped coming twenty-eight years ago.

Nobody agrees why. The old highway survives as a thinning chain of businesses selling souvenirs of something almost no young person remembers.

### The newcomers

**Nell, eighteen**, is a young griffin who has moved inland to live with her father after failing out of a vocational program. She takes a temporary job photographing and cataloguing roadside signs before a highway decommissioning project.

She is embarrassed by the assignment and eager to leave. To her, the region’s nostalgia feels like a demand that she mourn a life she never had.

**Oaks, twenty-two**, is a jackalope employed by a regional historical association. He drives the survey truck, handles access permissions, and insists that Nell record the backs of signs as well as their picturesque fronts.

He is practical, dry, and occasionally unscrupulous: he can get them free rooms by implying they influence heritage grants. He doesn’t.

### The story

At a derelict attraction, Nell finds a recently shed plate of wayfarer hide—small enough to carry, but unmistakable.

Their survey becomes an investigation. Each stop offers a contradictory fragment: an old ranger’s notebook, a mechanic’s home movies, a restaurant menu that recorded passage dates, a motel owner who insists the last migration went through after the official final sighting.

There is still one wayfarer following the old route.

It is young, by its species’ standards, and travelling mostly underground. Its apparent disappearance has been caused partly by the new highways, drainage works, fences, and extraction sites that fragmented its route. No single project killed the migration. Each project made perfectly defensible local sense.

Now it has reached a dead end beneath the town where Nell’s father lives.

### The human-sized stakes

Finding a living wayfarer could save the region’s tourist economy. Oaks’s employer wants a public announcement and a managed viewing event. Business owners begin reopening mothballed rooms.

But the creature is not returning to perform the old spectacle. It is lost.

Nell wants to release the evidence immediately. Oaks wants to secure a route first. Their disagreement becomes personal when she learns he has been quietly promising different towns that they might host the first sighting, hoping to win cooperation. His habitual small deceptions have created expectations he cannot fulfil.

### The climax and landing

They reconstruct the migration route and discover that the surviving creature is trying to reach a dry inland basin—now occupied by a solar installation and several failing farms.

Helping it means negotiating a temporary passage rather than defeating one villain. Their collected photographs and oral histories become practical evidence: this culvert follows an old crossing; that motel was built facing a route now buried beneath a frontage road.

The final passage happens at night, without the promised grandstands. Some people are furious. Others stand beside their darkened businesses and hear, for the first time in decades, something immense moving beyond the headlights.

The creature reaches the basin. What happens next may take years.

Nell finishes the survey, but changes its purpose: not a collection of picturesque ruins, but a record of how to keep a route open. Oaks must remain in the region and face the people he misled.

**Why Oaks matters:** He loves the old road without having experienced its prosperous years. He has inherited nostalgia almost as a family obligation. His growth is realizing that caring for a place does not require recreating its best-selling moment.

---

### Which direction seems strongest?

- **Monument Basin** best combines ranger culture, natural grandeur, and unsettling mystery.
- **Genuine Wonders** gives Oaks the most personal stake and makes the fullest use of “Hoaxey.”
- **The Road That Used to Go Somewhere** most directly explores wear, nostalgia, and the dying embers of prosperity.

My strongest recommendation is **Genuine Wonders** if Oaks is the seed you’re most attached to, or **Monument Basin** if the landscape and atmosphere are what first made you want to write this. In either case, I’d preserve one feature: Oaks knows how to run the place, but he does **not** know what the place ultimately is. That gives him authority without letting him solve the story for the newcomer.

Sur le pain chaud, l’été s’étire,
Et chaque bouchée nous fait sourire.
Un peu de sucre, un fruit qui dure :
Le bonheur tient dans la confiture.

“Anybody who says the internet is ten percent of the work,” said Chen, “is paying somebody else to do the work.”

Lisa turned from the screen. “That your professional opinion?”

“That’s my professional resentment.”

A few people smiled. Captain Velez didn’t.

“Can we establish where the money came from?”

“Not yet,” Lisa said. “New car’s leased through an LLC. Condo belongs to a girlfriend. Watches might be fake.”

“Watch isn’t fake,” said Patel from the back.

Everyone looked at him.

“My wife sells them,” he said. “That one costs more than my first house.”

Velez studied the photograph. Alejandro Gonzales smiled back at him, handsome and apparently untroubled by the price of anything.

“All right. Find me a victim.”

***

By Thursday, Lisa had found fourteen.

The difficulty was that none of them considered themselves victims.

“He helped us,” said the woman across her desk.

Her name was Erin Bell. She wore hospital scrubs under a winter coat, and she’d brought a folder containing bills arranged by date. Lisa hadn’t asked her to bring them.

“My daughter needed a wheelchair the insurance wouldn’t cover. Somebody sent me his page. He came out, did a video with us, put it online. We got the chair.”

“How much did the fundraiser collect?”

“Forty-three thousand, I think.”

“And how much did you receive?”

“The chair. Seven thousand toward her therapy.”

“Did Mr. Gonzales explain what happened to the rest?”

Erin’s hand settled on the folder.

“He said there were expenses.”

“Thirty thousand dollars in expenses?”

“He got us more than anybody else did.”

Lisa let the silence sit. In the corridor, somebody laughed at something, then a door closed.

Erin leaned forward.

“Are you going to take the chair?”

“No.”

“Because people make promises all the time, Detective. They send links. They say they’ll pray. He actually showed up.”

***

Chen had Gonzales’s page on both monitors when Lisa returned.

Alejandro wasn’t Slick online. He was Alex Gives Back.

There he was carrying groceries up a porch. There he was hugging a veteran beside a repaired pickup. There he was kneeling next to Erin’s daughter, listening solemnly while she explained the controls on her new chair.

He was good at it. He never looked at the camera while someone was crying.

“Fourteen campaigns in four months,” Chen said. “Most of the beneficiaries got something. Enough to make a follow-up video.”

“How much stayed with him?”

“Can’t tell from the public totals. Some campaigns link to registered charities, some don’t. Financial Crimes is interested.”

Lisa watched Alejandro wipe his eyes with the heel of his hand.

“That genuine?”

“Could be. People can feel good about doing bad math.”

Chen clicked to another video.

A young woman sat on a motel bed, hands folded between her knees. The caption read: **HELP MARISOL GET HOME.**

Lisa stopped pulling off her coat.

“Go back.”

Chen paused it.

“What?”

“The woman.”

“You know her?”

“Print that.”

“Lisa—”

“Please.”

He did.

She took the warm page down the hall to Missing Persons.

***

Marisol was actually Rebecca Sloane, twenty-six, last seen leaving a restaurant job eleven months earlier.

Her mother had called every Tuesday for the first six months. After that, she’d started calling on Rebecca’s birthday, her own birthday, holidays. The detective assigned to the case remembered her apologizing.

Lisa watched the fundraiser again with headphones.

Rebecca described losing her identification, escaping a violent boyfriend, needing money to reach family in Arizona. Her voice was flat. At one point she looked past the camera.

Alejandro’s voice came softly from behind it.

“Tell them what you told me.”

Rebecca swallowed.

“I just want to go home.”

The campaign had collected sixty-eight thousand dollars.

Its last update said Marisol was safe and had asked for privacy.

“Could still be voluntary,” Velez said when Lisa brought it to him. “She could have left her life. Could be helping him run a scam.”

“Then I’d like her to tell me that.”

“So would I. Find where they shot it.”

***

The motel had changed its bedspreads.

That cost them most of Friday.

At four-twenty, a manager recognized the chipped headboard in the video. At five-ten, he found the reservation: three nights, paid by a media company whose mailing address was Alejandro’s girlfriend’s condo.

At five-forty, he remembered the second woman.

“Older,” he told Lisa over the phone. “She came to collect them.”

“Them?”

“The girl and the little boy.”

Lisa looked across Chen’s desk.

“What little boy?”

“Four, maybe five. Didn’t see him much.”

“Do you have the woman’s name?”

“No. But she’s been back. Last week, actually.”

Lisa reached for a pen.

“Same room?”

“No, ma’am. Same arrangement. She brings people in, the gentleman makes his movies, they leave.”

“Is anyone there now?”

The manager hesitated.

Through Lisa’s headphones came the faint clatter of a keyboard.

“Room nineteen.”

***

They were still waiting for a second unit when Gonzales’s livestream notification appeared on Chen’s phone.

He held it between them.

Alejandro stood beneath a motel walkway, rain shining on his jacket. He looked tired and earnest.

“Family, we’ve got an urgent one tonight.”

Behind him, a door stood open.

Lisa could see a small shoe on the carpet.

“These folks have been through something terrible,” Alejandro continued. “And we have a very small window to help.”

Lisa opened the car door.

On the phone, hearts floated up across his face.

She lowered the tablet and looked over the six of us.

“Questions?”

“Which gate has the bars?” asked Havel.

“The same gate has the hospital.”

“North or south?”

“Yes.”

Nobody else had questions.

She touched her tablet to the reader beside the door. Our temporary port passes appeared one by one in the dispenser, each with a photograph, ship registry, and a thick yellow stripe.

“Yellow means transient crew. Keep them visible. If somebody offers you money to carry a package between terminals, refuse. If somebody asks which gate you came through, show your pass. If you hear shooting, get behind something solid. Those advertisement screens are not solid.”

Havel glanced at the enormous illuminated woman selling insurance above the baggage belt.

“Wouldn’t have trusted her anyway.”

The officer did not smile.

Beyond customs, the port smelled of hot wiring, floor disinfectant, and food fried in oil that had seen too many ships come and go. Our freighter had spent nineteen days on recycled air. Even bad cooking smelled wonderful.

Captain Venn stopped beneath the departures board.

“Four hours,” she said. “Then back aboard. We unload, take on water, and leave before anyone finds a reason to delay us.”

“What about the reactor filters?” I asked.

“You find them. Havel carries them.”

Havel opened his mouth.

“You wanted shore leave,” she said.

The chandlery occupied three units between a currency exchange and a shuttered travel agency. Someone had painted over the travel agency’s window, but cheerful blue letters still showed through: DISCOVER THE SOUTHERN HIGHLANDS.

Inside the chandlery, shelves reached almost to the ceiling. There were suit seals in transparent drawers, boxes of ceramic fuses, and a perfectly preserved ship’s compass that could not possibly be useful within a hundred kilometres of a working fusion plant.

The man behind the counter examined my parts list.

“Two filters?”

“Three, if you have them.”

“I have six.”

“That sounds promising.”

“Unfortunately, they belong to somebody.”

Havel leaned against the counter. “Everybody says that before telling you the price.”

The shopkeeper looked past him toward the door.

A woman had come in carrying an empty canvas bag. Her left sleeve was pinned above the elbow. She wore ordinary dockworker’s clothes, but the shopkeeper straightened as if she had arrived with a squad behind her.

“Your order isn’t ready,” he said.

“You told me noon.”

“The warehouse hasn’t released it.”

“It’s half past.”

“I know what time it is, Mara.”

She put her bag on the counter and noticed our yellow passes.

“What ship?”

“Merchant freighter,” I said.

“I can see that. Which one?”

“The *Patient Venture*.”

Her eyes moved to the parts list under the shopkeeper’s hand.

“Reactor filters?”

I reached for the paper. The shopkeeper let me take it.

“Sorry,” I said. “We don’t want any trouble.”

“You and everyone else.” She turned back to him. “I need all six, Dav.”

Havel stopped leaning.

Outside, a baggage tractor rattled past with one wheel squealing. Somewhere farther along the concourse, a child was crying.

The shopkeeper rubbed his forehead.

“I can give you three today.”

“No. You can give me six today. That was the arrangement.”

I folded the list and put it in my pocket.

“We’ll try another supplier.”

“There isn’t another supplier,” Havel said.

“We’ll try anyway.”

Mara stepped aside to let us pass. As I reached the door, she spoke again.

“Your ship has a machine shop?”

I kept my hand on the doorplate.

“A small one.”

“Can it cut a filter collar? Standard forty-millimetre thread.”

“Depends on the alloy.”

She took a metal ring from her pocket and set it on the counter. One edge had split. Someone had tried to repair it with wire.

I should have left. The officer’s instructions were fresh enough that I could remember the tired way she had said *completely on your own*.

Instead, I went back and picked up the ring.

“This isn’t from a ship.”

“No.”

“Coolant plant?”

“Water purification.”

Havel looked at me. I knew that look. It meant the captain had given us four hours, and he would be happy to remind her whose idea this had been.

I turned the ring over. The wire repair had worn a shallow groove into the metal.

“Where is it?”

Mara hesitated.

“Outside the fence,” she said.

I put the ring down.

She did not argue. That was worse, somehow. She just picked it up again and slipped it into her pocket.

### La maison au bord du soir

Au bout d’un petit chemin bordé de fougères se trouvait une maison basse, avec un toit bleu et une cheminée qui ne fumait jamais trop.

On l’appelait la maison au bord du soir.

On pouvait y arriver à n’importe quelle heure. Personne ne demandait pourquoi on marchait lentement, pourquoi on s’arrêtait si souvent, ni pourquoi certaines journées semblaient plus longues que d’autres.

Près de la porte, une petite pancarte disait :

*Entrez comme vous êtes. Nous avons tout notre temps.*

Une personne arriva un soir, portant six sacs.

Ils étaient de tailles différentes. Certains se voyaient bien ; d’autres ressemblaient presque à de simples plis dans son manteau. Pourtant, chacun avait son poids. Et plusieurs tiraient douloureusement sur ses épaules.

La gardienne de la maison ouvrit avant même qu’il soit nécessaire de frapper.

— Bonsoir, dit-elle. Tu peux entrer.

Elle ne s’exclama pas devant les sacs. Elle ne demanda pas comment ils étaient devenus si lourds. Elle écarta seulement une chaise du passage pour laisser davantage de place.

Dans le salon, le feu faisait un bruit doux, comme du papier qu’on froisse très loin. Une lampe éclairait un tapis couleur de miel. Il y avait un fauteuil, un canapé, une chaise longue, et des coussins que l’on pouvait déplacer sans devoir demander la permission.

— Où serais-tu le moins mal ? demanda la gardienne.

La personne regarda autour d’elle.

C’était une question agréable. On ne lui demandait pas de trouver un endroit merveilleux. Seulement un endroit un peu plus doux.

Elle choisit le canapé près de la fenêtre.

La gardienne apporta un petit banc pour soutenir les sacs. Ils restaient là, à portée de main, mais le banc en portait une partie du poids.

Puis elle ajusta la lampe.

— Comme ça ?

— Un peu moins de lumière, peut-être.

— Bien sûr.

Et cela fut aussi simple que cela.

Dehors, le jardin entrait lentement dans la nuit.

Un merle sautillait sous une haie. Il retournait les feuilles avec beaucoup de sérieux, comme s’il cherchait une chose minuscule et très importante. Plus loin, un arrosoir oublié recueillait les dernières gouttes d’une pluie déjà passée.

Sur le rebord de la fenêtre, un chat gris dormait, le nez caché sous sa patte.

— Il s’appelle Demain, dit la gardienne.

La personne sourit un peu.

— Pourquoi ?

— Parce qu’il peut presque toujours attendre.

Demain remua une oreille, puis reprit son sommeil, manifestement satisfait de cette explication.

La gardienne s’assit à l’autre bout de la pièce avec un ouvrage de laine. Ses aiguilles avançaient lentement. Un rang, puis un autre. Parfois, elle s’arrêtait pour regarder le feu.

Il n’était pas nécessaire de parler.

La personne sentait encore ses sacs. L’un pesait davantage ce soir-là. Un autre semblait changer de place sans prévenir. La douleur n’avait pas disparu en passant la porte.

Mais ici, personne ne lui demandait de faire semblant.

Elle pouvait changer de position. Replacer un coussin. Garder les yeux ouverts ou les fermer. Même soupirer sans qu’on lui pose aussitôt une question.

Après un moment, la gardienne montra la fenêtre.

— Tu vois la petite lumière, au fond du jardin ?

Entre les arbres brillait une lanterne.

— Elle éclaire quoi ?

— Une marche.

— Une seule ?

— Oui. Le chemin tourne juste après. Depuis la maison, on ne voit pas la suite.

La personne observa le petit cercle doré. On y distinguait le bord d’une marche en pierre, une feuille humide et quelques brins d’herbe. Tout le reste demeurait dans l’ombre.

C’était joli, cette petite lumière qui n’essayait pas d’éclairer tout le jardin.

Le chat Demain se réveilla pour accomplir une tâche importante : s’étirer. Il allongea une patte, puis l’autre, hésita longuement, et choisit finalement un coussin voisin.

La gardienne reprit son ouvrage.

Dans la cuisine, une horloge marquait les heures avec tant de discrétion qu’on pouvait aussi bien croire qu’elle comptait les silences.

La personne laissa son regard se poser sur les choses simples.

Le bord rond d’une tasse.

Une couture sur le coussin.

L’ombre d’une branche qui bougeait contre le mur.

Rien de tout cela ne résolvait les six maladies. Mais ces petites choses existaient à côté d’elles. Elles avaient, elles aussi, une place dans la soirée.

Peu à peu, la maison devint plus calme encore.

La gardienne posa sa laine dans un panier.

— Je serai dans la pièce voisine, dit-elle. Tu peux m’appeler si tu as besoin de quelque chose.

Elle laissa la porte entrouverte.

Sur son banc, chacun des six sacs avait trouvé sa place. Il n’était pas nécessaire de les ouvrir maintenant, ni d’en vérifier le contenu.

Dehors, la lanterne éclairait toujours la marche.

Le merle s’était abrité dans la haie.

Le chat dormait de nouveau.

Et dans la maison au bord du soir, on avait gardé du temps, de la place et une lumière douce pour cette personne fatiguée.

Le sommeil pouvait venir bientôt, ou prendre son temps.

En attendant, il n’y avait plus d’histoire à suivre, plus de chemin à parcourir.

Seulement le canapé près de la fenêtre.

Le coussin, ajusté comme il fallait pour cet instant.

Et, de l’autre côté de la porte entrouverte, le bruit tranquille d’une tasse que l’on rangeait.

## The Uses of Air

I bought the kayak on a Sunday in August. The man selling it lived in Edison, in a house with no shade. He had laid the boat on his driveway beside a lawn mower. In the sunlight the yellow vinyl was almost white.

“Does it hold air?” I asked.

“Mostly,” he said.

He wanted forty dollars. When I hesitated, he offered to include a bicycle helmet with green dinosaur spikes. It was large enough for an adult. He pressed one of the spikes with his thumb and let it spring back.

I paid him. There seemed no reason to prolong our acquaintance.

By two o’clock the inside of my Pontiac Aztek was so hot that the seat-belt buckle burned my wrist. The air conditioner had stopped working in June. With the windows down, I could hear the kayak shifting in the back whenever I turned. I had purchased it because I wanted to spend less of my life in the car. Now I was driving it to water.

At a pharmacy outside New Brunswick, I stopped to look for swimming trunks. There were none. There were greeting cards, bags of charcoal, and a revolving display of reading glasses. In the last aisle I found adult-sized Depend diapers. The package showed a man whose expression suggested that an important difficulty had been overcome.

I bought them and a bottle of warm water.

The cashier asked whether I wanted a bag.

“Yes,” I said.

***

At three that afternoon I reached the Raritan at Donaldson Park in Highland Park. The tide had exposed a strip of dark mud. Beyond it, the river carried the sun in broken pieces.

The smell became stronger as I approached the bank. It came from the warmed mud and the wet vegetation left behind by the falling water. There was a sourness underneath it, like something forgotten in a closed refrigerator. I could not tell how much belonged to the river and how much had been given to it.

I changed in the car. The diaper fitted closely and made a dry rustling noise when I walked. Then I put on the dinosaur helmet. The chin strap was hot.

Only after inflating the kayak did I discover that I had no paddle.

I searched the trunk. There was a jack, an empty washer-fluid bottle, and a spatula left over from a cookout. The spatula had a black handle and three slots in its metal blade. I held it for a moment. Through the slots I could see the river.

A man walking a small dog stopped beside me.

“Going out?”

“Yes.”

“With that?”

“It’s what I have.”

He looked at the kayak, then at my helmet. His dog was busy smelling the mud. After a while they continued along the bank.

I pushed off.

For several seconds nothing happened. I sat in the shallow boat, very hot, while the river moved beneath me. Then I leaned over and pulled the spatula through the water. Most of the water passed through its slots. The kayak turned toward shore.

I tried the other side. It turned back.

There was work to be done, and I did it.

***

Ten feet from land, the heat seemed greater than it had beside the car. It rose from the yellow vinyl and struck my bare chest. Sweat collected beneath the helmet. I could feel each place where the foam touched my skull.

The left side of the kayak was softening.

The seller had told the truth. It held air, but not all of it, and not indefinitely. When I shifted my weight, a wrinkle opened beside my thigh. A little river water entered and spread across the floor.

The diaper absorbed it.

Until then, I had thought of this garment as an embarrassment. Now it had become a weight. It swelled against me with a patience I could do nothing to interrupt.

Across the water, traffic crossed the bridge. The cars shone briefly and disappeared. Their occupants were going somewhere. I watched them while making small, laborious circles with the spatula.

I had imagined that buying a boat would alter the character of my afternoons. In one respect I had been right. Ordinarily, at this hour, I was not sitting in warm river water wearing a dinosaur helmet.

A gull landed nearby. It remained beyond my reach without appearing to make an effort.

When I returned to the bank, I had traveled perhaps thirty yards. My shoulder hurt. Getting out, I slipped to one knee in the mud. The smell rose around me, immediate and intimate.

I stood up because there was nothing to be gained by remaining on my knees.

***

The following Saturday I tried the Passaic in Rutherford, near the public launch at River Barge Park. I arrived at eleven in the morning. Another hot day was beginning.

During the week I had put a patch over the leak. I had also had several opportunities to purchase a paddle. Each time I remembered it, I was occupied with something else.

The spatula was still in the trunk.

Here the water smelled of damp wood, old leaves, and something faintly oily near the bank. Small debris had gathered in the slack water. A plastic cup turned slowly against a branch. Behind me, a truck reversed with a succession of clear, indifferent beeps.

I inflated the kayak. The patch lifted at one corner.

For a moment I considered going home. At home there was a fan and a chair beside it. I could see the chair distinctly. But the boat was already inflated, and I had put on the diaper.

I launched.

This time I stayed close enough to shore to see individual stones beneath the shallow water. I paddled until my wrist grew tired. Then I stopped.

Without my efforts, the boat moved more steadily.

There was no revelation. The river stank. My helmet pinched. Along the seam beside my leg, air escaped with a faint sound that I could hear only when I bent toward it.

Yet a breeze had come up. It touched my wet shoulders and passed on toward the road. For the first time that morning, I was not entirely hot.

I sat still to receive it.

Later I would drag the boat ashore, empty it, and fold its damp sides into the Pontiac. But for another minute there was enough air.

Inside the bookstore, Jason discovered a button he hadn’t noticed before.

It was tucked beneath the remote’s sliding battery cover, beside a tiny symbol resembling an open book. When he pressed it, green lettering scrolled across the display:

**COVER MODE: HUMAN SUBJECTS ONLY. ONE MALE, ONE FEMALE.**
**PRINTED EXPRESSIONS AND POSES REMAIN FIXED.**

Jason glanced at the nearest display.

A business magazine featured a silver-haired woman in a navy suit, standing with folded arms against a city skyline. The caption identified her as Eleanor Vale, sixty-two, founder of an international shipping company.

Beside the display, a young male bookseller was pushing a cart of returns. His name tag read **BEN**, and beneath it, **ASK ME ABOUT MYSTERIES**. He wore a green shop apron over a checked shirt.

Jason selected the woman on the magazine, then Ben.

The remote blinked.

Ben’s head remained exactly where it was, his unruly hair falling over one eyebrow. Below his neck, however, he now wore Eleanor Vale’s navy suit on her older frame. His name tag was neatly pinned to the lapel.

He continued shelving books.

“Crime goes upstairs,” he told a customer, gesturing with a hardback. “Unless it’s true crime. That’s downstairs, for reasons nobody has successfully explained to me.”

Jason looked at the magazine.

Eleanor’s silver-haired head and composed smile were unchanged. So were the angle of her shoulders and her folded-arm pose. But beneath her head were Ben’s younger build, checked shirt, and green apron.

The skyline remained untouched.

The headline now read:

**ELEANOR VALE: THE BOOKSELLER WHO BUILT A GLOBAL EMPIRE**

Jason leaned closer. Even the folds of the apron followed her original pose. The printed woman hadn’t moved; the image had simply acquired a different body and outfit.

He tried a second experiment.

Near the café, an elderly man in a brown cardigan was studying a railway timetable. Across from him stood a manga display. One cover showed an adult female detective in a long raincoat, holding an open notebook beneath a streetlamp.

Jason aimed at both.

A small warning appeared:

**ILLUSTRATED HUMAN CONFIRMED.**

He pressed the button.

The elderly man kept his lined face, round spectacles, and thoughtful frown. His body and clothes became those of the detective, rendered as ordinary flesh and fabric rather than ink. The long raincoat brushed against his chair.

He turned a page of the timetable.

On the manga cover, the detective retained her sharply drawn face and intent expression. Her new cardigan-clad body occupied precisely the same stance as before, one hand still supporting the notebook beneath the illustrated streetlamp.

Jason checked the notebook. Its angle hadn’t shifted at all.

Then he noticed another copy of the same manga farther down the shelf.

That cover had changed too.

So had every copy behind it.

For a moment, his thumb hovered over the button. He opened one of the books. The detective inside still wore her raincoat.

Only the covers.

“Finding everything all right?”

Ben had come around the display, carrying a stack of bookmarks.

Jason hastily lowered the remote. “Just looking.”

“Take your time.”

As Ben walked away, Jason examined the display again. Beneath the targeting symbols, a number had appeared:

**MATCHING COVERS UPDATED: 38,416**

His grin faded.

He had thought he was experimenting with one magazine and one book.

The remote, apparently, had been working on the entire print run.

# El jardín de la armonía 🌼

**Cuento para niños de primero**

En la escuela de Ana había un pequeño jardín. Cada niño cuidaba una planta.

Una mañana, Ana quiso poner su flor amarilla en el centro.

—¡Mi flor debe estar aquí! —dijo.

—¡No! ¡Aquí va la mía! —respondió Tomás, que tenía una flor roja.

Los dos empezaron a discutir. Mientras tanto, Sara esperaba con una pequeña planta de flores blancas.

La profesora se acercó y les preguntó:

—¿Han escuchado cómo cantan los pájaros? Cada uno tiene una voz diferente, pero juntos hacen una canción hermosa. Nosotros también podemos vivir en armonía.

—¿Qué es la armonía? —preguntó Ana.

—Es vivir con respeto, amor y paz. No significa que todos pensemos igual, sino que aprendamos a escucharnos y a cuidarnos. La armonía empieza en nuestro corazón y se nota en lo que hacemos.

Ana respiró despacio y escuchó a Tomás. Él quería poner su flor donde recibiera suficiente luz.

—Podemos buscar un lugar bueno para las dos plantas —propuso Ana.

—¡Sí! Y también para la planta de Sara —respondió Tomás.

Los tres organizaron las materas sin dejar ninguna por fuera. Después, compartieron la regadera y limpiaron juntos el jardín.

Antes de regresar al salón, guardaron un momento de silencio. Escucharon los pájaros, sintieron el viento y dieron gracias por la naturaleza y por su amistad.

—Nuestro jardín tiene flores diferentes y todas son importantes —dijo Sara.

Ana sonrió. Había descubierto que la armonía no era hacer todo a su manera, sino ayudar a que todos se sintieran escuchados y queridos.

**Enseñanza:** La armonía es un valor espiritual que cultivamos cuando llenamos nuestro corazón de paz y tratamos con amor y respeto a los demás y a la naturaleza.

*Lee cada pregunta con ayuda de tu docente o familiar. Marca una sola respuesta.*

### 1. ¿Dónde ocurre la historia?
A. En una playa.  
B. En el jardín de la escuela.  
C. En una tienda.

### 2. ¿Por qué discutieron Ana y Tomás?
A. Porque querían poner sus flores en el mismo lugar.  
B. Porque no encontraban sus cuadernos.  
C. Porque querían ir a casa.

### 3. ¿Para qué habló la profesora sobre los pájaros?
A. Para enseñarles a volar.  
B. Para pedirles que cantaran fuerte.  
C. Para mostrarles que pueden ser diferentes y vivir en armonía.

### 4. ¿Qué hizo Ana para ayudar a resolver el problema?
A. Escondió la flor de Tomás.  
B. Escuchó a Tomás y propuso una solución.  
C. Se llevó todas las plantas.

### 5. ¿Cuál de estas acciones muestra armonía?
A. Compartir la regadera y cuidar juntos el jardín.  
B. Gritar para conseguir el mejor lugar.  
C. Dejar a Sara sin espacio para su planta.

### 6. ¿Qué aprendieron los niños?
A. Que todas las flores deben tener el mismo color.  
B. Que solo una persona puede cuidar el jardín.  
C. Que todos son importantes y merecen respeto.

### 7. Si tú y un compañero quieren usar el mismo color, ¿qué puedes hacer para vivir en armonía?
A. Quitárselo de la mano.  
B. Conversar y acordar turnos para usarlo.  
C. Esconderlo para que nadie lo use.

### മഴയുടെ കണക്ക്

രണ്ടായിരത്തിയിരുപത്തൊന്നിലെ മഴയ്ക്ക് ഒരു മര്യാദയുമില്ലായിരുന്നു. രാത്രി വന്നാൽ രാവിലെ പോകണം എന്നില്ല. വന്നുകേറി താമസമാണ്. വാടകയില്ല. വൈദ്യുതിക്കാശില്ല.

എന്റെ വീട്ടിൽ അന്ന് മൂന്നു പാത്രങ്ങളുണ്ടായിരുന്നു. ചോറുവെക്കാൻ ഒന്ന്. കറിവെക്കാൻ ഒന്ന്. മേൽക്കൂരയിൽനിന്നു വീഴുന്ന വെള്ളം പിടിക്കാൻ ഒന്ന്.

മഴ കനത്തപ്പോൾ മൂന്നിനും ഒരേ പണിയായി.

“ഇനി ചോറോ?”

ഭാര്യ ചോദിച്ചു.

“വെള്ളം കുറയട്ടെ.”

“വയറ്റിലെ വിശപ്പും വെള്ളം കുറയുന്നതു നോക്കി നിക്കുവല്ലേ!”

അതു ശരിയായിരുന്നു. പക്ഷേ ശരിയായ കാര്യങ്ങൾക്കെല്ലാം മറുപടി പറയേണ്ട ആവശ്യമുണ്ടോ?

ഞാൻ വാതിൽക്കൽ ഇരുന്നു മഴയെ നോക്കി. അപ്പോഴാണ് അബ്ദുക്ക വന്നത്. തലയിൽ പ്ലാസ്റ്റിക് സഞ്ചി. മുഖത്ത് മാസ്‌ക്. കൈയിൽ നനഞ്ഞൊരു പൊതിയും.

“എന്താ പൊതീല്?”

“നിനക്കുള്ളതല്ല.”

എനിക്കു സമാധാനമായി. എനിക്കുള്ളതാണെങ്കിൽ ഒന്നുകിൽ കടത്തിന്റെ കണക്കായിരിക്കും. അല്ലെങ്കിൽ പഞ്ചായത്തിൽനിന്നുള്ള നോട്ടീസ്.

അബ്ദുക്ക പൊതി തുറന്നു. നാലു ചൂടൻ പഴംപൊരി.

“തിന്ന്.”

“എനിക്കുള്ളതല്ലെന്നു പറഞ്ഞിട്ട്?”

“ചോദിക്കുമ്പഴേക്കും എല്ലാം പറയണോ?”

ഞങ്ങൾ രണ്ടെണ്ണം വീതം എടുത്തു. ഭാര്യ വാതിൽക്കൽ വന്നുനിന്നു. ഞാൻ എന്റെ കൈയിലെ ഒരെണ്ണം അവൾക്കു നീട്ടി.

“എനിക്കു വേണ്ട,” അവൾ പറഞ്ഞു.

ഞാൻ തിരികെയെടുക്കാൻ തുടങ്ങിയപ്പോൾ അവൾ വാങ്ങി.

മഴ മുറ്റത്തേക്കു കയറി. വഴിയും തോടും തമ്മിലുള്ള അതിർത്തി പോയി. ഒരു ചെരുപ്പ് വെള്ളത്തിലൂടെ ഒഴുകിവന്നു.

“നിന്റെതാണോ?” അബ്ദുക്ക ചോദിച്ചു.

“അല്ല. എന്റേതാണെങ്കിൽ മറ്റേതും പിന്നാലെ വരും. ഒറ്റയ്ക്കു സഞ്ചരിക്കാനുള്ള ത്രാണിയില്ല.”

അബ്ദുക്ക ചിരിച്ചില്ല. അങ്ങേപ്പുറത്തെ വീടുകളിലേക്കു നോക്കിയിരിക്കുകയായിരുന്നു.

“സൈനബാടെ വീട്ടില് വെള്ളം കേറി,” അയാൾ പറഞ്ഞു. “ഓളും കുട്ടിയും പള്ളിക്കൂടത്തിലേക്കു പോയി.”

ഭാര്യ അകത്തേക്കു പോയി. മടങ്ങിവന്നപ്പോൾ ഒരു പൊതിയുണ്ടായിരുന്നു. ഞങ്ങളുടെ അവസാനത്തെ അരി.

“ഇതു കൊണ്ടോയ്ക്കൊടുക്ക്.”

ഞാൻ അവളെ നോക്കി.

“നാളെ നമുക്കോ?”

“നാളെ നിങ്ങള് ചോദിച്ചുകൊണ്ടുവാ.”

അബ്ദുക്ക അരിയും വാങ്ങി മഴയിലേക്കിറങ്ങി. കുറച്ചുദൂരം ചെന്നിട്ട് തിരിഞ്ഞുനിന്നു.

“പഴംപൊരീടെ കാശ് നിന്റെ കണക്കിലിട്ടിട്ടുണ്ട്!”

“എത്ര?”

മഴയുടെ ഒച്ചയിൽ മറുപടി കേട്ടില്ല.

ഞാൻ വാതിലടച്ചില്ല. അബ്ദുക്ക തിരിച്ചു വരുമ്പോൾ ചായ കൊടുക്കണം. ചായപ്പൊടി അയാളോടു തന്നെ വാങ്ങിക്കൊണ്ടുവരാൻ പറഞ്ഞില്ലല്ലോ എന്നു പിന്നെയാണ് ഓർത്തത്.

*These stories are fictional, but their setting is historical. One distinction matters: the German-held enclave around Chania remained under occupation until the surrender of 9 May 1945, effective the following day. Afterward, British arrangements temporarily left German troops armed pending disarmament and removal; maintaining order and preventing weapons from reaching ELAS were among British concerns. Italians on Crete had varied circumstances after Italy’s 1943 armistice, including service under German control and compulsory labor.*

### 1. The Price of a Bell  
*Outside Chania, March 1945*

Every morning, Paolo counted the transport mules. Every morning, his German supervisor counted them again, as though an Italian could not be trusted with numbers smaller than twelve.

There were eleven.

The twelfth had died in February, but its ration remained on a piece of paper. Paolo regarded that paper as the most generous animal in Crete.

He exchanged part of its barley allowance for potatoes, and some potatoes for olive oil. The oil went to a woman who repaired his trousers. Nothing traveled in a straight line anymore except German orders, which generally arrived at places where they could not be obeyed.

One afternoon, a man brought him a goat.

“Found wandering,” the man said.

“With a rope around its neck?”

“It was a very orderly goat.”

Paolo paid with salt and a German army blanket. By evening, he had exchanged the goat for wine, onions, and a promise of eggs.

The difficulty began next morning when a widow named Despina arrived at the mule yard carrying a small brass bell.

“My goat wears this,” she said.

“Then your goat is elsewhere.”

“I removed it yesterday because the clapper was broken.”

Paolo looked toward his supervisor’s hut.

Despina followed his glance. “You can fetch him. Then I shall tell him about the barley.”

For the first time in months, Paolo wished the twelfth mule were alive.

They went to the village secretary, whose office possessed a cracked portrait, three kinds of obsolete forms, and no authority that armed men were obliged to respect.

The secretary heard both sides.

“Was the goat stolen?” he asked.

“Almost certainly,” Paolo admitted.

“Excellent. We have established something.”

Recovering it required the return of the blanket, two bottles of wine, and onions already simmering in somebody’s supper. The secretary substituted potatoes for the onions and wrote the settlement on the back of an occupation requisition.

On the way home, Despina’s nephew emerged from an orange grove. Paolo recognized the concealed bulk beneath his jacket.

“Next time,” the young guerrilla said, “bring cartridges.”

“Next time,” Despina replied, “he brings eggs. You cannot feed your cousins cartridges.”

Paolo returned after dark. His supervisor demanded to know where he had been.

“Transport difficulties.”

That night, Despina left three eggs beside the mule-yard gate. Paolo ate one, traded one, and kept the third until morning simply for the pleasure of possessing tomorrow’s breakfast.

End of 1st story

### 2. The Book of Receipts  
*The foothills south of Chania, April 1945*

Maria kept two notebooks beneath the counter of her father’s shop.

In the first she recorded ordinary debts: oil, salt, potatoes, a little wine.

In the second she recorded what men with weapons took.

She had begun by separating Germans from Greeks. By April, she separated those who gave receipts from those who did not. Neither category paid very often.

A German foraging party arrived before noon: four soldiers, a corporal, and an Italian laborer pushing a handcart with a crooked wheel.

The corporal wanted poultry.

“We have no poultry,” Maria said.

A hen answered from the courtyard.

The Italian closed his eyes.

They took the hen, a sack of potatoes, and two tins of oil. The corporal offered a requisition slip bearing an impressive stamp. Maria entered its number carefully.

“You expect payment?” the Italian asked quietly.

“No. I expect to remember.”

At the bend above the village, shots broke out.

Maria dropped behind the counter. Her father, whose knees seldom permitted haste, reached the floor before she did.

The firing lasted less than a minute. Then came shouts, a mule screaming somewhere, and the grinding wheel of the abandoned cart.

At dusk, her brother Nikos appeared with another guerrilla. They carried a wounded companion on a shutter.

“We stopped them taking the food,” he said.

“Did you?”

He looked at the empty shelf.

Maria boiled water. Her father tore strips from the least worn sheet in the house. The wounded man bit on a folded belt while the other guerrilla held the lamp.

Beyond the doorway, villagers argued in whispers about retaliation. They had lived through enough occupation to understand that a brief exchange of fire could leave consequences far beyond the men who fired. News of shootings and punitive raids still reached them, even as everyone said Germany was finished.

“Move him before dawn,” Maria told her brother.

“He may not survive the journey.”

“He may not survive staying.”

Later, the village president arrived. He wanted names for a petition stating that the inhabitants had taken no part in the attack.

Nikos stood in the dark behind the storeroom curtain.

Maria signed.

Before dawn, the wounded man was carried uphill. At sunrise, the Italian returned alone with the empty handcart. Without looking at her, he placed one tin of oil on the counter.

“It fell off,” he said.

She did not thank him aloud.

In her second notebook she crossed out one tin, leaving the original entry readable beneath the line.

End of 2nd story

### 3. Surrender, with Inventory  
*Chania enclave, May 1945*

The war ended for Sergeant Arthur Bell in a room containing six chairs, seven men, and nobody willing to sit first.

He had arrived with a small British party after the surrender. Back in Britain, people were celebrating. Here, a German sentry still stood outside with a rifle.

Bell glanced at the sentry, then at the German quartermaster.

“Yes,” the quartermaster said in English. “We have noticed the contradiction.”

Bell’s instructions concerned inventories, depots, guards, and the arrangements preceding removal. Weapons were not to disappear into the countryside. Until Allied arrangements caught up with the surrender, German personnel continued guarding stores with German weapons.

It was an arrangement that could be explained in a headquarters memorandum more easily than in a Cretan street.

The Greek interpreter, Eleni, translated the discussion for a local official.

“Ask when our police take over,” the official said.

Bell consulted his papers.

The official watched him. “That is not an answer.”

“No,” Bell admitted. “It is where I hoped to find one.”

Outside, an Italian cook named Vittorio was making soup from potatoes and greens. He had been told to prepare meals for a hundred men, then sixty, then ninety-three. Surrender, he observed, had not improved military arithmetic.

An ELAS veteran waited beyond the gate. He had come down from a nearby village to ask about a missing relative and the return of requisitioned livestock. The sentry barred his way.

Eleni went out before the argument grew louder.

“He stood here last week,” the veteran said, pointing at the German. “Now you tell me he stands here because the British want him here.”

“For the stores,” she said.

“My brother is not a store.”

She brought him inside.

The quartermaster had lists of flour, fuel, ammunition, boots, and veterinary supplies. He had no list that answered the man’s question. Bell wrote down the missing relative’s name, careful not to promise news.

Then they returned to the weapons inventory.

One machine gun was missing.

The quartermaster became rigid. Bell stopped writing. The Greek official gave a small, humorless nod, as though this confirmed something.

Vittorio was summoned because he had been seen near the store.

“I moved it,” he said.

“Why?”

“Rain through the roof.”

“Where?”

“Under my bed.”

They found it there, wrapped in sacking, beside six oranges and a saucepan.

By evening the inventory had advanced twelve pages. The veteran left with a written acknowledgment of his inquiry, not an answer. The local official left with another appointment.

Vittorio served the soup.

Eleni carried a bowl to the interpreter’s table and another to the man guarding the gate. She disliked that second journey, but made it.

Next morning, there would still be armed Germans outside Chania. There would also be another British lorry, another meeting, and another list. For now, Bell put down his pencil and ate before his soup went cold.

End of 3rd story

# Eternal Love

### Verse 1
You left your coffee cooling by the door,  
I heard your footsteps cross the kitchen floor.  
No grand arrival, just an ordinary day—  
Then you smiled, and the silence slipped away.  

### Verse 2
We learned each other slowly, scar by scar,  
Made a little home beneath the city stars.  
With empty pockets and a window full of rain,  
We found a thousand ways to choose again.  

### Chorus
I’ll love you when the summer leaves the trees,  
When silver fills your hair like winter seas.  
When years have changed the faces that we knew,  
I’ll find another way to fall for you.  
Let every season take what seasons do—  
My heart will keep a place made just for you.  

### Bridge
And if the words grow harder to recall,  
We’ll leave our photographs along the hall.  
I’ll sit beside you, let the record play,  
And ask you for a dance like yesterday.  

### Verse 3
One day we’ll move a little slower down the street,  
Still matching every other step our feet can meet.  
You’ll steal my scarf; I’ll say it looks like rain,  
And take the long way home with you again.  

### Chorus
I’ll love you when the summer leaves the trees,  
When silver fills your hair like winter seas.  
When years have changed the faces that we knew,  
I’ll find another way to fall for you.  
Let every season take what seasons do—  
My heart will keep a place made just for you.  

### Outro
Leave your coffee; come and watch the morning rise.  
There’s that same familiar sunlight in your eyes.  
Forever starts the way it always does:  
Another day, another choice for us.

“Let go! Oh my gosh—let go of me!”

Kessa’s wings hammered the water. Below her, the young plesiosaur tightened her grip and rolled one dark eye upward.

“Maybe,” she said around her captive, “don’t skim my lagoon.”

“I was catching a fish!”

“Yeah? So was I.”

Kessa screamed as the teeth at her abdomen caught more firmly. Her wingtip slapped the plesiosaur’s cheek, throwing spray over them both.

“I can’t get any lift! Everything hurts!”

Above the lagoon, two other pterosaurs circled so tightly their shadows kept crossing.

“Okay, this is literally a nightmare,” Velli cried. “Kessa, pull up!”

“What do you think I’m trying to do?”

“I don’t know! I can see your wings going, but you’re not—”

“Velli, stop narrating!” said Sira.

“Well, help her!”

Sira swooped toward the water, saw the long neck turn, and climbed again.

“I can’t. I’m sorry, Kess. I can’t get close.”

The plesiosaur gave a muffled laugh.

“Smart friend.”

Something struck her left foreflipper.

Her jaws opened.

Kessa tore free with a shriek and beat at the surface, half flying, half scrambling across it.

“What—hey!” The plesiosaur twisted. A young mosasaur had clamped onto her flipper. His tail thrashed so hard that bubbles streamed along his sides.

“I got her!” he called, his words blurring through the water. “Mother, I got her, but she’s pulling!”

“Keep your body straight, Renn.”

The answering voice came from deeper water.

A second young mosasaur flashed beneath the plesiosaur and seized her other foreflipper.

The plesiosaur cried out.

“Seriously? Two on one?”

“She’s stronger than the fish,” the second hunter said. “Much stronger.”

“Of course she is, Mira,” their mother replied. “Don’t wrestle against her whole body. Turn with her.”

Overhead, Kessa finally caught the air.

“I’m up,” she gasped. “I’m up. Don’t touch me.”

“We’re not touching you,” said Sira, flying close enough to steady her if she fell.

“I know. Just—everything feels awful.”

A thin red trail washed away below her.

The plesiosaur plunged, dragging both young hunters beneath the surface.

“You picked the wrong girl,” she shouted. “I’m not some slow old turtle!”

Renn’s grip slipped.

For an instant she was free on one side. She swung her neck, struck at him, and missed as he recoiled.

“That almost got my face!”

“Then stop hanging around my face!”

“Renn,” said his mother, “behind her.”

He darted past the sweeping neck and caught the plesiosaur at the hindquarters.

She jerked forward with a sharp cry.

“Oh—that feels different,” Renn said, startled. “Softer. Sort of squishy.”

“Keep your attention on her movements.”

“I am! I just didn’t expect—”

The plesiosaur lashed her rear flipper into his shoulder.

“Ow!”

“Good!” she snapped.

Mira released the foreflipper only long enough to dive beneath her. The next bite caught the plesiosaur’s vulnerable underside.

Her whole body buckled.

“No! Get off!”

“I’ve got her,” Mira said, though she sounded frightened now. “I think I’ve got her.”

The plesiosaur lunged upward. She broke the surface with both hunters still attached, dragging a sheet of water behind her.

“Help!” she shouted.

The word surprised even her.

Above, Velli faltered in mid-flap.

“Oh, now she wants help.”

“Not so smug anymore,” Sira called.

Kessa landed awkwardly on a low rock. She held her wings out for balance, trembling.

“You bit me!” she cried. “You don’t get to act like this is unfair!”

“I wasn’t talking to you!”

The plesiosaur bent her neck beneath herself and caught Mira near the shoulder.

Mira squealed but did not release her.

“It hurts! Mother, she’s biting me!”

“Move closer to her body. Give her less room.”

“I’m trying!”

The plesiosaur bit again. Mira flinched, her tail beating wildly.

For a moment the pressure beneath the plesiosaur eased.

“Yes,” she gasped. “That’s right. Let go.”

But Mira shifted closer instead.

“I can still hold,” she said, almost to herself. “I can still hold.”

“Together now,” their mother instructed. “Down and turn.”

Renn pulled. Mira followed.

The plesiosaur’s head struck the surface sideways.

“Wait—wait!”

Her flippers churned, one stroke missing its rhythm, then another. She stretched her neck toward the air, toward the bright patch between the circling wings.

“I can’t—”

Water closed over her voice.

On the rock, Kessa stared at the spreading ripples.

Velli landed beside her. “Well. Maybe don’t skim her lagoon.”

No one laughed.

A few bubbles rose. Farther out, a dark tail passed beneath the surface.

“Did we do it?” Renn asked below.

Their mother watched until the struggling stopped.

“Yes.”

Mira finally loosened her jaws.

“My shoulder hurts,” she said quietly. “I thought she was going to make me let go.”

Above them, Sira folded her wings.

“Can you fly home, Kess?”

Kessa looked once more at the empty water.

“Not yet,” she said. “Just sit with me.”

从歌曲创作的角度看，这首词有一个值得保留的核心：**借“潘金莲”的戏中形象，写一个普通女子从错付感情到找回自我的过程。**“戏台、红袖、人群、背影”也有画面感，适合发展成一首带戏曲元素的流行情歌。

但目前更像一篇已经表达清楚主题的抒情文字，距离容易被唱出来、被记住的歌词，还需要做几处关键调整。

## 一、先明确：“我不是潘金莲”，究竟要表达什么？

这是整首歌最有辨识度的一句，但现在它承担了几种不同含义：

- 第一段：我没有她的妖娆；
- 第一遍副歌：我不敢放肆爱恨；
- 第二遍副歌：我不需要惊天动地的爱情；
- 结尾：我要寻找真正适合我的人。

这些意思并不完全冲突，但核心有些分散。建议统一为：

> **我不是你安排的戏中人，也不愿为一段不属于我的感情失去自己。**

这样，“潘金莲”就不只是一个吸引注意的名字，而能与“戏台、角色、看客、散场”等意象形成完整的表达。

另外，“你是谁的西门庆”会让听众自然联想到背叛、欲望或不忠。如果故事只是在写单恋，这个人物比喻就可能显得过重。**要么把对方的薄情写得更具体，要么适当弱化“西门庆”，把重点放在“戏里戏外”的关系上。**

## 二、主歌：保留画面，减少直接解释

开头的戏台很好，但后面很快进入“平凡女子渴望爱情”的概括，画面没有继续推进。

原句：

> 我站在人群边缘，遇见了你的背影，  
> 却发现你眼中的光，不是为我而停。

这里从“背影”直接跳到“眼中的光”，视角略有断裂。可以补一个转身动作，例如：

> 我站在人群边缘，看你回身笑得轻，  
> 才知你眼底的光，落在另一个身影。

这只是示意，重点是：**让听众看见“我为什么伤心”，而不只是听见“我很伤心”。**

原句：

> 只是一个平凡的女子，渴望爱的怀抱。

意思明确，但比较通用。可以换成有动作、有生活感的表达，例如：

> 我只盼散场以后，有人为我等一等。

这一句既表达了渴望陪伴，也延续了开头的戏台场景。

## 三、预副歌：不要提前把情绪放下

现在的预副歌中：

> 我不奢求天长地久，只愿这一刻停留

已经有“退让、接受”的感觉；紧接着第一遍副歌又说“如今已不再执念”，情绪释放得太早，第二段便缺少继续发展的空间。

建议把情绪推进调整为：

**主歌一：看见他心有所属 → 预副歌：明知不该仍想靠近 → 副歌一：承认疼痛 → 主歌二：开始清醒 → 最后副歌：主动离开。**

例如，预副歌可以向这种矛盾感靠拢：

> 明知你的目光，从没为我停留，  
> 我却把一句问候，听成了天长地久。

另外，“让我们擦肩又别走”语义不够明确。如果想表达离别，可以改成“让我们相逢以后，又各自远走”；如果想表达挽留，就要明确“我想说别走”。

## 四、副歌：统一骨架，让记忆点真正留下来

目前两遍副歌几乎是两套歌词，句长也差异明显。若使用同一段旋律，填唱会比较困难；听众也不容易形成记忆。

建议：

- 两遍副歌保留相同的句式与核心句；
- 第一遍写“舍不得”，最后一遍写“终于舍得”；
- 只替换关键的两三句，制造成长感。

例如，可以把副歌往这个方向打磨：

> 我不是潘金莲，  
> 不必照着你的戏文上演，  
> 你把温柔留给谁的眉眼，  
> 我却还等在散场的屋檐。  
> 我不是潘金莲，  
> 也会为一句承诺失眠，  
> 明知你不会回到我身边，  
> 还舍不得说一句再见。

最后一遍保留前面的骨架，把结尾改成：

> 我把没说完的话留给昨天，  
> 这一次不再等你回到身边，  
> 散场以后，我也能走远。

这不是建议直接定稿，而是示范：**重复负责让人记住，变化负责让人感动。**

## 五、语言：少用结论，多给细节

以下几处建议重点精简：

| 原句 | 修改方向 |
|---|---|
| “你是谁的传说，我只是路过的过客” | “路过”和“过客”重复；“传说”也比较虚，可改成具体关系或动作。 |
| “深深的烙印，却又随风而逝” | “烙印”强调难以消失，“随风而逝”却强调消散，要说清消失的是人、承诺还是感情。 |
| “只在夜里飘散如梦” | “夜里、飘散、如梦”都偏朦胧，叠加后反而没有明确画面。 |
| “平凡人生自有我的精彩” | 偏口号，可以写一个“我开始为自己生活”的具体动作。 |
| “不需要那虚假的角色” | 可改为“不再演你要的角色”，表达更主动，也更贴合戏台意象。 |

“不羡慕那错误的情”也建议改。“错误”是在替听众下判断，不如写出代价，例如“不要靠谁的眼泪成全”。这样更有情感，也更耐听。

## 六、结尾：不必急着安排“幸福结局”

目前的结尾：

> 我会找到那个对的人，陪我走向幸福的结局。

意思积极，但比较常见，而且容易让“自我成长”又落回“等另一个人来完成”。

更有力量的结尾，是她暂时没有遇见谁，却已经能够独自离开：

> 戏台的灯一盏盏熄灭，  
> 我走出人群，不再回头看。

这会与开篇形成呼应：**开始时，她站在人群边缘看他；结束时，她走出人群，回到自己的人生。**

## 歌名建议

目前歌名空缺，可以考虑：

- **《我不是潘金莲》**：辨识度最高，但正文必须把这个人物借喻写透。
- **《不演你的戏》**：主题更直接，也更容易让不同听众代入。
- **《散场以后》**：偏抒情，适合突出从错爱到释然的过程。

**我最建议的修改方向是：保留“我不是潘金莲”这个钩子，贯穿“戏台—入戏—散场”的意象，删去泛泛的爱情宣言，让主人公用行动完成转变。**这首词不缺主题，真正需要增加的是具体性、情绪层次和可反复吟唱的副歌。

### Оливье и спор о главном

Под Новый год, в салатнице хрустальной,
Затеял спор Горошек скандальный:
— Без нас салат — не праздничный обед!
Мы — украшенье! Нам и равных нет!

— Подумаешь! — фыркнула Картошка. —
Да вас кладут-то — маленькую ложку.
А я кормлю! Без сытности моей
Хозяева не соберут гостей.

Морковка заявила:
— Я всех вас нарядила!
А Огурец заметил:
— Зато я за вкус в ответе!

— Ну, хватит! — Колбаса сказала строго. —
Вас без меня не съели бы и много.
— А я нежней любого молодца! —
Вступили в спор кусочки от Яйца.

Тут Майонез воскликнул:
— Что за спесь!
Да я один связую вас здесь всех!

И каждый так раздулся от почёта,
Что стал считать других за недочёты.
Решили: «Врозь покажем, кто важней!» —
И разошлись по блюдцам поскорей.

Пришли к столу домашние гурьбою.
Хозяйка только всплеснула рукою:
— Всё нарезала, а смешать забыла!
И ложкой спорщиков соединила.

Салат смели. Хвалили всей семьёй.
А кто в нём главный — не спросил никто.

**Мораль:**
Коль общее для каждого — лишь повод похвалиться,
Не выйдет ничего, пока не прекратится
Спор о заслугах — громкий, но пустой.
Хорош салат не частью, а собой.

**Refinement**  
Give each sensory element a practical job. Sound locates trouble. Texture guides a hand. Repetition measures rising water. Keep the danger physical and the outcome earned.

**Final prompt**  
Build a scene in which language changes behavior under pressure: dialogue stays spare; objects acquire force through compound verbs; spacing measures distance; punctuation carries impacts. ### Style synopsis: **Impact Weave**

Three kinds of expression share the scene:

- **Contact:** compressed, tactile sentences for whatever touches the body.
- **Signal:** speech, mechanical noise, and recurring words that register changes.
- **Travel:** spatially stretched phrases for movement across a room or through water.

Transitions happen through shared material: the vibration of a washer becomes vibration in a window; the window’s tapping becomes rain against a wrist. Invented compounds name precise actions rather than decorate them. Brief, ordinary dialogue keeps the scene anchored.

**DOOR → CURB**

She opens the door against the shove.

Rain pinpricks the warm strip inside her collar.

Left hand: railing.

Right hand: broom.

She advances by broom-depth:

tap  
step  
tap  
step

Under the water, the curb is still exactly where the curb was. This feels useful enough to trust.

She finds the drain with the broom handle.

Iron answers.

tak.

Another inch.

tak.

Then something soft.

The handle springs back.

From inside, her daughter has the phone torch against the window.

Its light reaches Mara in a trembling white sleeve.

“Lower.”

The sleeve drops.

“Stay.”

---

Mara kneels.

Water chin-slaps the glove cuffs.

Her fingers go into the brown and come back wearing leaves.

Again:

a crisp packet  
black hair  
a rope of grass

Something round stays wedged beneath the grate.

She presses.

It gives, then fills the gap again.

A tennis ball.

Wet felt. Split rubber. Swollen tight between two bars.

She hooks a finger into the split.

Pulls.

The ball bites the glove.

Pulls harder.

Yellow felt peels off in a strip.

Across the road, a car alarm begins its useless employment.

wee—  
wee—  
wee—

“Coat hanger!” Mara shouts.

---

Her daughter appears in the doorway with six.

“Stay on the step.”

“I am on the step.”

“Your toes aren’t.”

The toes withdraw.

Mara takes the wire bundle. Twists one hanger open against the railing. Bends its end into a narrow hook.

Back down.

Left hand flat on iron.

Right hand fishing through the ball’s torn mouth.

The hook catches rubber.

She winds the wire around the broom handle.

Turns.

Her forearms cord.

Turns.

The ball stretches a black tongue between the bars.

Then—

**pock**

Small sound.

Ridiculous sound.

The gutter drops beneath her wrist.

---

First a fist-sized hollow.

Then a turning bowl.

Leaves nose-dive. The crisp packet snaps straight and vanishes. Water rubs gravel over iron with the sound of a drawer full of cutlery being shut slowly.

Mara gets up.

One knee objects.

The other takes her weight.

She carries the burst tennis ball at arm’s length.

Her daughter opens the door.

“That?”

“That.”

They look at it.

Rain drips from its fur.

**22:18**

The floor squeegee makes long rubber complaints.

They push the street back outside.

Brown stripe. Clear stripe.

Brown stripe. Clear.

Under machine four, the girl finds a pound coin and a blue plastic dinosaur. She washes both in the sink.

Mara checks the outlets, leaves the breakers off, hangs the yellow gloves fingers-down.

The orange is still on the folding table.

Her daughter peels it.

One bright oil-pop catches Mara just below the eye.

“Sorry.”

“Give me half.”

They sit above the wet floor, eating.

Behind them, the blue towel waits with one corner folded.
