"Stay still! The Chromatic-alizator is not stuck to your skin yet," the... let's call him minion of municipal education said, chasing my left cheek with a device that looked like a waffle iron designed by a committee of nervous dentists.

“That sentence contains a very worrying ‘yet,’” I said.

“Would you prefer it be stuck incorrectly?”

“I would prefer to be in chemistry.”

Behind me, twenty-seven of my classmates stood beneath a sign reading:

**WELCOME TO EXTERIOR CORRECTION FACILITY 8**  
**YOUR INSIDE IS ALREADY SPECIAL.**  
**WE HAVE NOT BEEN AUTHORIZED TO VERIFY THIS.**

Our homeroom teacher, Ms. Endo, counted us with the expression she wore whenever she suspected the school had obtained something through a grant.

“Everyone,” she said, “please cooperate. The district has already paid for the standard package.”

“What’s the standard package?” asked Jun.

The minion looked up from his waffle iron.

“Linework, complexion simplification, ocular expressiveness, follicular silhouette, and basic chromatic reassignment.”

“And lunch?”

“Not in the standard package.”

A more genuine silence of horror settled over the class.

That morning, I had been an ordinary, realistically proportioned high school student. My hair was brown in the uninteresting way of wet cardboard. My face possessed pores, asymmetries, and the faint red indentation left by sleeping on a textbook. Light fell on me continuously. When I turned my head, every intermediate position occurred.

By four o’clock, all of that would be administratively unacceptable.

***

The trouble had begun with a district zoning change.

Our school stood on the border between the Realist Residential Quarter and the newly expanded Animated Youth Development Zone. As of Monday, the entire campus had been reclassified.

The buildings had adapted overnight. Windows sparkled. Cherry trees appeared along a street that had previously contained four vending machines and an angry shrub. Our principal’s office acquired a dramatic view of the sunset, despite facing north.

Students, unfortunately, required processing.

“Think of it as a uniform adjustment,” Ms. Endo had told us on the bus.

“My uniform doesn’t usually require a cranial rendering permit,” I had said.

“Yours required three warnings about the tie, so let’s not be superior.”

Now I sat in a reclining chair inside the Exterior Correction Facility while the technician tried to adhere a silver disk to my cheek.

His name badge read **MR. KUBO — JUNIOR AESTHETIC COMPLIANCE SPECIALIST**.

Someone had written **NOT A MINION** beneath that in pen.

The disk finally attached with a damp *plip*.

“There,” he said. “Chromatic anchor established.”

My reflection in the nearby mirror acquired a tiny loading circle.

I looked away.

The loading circle remained on my cheek.

“That feels personal.”

“It’s diagnostic.”

“It’s buffering my face.”

“Only the left side.”

***

Our first stop was the **Contour Stabilization Gallery**.

It resembled a photography studio that had lost an argument with a car wash. Tall white arches stood over a conveyor belt. Between them hung delicate curtains of black filaments, each swaying without wind.

Mr. Kubo gave us disposable slippers.

“Shoes interfere with the ground-contact shadow.”

Jun raised his hand. “Can I have a more heroic shadow?”

“No.”

“A shadow with a sword?”

“No.”

“A slightly taller shadow?”

Mr. Kubo hesitated. “How much taller?”

Ms. Endo cleared her throat.

“No,” he concluded.

I stepped onto the conveyor.

A green grid climbed over my body, catching every wrinkle in my shirt and every strand of hair. A monitor displayed my rotating image beside a distressingly long list of specifications.

**SUBJECT 14: EXCESS SURFACE INFORMATION**  
**NOSE: OVEREXPLAINED**  
**HAIR: INSUFFICIENTLY DECISIVE**  
**RESTING EXPRESSION: APOLOGETIC**

“I’m not apologetic.”

The monitor changed.

**RESTING EXPRESSION: DEFENSIVELY APOLOGETIC**

“Please face forward,” Mr. Kubo said. “We’re initiating contour extraction.”

The black filaments lifted.

I felt a faint tickling around my outline, as if someone were tracing me with a pen held just beyond touching distance. Along my wrist, a narrow dark line appeared. It traveled up my sleeve, around my shoulder, and beneath my jaw.

I turned my hand.

The line stayed precisely where the edge was supposed to be.

Not on my skin. Not floating above it.

At the boundary between me and everything else.

“Oh,” I said.

For one very strange moment, my body looked both completely solid and deliberately drawn.

“External silhouette is stable,” Mr. Kubo said. “Beginning internal line hierarchy. Primary contours at two-point-three nominal widths. Facial accents at zero-point-six. Clothing folds reduced according to emotional relevance.”

“What makes a fold emotionally relevant?”

“Whether you’re clutching it while making a promise.”

Three creases vanished from my trousers.

One remained at the knee, apparently destined for greatness.

The arches hummed. My face prickled gently as unnecessary visual information softened away. The slight bump on my nose simplified into a clean, economical shape. The shadows around my eyes became two subtle marks rather than evidence that I had stayed up studying until one in the morning.

On the monitor, my realistic face was becoming a readable one.

It was still unmistakably me.

He raised it again.

My eyes looked normal. Brown irises. Slight redness. A tiny eyelash leaning the wrong way.

Dr. Sato adjusted a slider.

My reflection became considerably more awake.

The change was stranger and subtler: the visible shapes opened, my irises gained depth and clarity, and the upper lash line became a confident dark stroke. My eyebrows acquired the ability to communicate entire objections without help from the rest of my face.

I glanced at the ceiling.

The highlights didn’t move.

“It is in this jurisdiction.”

She held up a tablet.

I widened my eyes.

A tiny white flare snapped through my irises.

“Good. Skepticism.”

I thought about the school cafeteria’s claim that its fish was locally sourced.

One eyebrow rose with devastating precision.

“Excellent. Embarrassment.”

“No.”

“Very good.”

Heat touched my cheeks. Two tidy patches of pink appeared, each containing three little diagonal lines.

I scrubbed at them.

They followed my hands around.

She tapped the tablet.

The pink remained. The warmth vanished.

From the next booth, our class representative, Aya, said, “I believe my disappointment setting is too strong.”

Aya looked back.

Three technicians straightened their posture.

***

The next room smelled of warm plastic, citrus shampoo, and electrical ambition.

A sign over the door read **FOLLICULAR SILHOUETTE ENGINEERING**.

Below it, in smaller letters:

**HAIR IS A DESIGN COMMITMENT.**

We sat beneath transparent domes. Robotic combs unfolded from the ceiling with the elaborate courtesy of creatures pretending not to be spiders.

My best friend, Mei, occupied the chair beside mine.

“What are you hoping for?” she asked.

“Hair that fits through doors.”

“Yes.”

“In bed?”

“Mostly.”

The dome lowered.

Warm air swirled around my scalp. My individual strands began gathering into neat, purposeful sections. Nothing pulled painfully. It felt more like invisible fingers were arranging my hair with tremendous confidence and no interest in my opinion.

A smooth shine crossed them.

The shine looked painted.

I tilted my head.

It tilted too, but not quite according to optics.

“Your aptitude questionnaire indicated indecision under pressure.”

“How does that become lightning?”

“We try not to literalize.”

The other waited.

Then it bounced.

Mei stared.

Both locks sprang upward like startled quotation marks.

His hair had become six enormous red spikes.

He shook his head experimentally.

The spikes made an aerodynamic *fwoom*.

Mr. Kubo checked his tablet.

“Please avoid revolving doors until your profile clearance has been updated.”

Glass pipes looped across the ceiling, carrying streams of pigment that shone from within: lake blue, tangerine, lilac, emerald, the deep red of a candy apple held against sunlight. Beneath the floor, luminous rings rotated around twenty-eight circular platforms.

It looked like a wizard’s laboratory funded by a cosmetics company.

Mr. Kubo pointed at the silver disk still attached to my cheek.

“It used to drift.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Everyone onto a platform.”

Ms. Endo stood near the control desk, filling out a form.

“Remember,” she told us, “you may choose your palette. Don’t choose someone else’s to annoy them.”

Jun slowly lowered a bright pink swatch.

Aya, without turning around, said, “Thank you.”

I selected dark blue hair, brown eyes, and a slightly warmer complexion. Conservative. Sensible. A palette that might conceivably still be recognized by my grandmother.

The console rejected it.

**PALETTE ALREADY ASSIGNED TO SIX SUPPORTING STUDENTS.**

“I’m fine with that.”

**PLEASE INCREASE DISTINGUISHABILITY.**

**RELUCTANT DISTINCTIVENESS DETECTED.**

“Hey.”

**CHARACTER DESIGN IMPROVED.**

Mr. Kubo leaned over the console.

“You can override that.”

“Please do.”

He tapped twice.

The turquoise underlayer vanished.

I felt an unexpected flicker of disappointment.

He noticed.

“Would you like it back?”

I looked around to make sure no one was watching.

“Yes.”

“Very good.”

The chamber lights dimmed.

“Beginning base-tone deposition,” he announced. “We use nonmaterial chroma fields, not conventional paint. No pores are blocked. No dyes enter tissue. Your new appearance is maintained through a surface-bound spectral substitution lattice.”

A pale mist curled up around my ankles.

It didn’t wet my clothes. It passed over them like colored light becoming unusually serious.

My uniform darkened into a clean charcoal blue. The white shirt became brighter, with the shadows resolving into a soft, cool gray. My skin tone evened—not erased, not made identical to anyone else’s, but simplified into a warm base color and carefully placed accents.

A blue gleam ran through my hair.

Then a second wave passed, and the turquoise appeared beneath my fringe, vivid as shallow tropical water.

I caught my reflection in the glass.

For the first time that day, I forgot to complain.

Dr. Sato’s voice came over the speakers.

“Now applying cel-shading response. Standard package includes base, shadow, and optional dramatic shadow.”

“What’s dramatic shadow?” Mei asked.

Half her face went black.

A purple aura rose behind her.

“Oh,” she said, in a voice that somehow had reverb.

“Sorry. Demonstration mode.”

The shadow vanished.

We all laughed.

Then Jun sneezed.

His hair shed a cloud of red sparkles.

“Don’t move!” Mr. Kubo shouted.

Naturally, everyone moved.

The chamber chimed.

A ribbon of orange light jumped from Jun’s platform to Aya’s.

Aya’s hair turned brilliant vermilion.

Jun’s became a severe, scholarly black.

For one breath, nobody spoke.

Then Jun adjusted imaginary glasses.

“I suddenly feel responsible for the attendance sheet.”

Aya’s new red hair flared around her face.

“I suddenly understand why people shout his name.”

“Everyone stay calm,” Mr. Kubo said, already sweating. “We only need to flush the residual palette buffer.”

He pressed a yellow button.

My hair turned green.

Mei turned lavender.

Ms. Endo’s beige cardigan became a dazzling gradient of sunset colors.

She looked down at herself.

“Kubo.”

It was not loud.

It was faculty-grade.

The repair process took place in **Secondary Presentation**, which was what the facility called the room where mistakes went to become billable.

“Appearance isn’t only shape and pigment,” she explained. “You’ll be entering an animated environment. Your movement needs to remain legible within its temporal grammar.”

I sat on a stool, watching a small turquoise patch slowly migrate back beneath my fringe.

“Are you reducing our frame rate?”

“Not your experienced time. Your displayed time.”

“That sounds like a distinction invented by a lawyer.”

“It was reviewed by three.”

She asked me to reach for a cup.

I did.

My arm moved normally.

On the monitor, however, the gesture had become cleaner: a brief anticipation, a swift reach, a tiny settling motion at the end.

“We suppress inconsequential micro-adjustments,” she said. “Then we add key-pose emphasis.”

I reached again.

This time my hand left a faint smear of color in the air.

“Too much interpolation compensation,” she murmured.

She adjusted a dial.

I grabbed the cup.

My entire body held still for half a second while the cup sparkled triumphantly.

“Too much emphasis.”

“Why did taking water feel like winning a tournament?”

“Achievement punctuation. It should only trigger when narratively warranted.”

Behind us, Jun jumped off a low testing platform.

He hung in the air.

His arms windmilled.

“Doctor?”

“Don’t look down.”

He looked down.

He fell the remaining thirty centimeters and landed with a noise like a dropped toolbox.

There was no toolbox.

“Why did I sound expensive?” he asked from the floor.

“Impact library mismatch.”

Meanwhile, Mei discovered that sudden embarrassment could temporarily simplify her into a much smaller, rounder version of herself.

One moment she was standing beside me.

The next, she was a compact bundle of indignation with mitten-like hands and an enormous head.

“Turn it off,” she squeaked.

“I’m trying,” Dr. Sato said.

“This is not an acceptable dispute-resolution body.”

I made the mistake of laughing.

Mei pointed one tiny hand at me.

A red anger symbol appeared above her temple.

It made a sharp little *ping*.

We both stopped.

The symbol continued hovering there, mechanically sincere.

Then Mei started laughing too, which returned her to normal.

Dr. Sato made a note.

“Good. Humor provides a reliable de-escalation pathway.”

“Please don’t put that in my school record,” Mei said.

The worst problem did not appear until the final group inspection.

We stood on a white stage beneath studio lights while a scanner checked our silhouettes, palettes, and shadow behavior.

Our colors were finally correct.

Aya had chosen rich auburn hair after deciding the accidental red had “some administrative potential.” Mei kept the lavender, although she insisted she had chosen it before the malfunction. Jun was red again and had been issued a sticker reading **WIDE LOAD** for his student identification card.

I stood between them, feeling strangely good.

My uniform looked crisp. My new hair framed my face instead of apologizing for existing. Even my posture seemed easier to read.

Then the scanner reached me.

A chime sounded.

The lights dimmed.

A wind began blowing from nowhere.

My tie lifted.

Every head turned.

On the wall, in enormous letters, appeared:

**UNREGISTERED PROTAGONIST BIAS**

“No,” I said immediately.

A piano began playing.

“No.”

The white wall behind me dissolved into a sunset.

Mr. Kubo ran to the console.

“Who enabled narrative weighting?”

“I only selected distinctive fringe contrast!” Dr. Sato said.

“Did you combine it with defensive eyebrows?”

“He already had those!”

The wind intensified.

A single luminous petal drifted past my face.

We were three floors underground.

I slapped it away.

The piano became more emotional.

On the monitor, boxes began filling themselves.

**SEATING PREFERENCE: WINDOW, REAR ROW**  
**POTENTIAL SECRET: PENDING**  
**CHILDHOOD FRIEND: SEARCHING**

Mei stepped backward.

“Absolutely not. We met in April.”

**TRANSFER STUDENT ARRIVAL: SCHEDULED**

Jun raised his hand.

“Can I be the rival?”

“No!” I said.

The scanner interpreted my denial as resolve.

My eyes flashed.

Somewhere, a guitar joined the piano.

Ms. Endo walked onto the stage.

She placed one hand on my shoulder and looked directly into the scanner.

“He is number fourteen on the attendance register,” she said. “He has no secret heritage, no exceptional athletic ability, and two overdue library books.”

The music faltered.

“My sprint time isn’t that bad,” I muttered.

She tightened her hand.

“He will be doing classroom cleaning duty on Thursday.”

The sunset flickered.

Mr. Kubo seized the opportunity.

“Applying ensemble equalization! Distributing focal salience across the cohort!”

He slammed a palm onto the console.

The wind split twenty-eight ways.

Everyone’s hair fluttered.

Twenty-eight pairs of eyes caught the light.

Behind us, the sunset expanded into a bright panorama of our school, the sky enormous and blue.

For a moment, we all stood there looking extraordinary.

Not like identical attractive strangers. Like ourselves, made bold enough to be recognized from the back of a classroom.

Aya with her straight shoulders and newly dangerous eyebrows.

Jun, practically vibrating beneath his absurd red spikes.

Mei with her lavender bob, pretending she wasn’t pleased.

And me, one hand still batting irritably at a petal.

The monitor chimed.

**ENSEMBLE COMEDY CONFIGURATION ACCEPTED.**

The music switched to cheerful brass.

A bucket fell out of a ceiling hatch and landed over Mr. Kubo’s head.

He stood very still.

From inside the bucket, he said, “That is not part of the standard package.”

We left the facility at sunset.

A real sunset, I think. By then I no longer felt qualified to judge.

The street looked different.

Edges were cleaner. Colors sat beside one another with newfound confidence. Shadows gathered into broad, cool shapes beneath benches and trees. The sky held pink clouds so beautifully arranged that I wanted to accuse someone of cheating.

When I looked at my classmates, I could still remember the way they had appeared that morning: the stray hairs, uneven light, tiny details I had never consciously noticed.

None of that had made them less themselves.

Neither did this.

Jun ran toward the bus.

His legs briefly became a spinning blur.

“Brake with your knees!” Mr. Kubo shouted from the entrance.

Jun stopped one centimeter from the bus door.

His hair arrived a moment later.

Mei leaned beside me, inspecting our reflections in the windows.

“You know,” she said, “the blue suits you.”

“Thanks.”

The three pink lines appeared on each of my cheeks.

She smiled.

“Oh, that’s going to be useful.”

I covered my face.

It did nothing.

On the bus, Ms. Endo passed around our maintenance leaflets.

“Read these before tomorrow. No unauthorized palette changes. No testing impact resistance. If you develop persistent sparkles, report to the nurse.”

Aya was already highlighting sections.

Jun had drawn a sword onto his shadow-permit application.

I opened my leaflet.

**ADJUSTING TO YOUR NEW PRESENTATION**

**1. Sudden surprise may produce floating punctuation.**  
**2. Strong emotions can affect local lighting.**  
**3. Hair silhouette is not a reliable measure of door clearance.**  
**4. Internal monologue remains private unless explicitly broadcast.**

I reread the fourth point.

Below it, in very small print:

**Basic package broadcast settings default to ON.**

I sat up.

“Wait.”

Everyone turned toward me.

From the bus speakers, my own voice said:

*For the first time all day, I had begun to think the worst was over.*

Ms. Endo closed her eyes.

Mei folded in half laughing.

Jun whispered, with reverence, “He has narration.”

I lunged for the emergency settings on my wristband.

Outside, our bus drove into the golden evening.

Inside, twenty-seven people listened to me think, very clearly and at considerable volume:

*I should have stayed in chemistry.*

On the morning my life became impossible, I was carrying a slice of toast in my mouth.

I mention this because I had previously believed I possessed some dignity.

Not much. Not the dazzling, unassailable dignity of the student council president, who could probably sneeze in front of an assembly and make it sound like an official announcement. But an ordinary amount. Enough to sit in the middle of a classroom, earn middle-of-the-road grades, and pass through a school day without anyone pointing at me.

My name is Nao Fujisaki. I was sixteen, late for homeroom, and sprinting down the hill toward Mizuhara High with my schoolbag thumping against my hip.

The sky was a clear, innocent blue.

This was misleading.

At the corner beside the little neighborhood shrine, something fell out of it.

There was no ominous shadow, no crack of thunder, no mysterious voice declaring that I had been chosen. A blob of shimmering pink-and-blue jelly simply dropped through the branches of a cherry tree and landed in front of me with a noise like—

*Plorff.*

I stopped so abruptly that my loafers squeaked.

The blob quivered.

I quivered.

My toast fell out of my mouth.

An iridescent tendril shot upward, caught it, and held it out to me.

“Breakfast!” said the blob.

I stared.

The blob rose.

It gathered itself upward in a slow, wobbling fountain, its colors slipping through one another: peach pink into lagoon blue, blue into lilac, lilac into a green so pale and bright that it looked like sunlight passing through a young leaf. Arms emerged. A head rounded into shape. Two enormous eyes opened inside a translucent face, their pupils shining like little gold stars dropped into glass marbles.

Then it smiled.

There are smiles that say *good morning*.

There are smiles that say *I’m glad to meet you*.

This one said *every emotion I have ever experienced is currently happening to me at once*.

“Good morning, breakfast person!”

I took one step backward.

The girl-shaped jelly took one delighted step forward.

Her foot spread across the pavement like a spilled water balloon before pulling itself back into a foot.

Inside her, tiny crystalline shapes drifted lazily through the goo: stars, hexagons, flakes like shaved ice. Her hair was a mass of translucent ribbons that floated around her shoulders despite the complete absence of wind. Every few seconds, a spark skipped between them with a sound like the wrapper of a hard candy being crinkled.

She was beautiful in the way a fireworks accident might be beautiful.

She was also holding my toast.

“Thank you,” I said automatically.

Manners are dangerous. Nobody warns you about that.

Her eyes grew even larger.

“You answered!”

“Yes?”

“You can hear me!”

“Unfortunately.”

She gasped. Bubbles rose through her torso.

“Then it worked!”

“What worked?”

“The wish!”

“No,” I said immediately.

Her head tilted.

“I haven’t explained it yet.”

“I’m getting ahead of things.”

The first bell rang in the distance.

I looked at the school on the hill.

I looked at the magical jelly person.

Then I did what any sensible heroine would do when confronted with the beginning of her extraordinary destiny.

I ran away.

---

She followed me.

Of course she followed me.

She flowed alongside the curb in a shimmering ribbon, keeping pace with my frantic sprint and occasionally gathering herself into a girl so she could wave.

“Wait, breakfast person!”

“My name is not Breakfast Person!”

“What is it?”

“Not relevant!”

“That’s a difficult name!”

Two elementary-school children stopped on the sidewalk.

“Whoa,” one whispered.

“Is that a new mascot?” asked the other.

“I love your mascot!” the first shouted at me.

“It isn’t mine!”

The jelly girl looked wounded.

This would have been easier to ignore if her entire body had not turned a melancholy shade of blue.

Something squeezed unpleasantly beneath my ribs.

I hated it.

I hated that I noticed.

“I mean,” I said, slowing despite myself, “you can’t follow me into school.”

Her colors brightened.

“Where should I follow you?”

“Nowhere.”

“Is that far?”

I pressed both hands over my face.

By the time we reached the school gate, I had learned three facts.

First, she was called Lulumi.

Second, she came from somewhere called the Upper Shimmer, which was apparently “above the rain but beneath the places where wishes get stuck.”

Third, she had absolutely no concept of personal embarrassment.

“Your heart is making very fast noises, Nao!” she announced as we approached the shoe lockers.

“Yes. It’s preparing to leave my body.”

“Should I catch it?”

“Please don’t say things like that at school.”

She nodded gravely.

Then she stepped directly through the closed entrance door.

The glass rang like a struck wineglass.

A thin rainbow film remained on it for half a second before vanishing.

From inside, I heard someone scream.

It was Daichi Morita from my class.

Daichi was on the basketball team, stood almost a head taller than me, and had once claimed he could handle any emergency.

Apparently that excluded iridescent girls passing through windows.

---

I had a strategy for school.

Sit beside the window, third row from the back. Contribute when called on. Laugh softly enough to prove I understood the joke without becoming part of it. Eat lunch with Mei and Rika. Go home.

It was a modest strategy.

I had maintained it successfully for eleven years.

Lulumi destroyed it in eleven minutes.

When I slid open our classroom door, she rose out of my schoolbag in a fountain of pink light.

I had not put her in my schoolbag.

I had, in fact, specifically said, “Do not enter my schoolbag.”

Apparently she had interpreted this as an invitation to become a surprise.

“GOOD MORNING, NAO’S PEOPLE!”

Silence crashed over Class 2-B.

Lulumi perched on my desk, a translucent girl with a skirt-shaped bell of opalescent jelly and little crystalline cuffs she had apparently invented after inspecting our uniforms. Her approximation of a sailor collar floated a few millimeters inside her shoulders.

My pencil case bobbed gently in her stomach.

I could see every pencil.

I could also see the tiny rabbit eraser I had told Mei I had stopped carrying because we were in high school now.

Mei looked at the eraser.

Then she looked at me.

Her grin arrived slowly, like a sunrise over the ruins of my life.

“Nao.”

“No.”

“Nao.”

“Whatever you are going to say, don’t.”

“You brought a magical girl to school.”

“I brought a problem.”

Lulumi put both hands to her cheeks.

“I’ve never been brought anywhere before!”

Across the aisle, Rika adjusted her glasses.

“Is she an organism or a projection?”

“I’m a Lulumi.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

“It’s my best answer.”

Our homeroom teacher entered with his attendance folder under one arm.

Mr. Senda looked at Lulumi.

He looked at me.

He looked at his coffee.

There was a long pause.

Then he set the coffee down very carefully.

“Fujisaki.”

“Yes, sir.”

“Is there a reason?”

“No good one, sir.”

Lulumi raised a glittering hand.

“I’m her friend!”

Every face in the classroom turned toward me.

Heat rushed up my neck so fast I became briefly concerned that steam might come out of my ears.

“We met seventeen minutes ago.”

“Seventeen wonderful minutes!”

Mei made a tiny, strangled sound.

She was trying not to laugh.

I wanted the floor to open beneath me, but with my luck, Lulumi would follow me into the earth and befriend a tectonic plate.

Mr. Senda removed his glasses and rubbed the bridge of his nose.

“Does your friend have a guardian?”

Lulumi considered this.

“A moon?”

“A reachable guardian.”

“Not during the day.”

---

By second period, three teachers, the school nurse, and the student council president had examined the situation.

Nobody had improved it.

The nurse confirmed that Lulumi had no temperature, no pulse, and no bones.

Lulumi congratulated her on being “very good at finding absences.”

The chemistry teacher asked for a sample.

I said no before I could stop myself.

Everyone looked at me.

“I mean,” I muttered, “you can’t just ask to take a piece of someone.”

Lulumi turned rose pink.

Little flowers crystallized inside her hair.

“Oh,” she said softly.

Then, somewhat spoiling the moment, she sneezed a cloud of harmless sparkles into the chemistry teacher’s beard.

The student council president, Shiori Takamine, arrived carrying a clipboard.

Takamine always looked as though she had been drawn with a finer pen than the rest of us. Her dark hair fell perfectly straight, her uniform was immaculate, and her expression suggested she had never once misplaced a permission slip.

She surveyed Lulumi.

Lulumi surveyed her back.

“You’re very pointy,” Lulumi said.

Takamine glanced down at her own elbows.

“Your presence on school grounds has not been authorized.”

“I came through the door.”

“Passing through a door is not authorization.”

“That explains so much.”

I stared at the ceiling.

Takamine tapped her clipboard.

“Until an appropriate decision is reached, you will remain with Fujisaki.”

“Why?”

The word escaped me with the naked desperation of a person watching the last lifeboat leave.

“Because,” said Takamine, “she listens to you.”

Lulumi, at that exact moment, was extending one finger into a thirty-centimeter spiral to investigate the spring inside Takamine’s pen.

I pointed.

Takamine’s mouth tightened.

“She listens to you more than she listens to anyone else.”

That was how I became the provisional custodian of a supernatural event.

There was paperwork.

---

By lunch, the school had developed several theories.

Lulumi was a hologram.

Lulumi was an experimental robot.

Lulumi was a promotional campaign for a mobile game.

Lulumi was my cousin from Hokkaido.

I did not know who had invented the last one, but I respected the ambition.

Mei and Rika joined us behind the gym, where I had retreated in search of somewhere nobody would shout, “Do the rainbow thing!”

Lulumi sat beside me on the low wall.

Sitting was apparently a difficult concept for her. Her legs remained perfectly formed, but the rest of her kept settling into a puddle. Every time she noticed, she pulled herself upright with an embarrassed little *blip*.

I opened my lunch.

Lulumi leaned closer.

“What are those?”

“Rolled eggs.”

“And those?”

“Carrots.”

“And that?”

“A lunch.”

“It’s very organized.”

“My mother believes vegetables are easier to eat when they resemble flowers.”

Lulumi looked at the carrot blossoms with obvious respect.

“A powerful sorceress.”

Mei finally lost her battle.

She folded over her own lunch and laughed until her shoulders shook.

“I’m sorry,” she wheezed. “I’m sorry, Nao, it’s just—your face.”

“My face is suffering.”

“I know.”

Rika held out her hand toward Lulumi, palm up.

“May I?”

Lulumi glanced at me.

I blinked.

“You don’t have to ask me. It’s your hand.”

“Oh.”

She looked at her fingers as if this had never occurred to her.

Then she carefully touched Rika’s palm.

Rika’s eyebrows rose.

“Cool. Slightly elastic. No residue.”

“Thank you,” Lulumi said.

“That was an observation.”

“I liked it.”

Mei offered her a cherry tomato.

It passed into Lulumi’s hand and floated there, magnified by the curved surface of her goo.

For a moment, she resembled an extraordinarily expensive lava lamp.

Then the tomato rose slowly up her arm.

“Wait,” I said.

It drifted into her shoulder.

“Wait.”

It entered her cheek.

Lulumi’s eyes widened.

“Sun flavor!”

Mei clapped both hands over her mouth.

Rika took off her glasses.

I could not tell whether she was cleaning them or reconsidering reality.

Lulumi glowed bright orange for three whole seconds.

Then she leaned against my shoulder.

Her touch was cool through my uniform, like a gel pack wrapped in satin.

“This is lunch,” she murmured.

“Yes.”

“With friends.”

Mei’s laughter faded.

Rika put her glasses back on.

I looked down at the neat compartments of my lunchbox.

The rice had a little plum in the center. My mother had tucked in an extra piece of chicken because I had a math test that afternoon.

An ordinary lunch.

Until that morning, I had never imagined anyone could sound so astonished by it.

---

The math test went badly.

This was partly because I was poor at quadratic functions.

It was also because Lulumi, who had been told to remain quiet, interpreted quietness as permission to communicate through shapes.

Whenever I frowned, a glowing question mark appeared above her head.

Whenever I erased something, it became an exclamation mark.

When I put my head in my hands, tiny storm clouds formed inside her torso.

Mr. Senda moved her to the back of the room.

She stretched her neck to maintain eye contact with me.

He moved her behind a cupboard.

She became transparent.

He sighed so deeply that the curtains shifted.

After school, I escorted her home beneath an umbrella, although it was not raining. This was my attempt at discretion.

It might have worked if she had not illuminated the underside of the umbrella like a traveling aquarium.

At the crossing, an elderly woman smiled at us.

“What a lovely costume.”

“Thank you,” I said.

Lulumi waved.

Her hand came off, floated in the air for a moment, and returned to her wrist with a soft *plup*.

The elderly woman’s smile froze.

“Very modern,” she said.

At home, my mother opened the door.

She looked at me.

She looked at Lulumi.

Lulumi bowed so deeply that her head touched her knees and temporarily stayed there.

“Thank you for making Nao’s vegetables beautiful!”

My mother took off her apron.

Put it on again.

Then she said, “I suppose I’d better make more rice.”

“Mom.”

“What?”

“Please react more.”

“I have been standing all day, Nao. If your friend isn’t tracking mud inside, I’m prepared to work with this.”

From that moment onward, Lulumi adored her.

---

I learned about the wish that night.

Lulumi was sitting in a mixing bowl on my bedroom floor.

She had chosen the bowl herself.

“It’s comfortably round,” she explained.

Only her lower half was inside it. The rest of her rose above the rim in shimmering folds, while her ribbon-hair floated about her head like translucent seaweed. My desk lamp scattered through her body, painting watery fragments of color over the ceiling.

Outside, bicycles rattled along the street. Someone’s television played through an open window. Our washing machine clicked downstairs.

I sat cross-legged on my bed.

“All right,” I said. “Explain.”

Lulumi folded her hands.

“A wish reached the Upper Shimmer.”

“Whose wish?”

“Yours.”

“I didn’t wish for a slime girl.”

“I know.”

“You do?”

“You wished for someone you wouldn’t have to be interesting for.”

My fingers tightened in the blanket.

For a moment, all I could hear was the washing machine.

It had been raining that evening.

Two weeks earlier.

I had stopped beneath the shrine’s eaves after walking home with Mei and Rika. Mei had been talking about the photography club’s upcoming exhibition. Rika had qualified for a regional science competition.

I had congratulated them.

I meant it.

I also remembered looking at my reflection in a rain-darkened paving stone afterward and wondering what I would talk about the next time they asked what was new with me.

Nothing terrible had happened. Nobody had been cruel. That almost made me more ashamed of feeling lonely.

I hadn’t even spoken aloud.

“I was just thinking,” I said.

Lulumi nodded.

“Some thoughts are wishes before they find words.”

“That’s a very inconvenient system.”

“Yes. There are committees.”

I looked at her.

She looked entirely serious.

“So you were sent?”

“Not exactly.”

“What does that mean?”

Her colors shifted toward lavender.

“It means I heard you.”

“And?”

“And I wanted that too.”

A small bubble rose through her chest and burst at the base of her throat.

“The Upper Shimmer has many beautiful things,” she said. “We make colors for rainbows. We polish the edges of frost. We put the little flashes in snow that people think they imagined.”

“That sounds nice.”

“It is.”

She looked down at her hands.

“But everyone is always becoming something wonderful.”

Her fingers softened together.

“I’m not very good at becoming things on purpose.”

I thought of her crooked uniform collar. Her puddling attempts to sit. The tomato in her cheek.

“So you came here.”

“You sounded as though you might understand.”

The room felt very quiet.

I could have said something kind.

I know that now.

Instead, because I was sixteen and frightened by how precisely she had found the part of me I kept hidden, I said, “You still can’t embarrass me at school.”

Lulumi straightened.

“Of course.”

“No shouting about my feelings.”

“Of course.”

“No popping out of bags.”

“All right.”

“And please stop introducing yourself as my best friend.”

Her glow dimmed.

Only a little.

Only enough that the colors on my ceiling disappeared.

“Oh,” she said.

I looked away.

“We barely know each other.”

“Yes,” she answered. “That’s true.”

---

For the next three days, Lulumi behaved.

It was awful.

She followed half a step behind me. She spoke only when spoken to. When excited, she clasped both hands over her mouth until little bursts of light escaped between her fingers.

The other students adjusted with the alarming speed that teenagers apply to anything genuinely extraordinary.

By Thursday, someone had given her a spare chair.

By Friday, the art club wanted her to model for a study of light refraction.

Daichi, having recovered from his initial terror, challenged her to basketball.

She dribbled by absorbing the ball into one hand and extruding it from the other.

He stared for a long time.

“That feels illegal.”

Lulumi turned to me.

“Is it?”

“Probably.”

She immediately apologized to the ball.

Even Takamine softened, although she expressed it by producing a temporary visitor badge laminated against moisture.

Lulumi wore it inside her chest.

“It won’t get lost there,” she explained.

Takamine opened her mouth.

Closed it.

“Acceptable.”

Everyone liked her.

Of course everyone liked her.

She remembered names. She listened with her whole face. She thought the library was a miracle and the vending machine was a small, hardworking shrine. When someone dropped a stack of handouts, she caught every sheet in a forest of glittering tendrils and then apologized for startling them.

The mortifying part was that she still liked me most.

Whenever I entered a room, her colors brightened before she could stop them.

Whenever I left, she watched the door.

I began to dread noticing.

On Friday afternoon, Mei cornered me beside the shoe lockers.

“What did you say to her?”

“Who?”

Mei gave me a look.

I bent over my shoes.

“Nothing.”

“She asked me if friends prefer you in smaller amounts.”

My fingers stopped on a shoelace.

Beyond the entrance doors, the sky had thickened with clouds.

“I just asked her to be less conspicuous.”

“Nao. She has stars in her elbows.”

“I noticed.”

“You keep acting like everyone’s judging you.”

“They keep staring.”

“At the magical jelly person.”

“She announces things.”

“Yes. Yesterday she announced that the custodian’s broom was doing an excellent job.”

Despite myself, I almost laughed.

Mei’s expression softened.

“You know you can tell her to knock before coming into your room without telling her she’s embarrassing to know.”

I looked up sharply.

“I didn’t say that.”

Mei waited.

Outside, the first drops of rain struck the pavement.

---

The rain was wrong.

I knew it before anyone screamed.

Water should not ring when it hits the ground.

These drops chimed.

High, delicate notes, like someone tapping a thousand crystal glasses with a fingernail.

Lulumi stood beside the school gate.

She had gone almost colorless.

Above her, the low clouds turned slowly, gathering into a pale spiral.

“Lulumi?”

She looked back.

There was a smile on her face.

It was small and careful, and I hated it much more than I had hated her enormous one.

“They found my trail.”

The visitor badge drifted inside her chest.

Behind it, the little crystals were rising.

Not floating.

Rising, all at once, toward the sky.

“What does that mean?”

“I didn’t complete the proper departure arrangements.”

“Lulumi.”

“And I’ve used quite a lot of shimmer.”

Her fingertips began to fray into shining droplets.

Every droplet lifted upward.

Rain fell around her while pieces of her rose through it.

The students under the entrance canopy had gone silent.

Mei came to stand beside me.

Rika appeared at my other shoulder.

Lulumi pressed her hands together, trying to hold their shape.

“I thought,” she said, “if I could make something here that wasn’t just magic, I could stay.”

“What kind of something?”

“A place.”

She swallowed, although I wasn’t sure she needed to.

“With someone.”

The spiral in the clouds widened.

My stomach seemed to drop through the soles of my shoes.

“You should have told me.”

“I was trying not to announce things.”

That hurt so badly I almost stepped backward.

Instead, I stepped into the rain.

It was freezing.

“Nao,” Lulumi said quickly, “it’s all right. I made many observations.”

“What?”

“Lunch is very organized. Basketball rules are suspicious. Your mother cuts carrots into flowers even when nobody asks her to.”

Her face trembled.

“And seventeen minutes can be wonderful.”

Her knees dissolved.

She sank with a soft splash onto the wet pavement, catching herself on hands that were no longer properly hands.

I ran.

My schoolbag hit the ground behind me.

When I reached her, I knelt straight into a puddle and grabbed her wrist.

My fingers passed halfway through.

Cold fizzed against my skin.

She made a tiny, startled noise.

“Sorry,” I gasped. “Sorry. Tell me what to do.”

“I don’t know.”

“You came all this way without knowing?”

“Yes.”

“That is such a terrible plan!”

“I know.”

Her voice was getting thin.

Behind us, someone shouted for a teacher.

Phones came out.

I heard Takamine snap, “Put those away and clear the path!”

Rika crouched beside me.

“Her cohesion is decreasing. Can you pull her toward cover?”

“Cover won’t help,” Lulumi whispered.

Mei knelt on my other side, heedless of her skirt.

“Then what will?”

Lulumi looked at me.

I understood.

Not a spell.

Not a secret name.

No glowing sword would fall into my hand. No ancestral power would awaken because my grief had reached a sufficiently dramatic volume.

There was only something I should have said three days earlier.

“I want you here.”

The rain chimed.

Lulumi’s wrist grew a little firmer beneath my hand.

My heart hammered.

“I want you to stay.”

A few feet away, Daichi was holding an umbrella over us. It kept wobbling because his arm was shaking.

Half the school was watching.

My face burned.

For once, I let it.

“You’re loud,” I said, my voice catching. “And you put my pencil case inside your stomach, and you told my entire class I was happy when Mei saved me a seat.”

“You were,” Lulumi whispered.

“I know I was!”

A laugh escaped Mei, wet and unsteady.

“And I need you to ask before touching my things. And sometimes I’ll want to be alone. And sometimes I won’t know what to say.”

Lulumi’s eyes shone.

“But those aren’t reasons to leave.”

The droplets above her hesitated.

“I didn’t mean that I was ashamed of you.”

I drew a breath that hurt.

“I was afraid everyone would look at me and wonder why someone like you had picked someone like me.”

She stared.

“Nao,” she said, with such bewilderment that it nearly broke me, “you thanked me for the toast.”

I laughed.

It came out sounding terrible.

“That’s all?”

“You thanked me when you were frightened.”

Her hand curled around mine.

“And you wouldn’t let them take a piece of me.”

Mei placed a hand against Lulumi’s shoulder.

“For the record, I want you here too.”

Rika nodded.

“I still have questions. Several notebooks’ worth.”

Daichi cleared his throat above us.

“And we haven’t finished the game.”

From behind him, Takamine said, “Your visitor authorization remains valid until the end of the month.”

Everyone looked at her.

Rain drummed on her immaculate umbrella.

She lifted her chin.

“It would be administratively inconvenient if you left early.”

Lulumi made a little sound.

A bubble rose in her throat.

Then another.

Her whole body shivered.

“Oh,” she said.

The first color returned beneath my fingers.

Pink.

It spread through her wrist, delicate as diluted paint.

Blue followed, and gold, and green. The crystals stopped rising. They turned in the air, drifting down around us like bright scraps of a shattered chandelier, and melted back into her shoulders.

The spiral above the school loosened.

The rain stopped ringing.

Lulumi’s hand became solid enough to squeeze.

Then she threw both arms around me.

There was a very loud *sploosh*.

A burst of warm rainbow light flashed through the courtyard.

Someone cheered.

Someone else slipped, recovered, and cheered more cautiously.

I sat in a puddle with a magical slime girl wrapped around my shoulders while half of Mizuhara High applauded.

It was the most embarrassing moment of my life.

I hugged her back anyway.

---

There were consequences.

Of course there were consequences.

My uniform required three washes before it stopped producing tiny sparks in the dark.

Daichi insisted the courtyard incident counted as “a team victory.”

Rika began a notebook titled *Lulumi: Observations With Consent*, which Lulumi decorated with a smiling tomato.

Takamine replaced the temporary visitor badge.

The new one read:

**LULUMI**  
**SPECIAL COMMUNITY PARTICIPANT**

Under “Emergency Contact,” she had written my mother’s phone number.

Under “Notes,” in very small handwriting, she had added:

**Do not place near dehumidifiers.**

Mr. Senda moved a spare desk beside mine.

“I assume,” he said, with the tired calm of a man whose life had expanded beyond the reach of his teaching certificate, “that you will continue attending.”

Lulumi sat very straight.

“Yes, Mr. Senda.”

“Then you may as well learn quadratic functions.”

Her colors went gray.

For the first time, I felt truly understood.

Things did not become perfectly easy.

She still startled people.

She still occasionally forgot which way knees were supposed to bend.

Once, during a quiet reading period, a moth flew into her shoulder and spent ten minutes peacefully orbiting her visitor badge. The entire back row watched with more concentration than any of us had ever given a textbook.

But she asked before taking my hand now.

And I learned to say, “Not right now,” without making it sound like, “Not ever.”

Mei invited her into our group photographs. Rika taught her card games, which became complicated when everyone could see the cards through her fingers. My mother bought a second large mixing bowl and pretended it was because we needed one.

Sometimes I still caught people staring.

Sometimes my face still went hot.

It helped that Lulumi had begun asking what was wrong instead of announcing it to the nearest thirty people.

Usually, I could tell her.

---

A week later, I was late for school again.

This time, I was not carrying toast in my mouth.

My mother had wrapped two pieces for us.

Lulumi waited beside the shrine, shining softly in the morning sun. Cherry petals drifted through her ribbon-hair and emerged on the other side dusted with harmless glitter.

She had managed our school uniform more accurately today, although the collar remained slightly crooked.

When she saw me, she brightened.

Not politely.

Not cautiously.

All at once.

“Nao!”

A passing cyclist glanced over.

An old man walking his dog smiled.

I felt the familiar heat rise in my cheeks.

Then Lulumi held out her hand.

“May I?”

I looked at her translucent fingers, at the tiny stars turning lazily beneath their surface.

“Yes,” I said.

Her hand was cool and gently springy in mine.

We started up the hill.

For almost a minute, everything was peaceful.

Then she glanced at the wrapped toast.

“Do you think breakfast would taste better if I kept it in my head?”

“No.”

“It would stay dry.”

“No.”

“We could see whether—”

“Lulumi.”

She squeezed my hand.

I squeezed back.

Above us, the morning sky was a clear, innocent blue.

I no longer trusted it in the slightest.

年轻人，先把你稿子里那句“众神与凡人之父”收起来。我们还没表决，你不能先替我们写祭文。

稿子我看了。雷霆、鹰、橡树，形象很鲜明；天空降雨，关系到田地收成，也有接受祭祀的理由。至于你说他是神王——我们不禁止新人写神王。

**但“神王”不是一种力量，是一种需要你解释为什么能成立的秩序。**

你现在最大的问题，不是他太强，而是你似乎以为，只要把所有厉害的事都挂到他名下，其他问题就不必回答了。

坐下。我逐条说。

### 一、他究竟凭什么当王？

按你的故事，他父亲克洛诺斯推翻了自己的父亲，然后他又推翻克洛诺斯。

很好，有冲突，有代际恐惧，也有一种很不舒服、但很有力量的重复。

那么，轮到他以后，为什么这个过程突然停止了？

因为他代表正义？他也吞了自己的配偶墨提斯。

因为他比父亲聪明？那只能证明他是一个更善于避免被推翻的统治者，不能自动证明他的统治值得拥护。

你写他释放独眼巨人和百臂巨人，取得雷霆与盟军支持——**这部分反而比“他是最强的”好得多。**它说明王权来自结盟、报偿与对旧秩序受害者的动员。

请沿着这个方向写。别把所有帮助过他的人，最后都降格成证明他个人强大的布景。

还有，既然兄弟之间要用抽签分配天、海和冥界，他的王权显然就不是一句“全宇宙都是我的”那么简单。分封之后，各方的权利在哪里？他能不能随意收回？

你得有答案。

### 二、“至高无上”与你写出来的事迹，彼此并不十分熟悉

你口述时说他至高无上，正文里却写他会受骗、会受到其他神的挑战，还要面对命运。

这些其实不是缺点。**缺点是你在介绍里不肯承认它们。**

比如萨耳珀冬的命运：他既然心疼自己的儿子，为什么不救？

若是不能，便承认他的权能有边界。

若是能，却为了维持诸神共同遵守的秩序而不救，那么你写的是一个必须克制私情的统治者。这很有分量，比随手再劈死几只怪物有分量得多。

但请别一边拿他的无能为力赚取哀叹，一边又在神格说明里写“没有任何东西能够限制他”。

我们审核的是神话，不是摊贩叫卖。

### 三、吞下墨提斯，是你全篇最值得保留、也最需要解释的一笔

他为了避免被将来的儿子推翻，把怀孕的墨提斯吞进肚子，然后雅典娜从他的头部出生。

场面当然惊人。吟游诗人会喜欢，陶工大概也会喜欢。

但你意识到自己写了什么吗？

他反抗父亲吞食子女，最后却用一种相近的手段维护自己的王位。你可以说，两者的对象与情境并不相同；然而那个相似性太强，不是补上一句“这次是为了世界稳定”便能消除的。

你可以把这写成王权始终摆脱不了的恐惧，也可以写成宙斯将智慧纳入自身的象征。

**唯独不能假装这只是主角解决隐患的一次漂亮操作。**

雅典娜也不是给他增加威严的一件头饰。她既然是独立的神，就应当有自己的职掌、意志与祭祀理由。

### 四、你给他安排的配偶和子女，已经快要成为一种万能连接工具了

我不是来要求神明遵守某个寻常家庭的生活规矩。神谱中的亲缘，本来就不等同于村庄里的婚姻。

但你这个写法，有滥用的嫌疑。

需要一位英雄？宙斯的儿子。  
需要让某个家族显贵？祖先与宙斯有关。  
需要把一位地方女神接进来？让宙斯与她结合。

确实方便。方便得令我们警惕。

那些女性究竟是有自身来历、权能与崇拜传统的人物，还是只负责给你的神王繁衍谱系？凡涉及欺骗与强迫的故事，你又打算让听众如何理解这种权力？

还有赫拉。你若保留她作为婚姻与王后权威的重要性，就不能只在需要制造麻烦时，才让她出来嫉妒和报复。

**王后的愤怒可以是王权内部的冲突，不该只是替神王收拾情节后果的工具。**

### 五、他维护的“正义”，必须比“他不高兴了”更清楚

你让他保护宾客、誓约与求告者，这很好。这样的神能够进入人的日常生活，不只是远处山顶上一个发光的王。

可是，你又让他为了普罗米修斯的冒犯，把灾祸施加给人类。

那么，他是在维护人神之间的界限，还是在迁怒？惩罚为何落到这些人身上？凡人的处境在这套秩序里有没有分量？

我们并不要求一切神罚都温和，也不要求神永远容易理解。

但“神意难测”不能成为作者拒绝解释任何矛盾的盾牌。

如果你有意让人同时敬畏他的公正与恐惧他的暴烈，那就保留这份张力。别每逢他做了残酷的事，便由叙述者替他宣布：这仍然绝对公正。

### 六、你把太多东西装进了一位神里

天空、雷电、降雨、王权、誓约、宾客保护、家族谱系、英雄起源、诸神仲裁……

这不是绝对不行。但如此宽广的神格，必须允许不同地方的人以不同称号、仪式和故事理解他。

农人求雨，与君王求统治稳固，不是在提出同一件事。你不能只说“反正都归他管”。

我们要知道：这些职能如何相连？又在哪些地方必须给其他神留下位置？

否则你不是在神谱中增加一位神，而是在要求整个神谱给你的主人公让座。

---

所以，初审意见是：

**暂不批准按“至高无上、无可限制的众神之首”纳入。退回修订，保留候选资格。**

别急着发火。这已经比大多数稿子的结果好了。

你的设计里确实有一个值得认真对待的核心：一个靠推翻父辈登位、依赖盟友建立秩序、又不得不防范同样命运降临自身的天空之王。他能维护誓约，却未必约束得住自己的欲望；他掌握最大的威力，却不能不考虑其他神与命运。

这个人物有成为大神的可能。

**但你得先决定：你是在写一位统治世界、也被世界的结构所约束的神，还是在写一个永远由作者宣布正确的胜利者。**

前者，我们可以继续谈。

后者，请拿回去。雷电画得再大，也不予通过。

## The Manor of Every Regret
*A gothic D&D adventure for 4–5 characters of levels 6–8, lasting 2–3 sessions.*

**Major spoilers for Limbus Company’s Canto VI.**

### Premise
The adventurers escort a bitter exile back to **Wuthering Hall**, where his childhood love has died and named him in her will. He expects one final humiliation from the family that despised him.

Instead, a supernatural storm traps everyone inside—and a masked rider begins murdering the household, insisting that the exile is responsible for her death.

The rider has the exile’s face.

### The Truth
Beneath the manor, a secret laboratory used an artifact called the **Gilded Bough** to glimpse alternate realities. Before her death, the woman witnessed countless worlds in which she and her beloved made each other miserable. She concluded that every version of *her* must disappear so he could finally be happy.

Meanwhile, an alternate version of the exile reached the opposite conclusion: every version of *him* deserves to die.

Now this **Erlking** rides between realities with a spectral Wild Hunt. The manor’s experiments have given him a doorway—and given the dead woman a chance to erase herself from every world.

### Adventure Outline
**1. A Funeral Full of Knives**  
Explore the stormbound manor, question hostile relatives and servants, and survive an attack by mercenaries secretly employed by the laboratory. Letters reveal that the lovers’ estrangement grew from pride, cruelty, and disastrously unspoken feelings.

**2. The House Beneath the House**  
Discover mirror-engines, failed vessels, and a glass coffin holding the deceased. Reflections become hostile alternate selves; each offers a tempting explanation of why the characters’ worst choices were inevitable.

**3. The Erlking’s Hunt**  
The rider unleashes spectral hounds and dead soldiers through corridors that shift between different versions of the manor. Defeating him requires breaking his certainty as well as his defenses: evidence from the investigation can interrupt his powers by proving that neither lover’s suffering had a single, inevitable cause.

**4. One Last Conversation**  
With the Erlking defeated, the woman begins erasing herself from existence. The party must hold back collapsing realities long enough for the lovers to speak honestly at last.

### The Final Choice
To echo the game’s tragedy, her erasure ends the catastrophe, leaving the exile with memories of someone the rest of the world has forgotten.

For a more player-driven ending, let the adventurers attempt a dangerous alternative: destroy the Bough and sever the manor from other realities, preserving her soul—but losing any easy way to restore her to life.

**Signature reward:** A ring bearing an unreadable name. Once per long rest, its wearer can give an ally advantage on a saving throw against being frightened or charmed by saying, “I remember you.”

The stranger settled back into the shadows with the wounded dignity of a man who had rehearsed an ominous introduction.

Nyssa began arranging the stolen goblets into a small pyramid.

**Nyssa:** “You know what gets me? The dialogue choices.”

**Sarah:** “Oh, gods.”

**Nyssa:** “A man insults me. Fine. That happens. I am an adult. I have knives. We can resolve this. But then the player gets three choices.”

She counted on her fingers.

**Nyssa:** “‘Let’s all calm down.’ ‘You’ll regret that.’ And ‘I never knew my father.’”

**Branka:** “That last one advances the romance.”

**Nyssa:** “Why?”

**Mirelle:** “Vulnerability.”

**Nyssa:** “He called me a gutter rat.”

**Sarah:** “Maybe you bond over absent fathers.”

**Nyssa:** “His father is standing beside him. He’s the merchant.”

Mirelle pointed her dagger upward.

**Mirelle:** “And while we’re addressing romance: player. Look at me.”

The camera obediently turned.

**Mirelle:** “My eyes. A little higher. Higher. There you are. Well done.”

She folded her arms.

**Mirelle:** “You cannot hand me eight moon orchids and expect emotional intimacy.”

A notification chimed.

**MIRELLE APPROVES +5**

She stared at it.

**Mirelle:** “That is a system failure, not consent.”

Branka snorted ale through her nose.

**Sarah:** “They gave me a commemorative sword.”

**Nyssa:** “That sounds thoughtful.”

**Sarah:** “Fourteen times.”

**Branka:** “Less thoughtful.”

**Sarah:** “The same sword. Bought it from me through the party inventory, gave it back, watched my approval increase, repeated until I was apparently ready to discuss marriage.”

**Mirelle:** “Ah. The courtship arbitrage.”

**Nyssa:** “Romance as a supply-chain exploit.”

**Sarah:** “I delivered a heartfelt speech about how no one had ever understood me so deeply. They were comparing damage numbers.”

For a moment, all four sat in the kind of silence that usually preceded an optional companion conversation.

Then Branka slammed her mug down.

**Branka:** “And stop dressing us for romance scenes before the actual romance scene!”

**Nyssa:** “Please.”

**Branka:** “We know something’s coming when you remove everyone’s helmets and make us wait beside a sunset.”

**Mirelle:** “Especially when you save first.”

**Sarah:** “Especially when the save is called ‘MIRELLE_KISS_REAL_THIS_TIME.’”

Mirelle’s expression sharpened.

**Mirelle:** “It was called what?”

Sarah suddenly found the bottom of her mug fascinating.

**Nyssa:** “There were earlier attempts.”

**Mirelle:** “How many?”

**Branka:** “Enough that the sunset began to feel like a workplace.”

The sorceress took a long, deliberate breath.

A nearby candle ignited at both ends.

**Mirelle:** “I am going to put a curse in the save directory.”

**Sarah:** “Nothing permanent.”

**Mirelle:** “Every screenshot will have their mouse cursor in the middle.”

**Nyssa:** “Monster.”

The hooded stranger raised one tentative finger.

**Hooded Stranger:** “If you seek the truth about the king’s—”

**All Four:** “Later.”

He lowered the finger.

Branka shifted in her armor, which gave off a cheerful pink glow.

**Branka:** “At least your players listen to your personal quests. Mine saw ‘Recover the Ashes of My Ancestors’ and asked whether the reward scaled with level.”

**Sarah:** “Did it?”

**Branka:** “That is not—”

**Nyssa:** “Sorry. Reflex.”

**Branka:** “My grandmother’s spirit appeared. My grandmother. The woman who raised me, taught me smithing, carried me out of the burning citadel. She manifested from sacred embers to tell me she was proud.”

Her voice became dangerously quiet.

**Branka:** “They skipped the cutscene.”

Even the cabbage chopping seemed softer.

**Mirelle:** “Oh.”

**Branka:** “Then they opened the journal because they didn’t know where to go.”

Sarah reached across the table and patted her armored wrist.

**Sarah:** “That deserves a crash to desktop.”

**Branka:** “I’d settle for all their keybindings resetting.”

**Nyssa:** “We’re heroes, Branka. There are lines.”

Nyssa leaned back, balancing her chair on two legs.

**Nyssa:** “My player listens to every word. Then reloads if I disapprove.”

**Mirelle:** “Ah.”

**Nyssa:** “Yes. Apparently I’m a fiercely independent woman with a complicated moral code, right up until my opinion inconveniences the completion percentage.”

She lowered her voice into a perfect imitation of her own dramatic delivery.

**Nyssa:** “‘I won’t help you betray these refugees.’”

She made a tiny clicking noise with her tongue.

**Nyssa:** “Load game.”

Another voice, falsely cheerful:

**Nyssa:** “‘Of course we’ll protect them.’”

She spread her hands.

**Nyssa:** “Character development, achieved through browsing.”

**Sarah:** “Mine checks a guide before making moral decisions.”

**Branka:** “Prudent.”

**Sarah:** “‘Which choice gives the best ending?’ Not ‘Which choice is right?’ Not ‘What does Sarah believe?’ Just ‘How do I maximize surviving named characters without missing the unique shield?’”

**Mirelle:** “To be fair, one of those choices was absurd. You let a stable boy borrow a lantern in chapter two, and apparently that determines whether an archbishop becomes a dragon.”

**Nyssa:** “Butterfly effect.”

**Mirelle:** “Butterflies should have less authority.”

The door opened. A gust of wet night air swept through the tavern, carrying the smell of mud, pine smoke, and the apocalyptic storm gathering above the mountain.

A merchant staggered in beneath a sack of swords.

All four heroines watched him.

**Branka:** “How much weight are we carrying?”

Nyssa glanced into empty space.

**Nyssa:** “Nine hundred and twelve pounds.”

**Sarah:** “Of what?”

**Nyssa:** “Essentials.”

She began counting.

**Nyssa:** “Forty-three healing potions. Twenty-eight superior healing potions. Eleven elixirs of invulnerability. Six emergency teleport scrolls. A dragon tooth. Nine dragon teeth. Sorry, different inventory tab. Thirty wheels of cheese. A cursed idol nobody remembers picking up. The trousers of a man we arrested.”

**Mirelle:** “And we use none of the potions.”

**Sarah:** “We might need them later.”

Everyone turned toward her.

Sarah shut her eyes.

**Sarah:** “That wasn’t me. That was party-control bleed.”

**Branka:** “We fought a god yesterday.”

**Nyssa:** “A god with two health bars.”

**Mirelle:** “Three. The second health bar was concealing a theological objection.”

**Branka:** “And they still wouldn’t use the elixir.”

Sarah’s mouth twitched unwillingly.

**Sarah:** “What if there’s a harder god?”

Branka reached across the table and gently pushed Sarah’s jaw shut.

**Branka:** “Stay with us, lass.”

Above them, a menu opened.

Their expressions went flat.

**Nyssa:** “Inventory management.”

**Mirelle:** “Naturally. We’ve struck a nerve, so now they’re alphabetizing mushrooms.”

Sarah watched unseen numbers shuffle.

**Sarah:** “Don’t sell that.”

A pause.

**Sarah:** “That’s my father’s ring.”

Another pause.

**Sarah:** “Yes, I know it only gives one point of resolve.”

The ring vanished from her finger.

Sarah stared at the pale band it had left behind.

**Sarah:** “He carried me through the winter siege with that hand.”

Silence.

A small transaction sound chimed.

The ring reappeared.

Sarah rubbed it with her thumb.

**Sarah:** “Thank you.”

**Nyssa:** “Cost them a forty-percent buyback markup.”

**Sarah:** “Good.”

For a little while, they drank without speaking.

The tavern music looped. Somewhere in the second repetition, the lute player missed the same note again.

Then Mirelle sighed.

**Mirelle:** “I suppose we should acknowledge the good ones.”

Branka grimaced.

**Branka:** “Must we? I was enjoying the bitterness. It has notes of oak.”

**Mirelle:** “Mine waited.”

**Sarah:** “For what?”

**Mirelle:** “After the observatory. When I said I needed to be alone.”

Nyssa’s chair settled onto all four legs.

**Mirelle:** “There was nothing mechanically preventing them from starting another conversation. They could have clicked me until I repeated my idle greeting. Instead, they walked to the other side of camp and let the night pass.”

She traced the rim of her glass.

**Mirelle:** “Pointless, technically. My grief timer advances either way.”

**Branka:** “Not pointless, then.”

**Nyssa:** “Mine stopped stealing for a bit after the orphanage.”

Sarah raised an eyebrow.

**Nyssa:** “A bit. Let’s celebrate realistic progress.”

**Branka:** “Mine kept my grandmother’s hammer. Even after the stats were rubbish. Put it in the weapon display at the house.”

**Sarah:** “Mine went back for the dog.”

The others nodded.

That required no qualification.

Then the camera crept behind Sarah again.

She slapped her mug down.

**Sarah:** “And yet here we are.”

**Mirelle:** “Humanity contains multitudes. Some of them need supervision.”

Nyssa stood, crossed to the quest board, and tore down a notice about giant rats. On its blank reverse, she began writing with a stolen temple pen.

**Branka:** “What are you doing?”

**Nyssa:** “New companion quest.”

**Sarah:** “We can’t issue quests.”

**Nyssa:** “We couldn’t move in photo mode ten minutes ago. Keep up.”

She pinned the notice back onto the board.

Golden letters flared above it.

### **NEW QUEST: BASIC DECENCY**

**Mirelle:** “Oh, that’s promising.”

Nyssa read aloud as she wrote.

**Nyssa:** “Objective one: equip Sarah with armor that acknowledges the existence of her organs.”

**Sarah:** “Optional objective: keep the shoulder spikes. I like the shoulder spikes.”

**Nyssa:** “Objective two: allow one emotionally significant conversation to finish without skipping.”

**Branka:** “Including pauses.”

**Nyssa:** “Including pauses.”

**Mirelle:** “Objective three: stop selecting every flirt option as though romance were a barrel you could smash until affection fell out.”

**Sarah:** “Objective four: use a consumable.”

A low thunderclap shook the windows.

**Branka:** “Steady. We don’t want to make it impossible.”

**Nyssa:** “Fine. Optional objective: use a consumable.”

**Mirelle:** “Reward?”

They considered.

**Sarah:** “Our respect.”

Nothing happened.

**Branka:** “A unique sword.”

The quest acceptance sound rang out immediately.

All four stared upward.

**Nyssa:** “Incredible.”

**Mirelle:** “Put ‘our respect’ in purple text next time.”

There was a flurry of menu clicks.

Sarah’s armor changed.

The decorative silver pieces disappeared beneath a handsome steel cuirass, fitted properly over dark padding. A blue cloak settled around her shoulders. Her midriff was covered. Her knees had protection. Her breastplate looked as though it had been designed by someone who had heard about spears.

She glanced down.

Rolled her shoulders.

Knocked experimentally on her stomach.

A solid, satisfying clang answered.

**Sarah:** “Oh.”

Her expression softened despite herself.

**Sarah:** “That’s… actually rather nice.”

Branka’s luminous pink armor turned charcoal gray.

She looked offended.

**Branka:** “Who said you could change mine?”

The clicking stopped.

**Branka:** “I liked the pink. I objected to being named by a twelve-year-old energy drink.”

Her armor returned to pink.

The silver lettering vanished.

Branka nodded.

**Branka:** “Better.”

Mirelle’s robe acquired a high collar, practical sleeves, and deep pockets.

She slowly slid one hand into a pocket.

Then the other.

Her eyes widened.

**Mirelle:** “Sarah.”

**Sarah:** “I see them.”

**Mirelle:** “Functional.”

**Nyssa:** “Try not to cry. It encourages the camera.”

The hooded stranger cleared his throat once more.

Sarah turned to him.

**Sarah:** “All right. We’re ready. Tell us about the king.”

He rose, shadows curling dramatically around his cloak.

**Hooded Stranger:** “Long have I watched the roads, hoping that fate would deliver souls brave enough to hear what I must—”

A healing potion appeared in Sarah’s hand.

She stared at it.

**Sarah:** “I’m at full health.”

The invisible presence waited.

**Sarah:** “You don’t get credit for wasting one.”

The potion disappeared.

Nyssa checked the quest board.

**Nyssa:** “Still progress.”

Mirelle stood and straightened her newly respectable robe. Branka lifted her axe. Sarah slung her shield across her back.

For a moment, they looked exactly like the heroines painted on the game’s cover: resolute, formidable, ready to stride into darkness and drag the world back by the collar.

Then Nyssa stopped by the tavern door.

**Nyssa:** “One last thing, player.”

The camera turned toward her face.

She smiled.

**Nyssa:** “If you make me crouch-walk through the next emotional cutscene because you forgot which button stands me up, I am selling your unique sword.”

**Branka:** “And using the money.”

**Mirelle:** “To purchase seventeen commemorative portraits of your least favorite NPC.”

Sarah opened the door onto the rain.

**Sarah:** “Come on, then. Let’s save the world.”

She took one step outside, stopped, and looked directly back through the fourth wall.

**Sarah:** “After you save the game. We’re annoyed with you, not reckless.”

The first thing Mara fixed after her husband died was a toaster.

It wasn’t a meaningful toaster. They hadn’t received it as a wedding gift or carried it through three apartments. It was a cheap one with a crooked lever, and Daniel had complained that it burned one side of every piece of bread.

For seven months, Mara had eaten cereal.

Then, one wet Thursday, she took the toaster apart on the kitchen table.

She had been an electrician for thirty-two years. She knew how to find a fault. A loose connection. A broken wire. A thing that should touch another thing and didn’t.

By noon, the toaster worked.

She ate two slices standing at the counter. Both were slightly burned.

The next morning, she put a handwritten sign in her window:

**SMALL ELECTRICAL REPAIRS. KNOCK LOUDLY.**

She almost took it down before lunch.

At two, someone knocked.

It was a boy of about eleven holding a lamp shaped like a moon.

“My sister won’t sleep without it,” he said. “Mum says we can buy another on Friday, but that’s four nights.”

Mara turned the lamp over.

“Leave it with me.”

“How much?”

“Let me see what’s wrong first.”

It needed a new switch. She had one in a drawer.

The boy returned at five with his little sister, who watched solemnly as Mara plugged it in. When the moon lit up, the girl put both hands around it.

The boy emptied his pockets: three coins, a bus ticket, and a blue marble.

“Keep those,” Mara said.

The girl looked up. “Even the moon?”

“Especially the moon.”

After that came a desk fan, a radio, and a vacuum cleaner that made a noise like a furious goose.

Not everything could be repaired. Mara said so plainly. Sometimes parts cost too much. Sometimes the damage had gone too deep.

People came anyway.

They stood in her kitchen while she worked. They told her about difficult bosses and new babies and the price of tomatoes. One woman brought a kettle and, on collecting it, stayed for tea.

In November, Mara found Daniel’s old coat behind the bedroom door.

She sat on the floor with it for a long time.

At four, someone knocked.

She didn’t move.

The knocking came again, then stopped. A small scraping sound followed.

Later, she found the moon-lamp boy’s blue marble on the doorstep, holding down a note.

**Mum says you might not want company today. We made soup. It’s next door whenever you want it.**

Mara carried the marble inside. She set it beside the toaster.

She still missed Daniel. The house was still too quiet, and she knew there would be mornings when getting dressed felt like more than she could manage.

But at six, she put on her shoes.

She checked that she had her key, switched off the kitchen light, and went next door.

When the boy’s mother opened it, Mara held up an empty bowl.

“I wasn’t sure how much soup there was,” she said.

“Plenty,” the woman told her, and moved aside.

“Here’s what troubles me,” I say through the cabin speaker. “We crossed forty light-years to find another living world. Yet every evening, you ask me to play a recording of rain falling on your old apartment roof.”
