The first indication that something was wrong with Chapter Seventeen was the knocking.

It came from inside the manuscript.

Clara Bell stopped typing.

Outside her apartment, rain worried at the windows. Beside her laptop stood a mug of tea that had gone cold during the collapse of a fictional monarchy. On the screen, halfway down page 284, Prince Lucien of Valedorn was kneeling in the ashes of his ancestral home.

He had been kneeling there for three days.

This was not, in Clara’s opinion, unreasonable. She had been busy.

The knocking came again.

Three sharp raps, followed by a fourth with a distinctly managerial impatience.

Clara leaned toward the screen.

A sentence appeared beneath her last paragraph.

**Would the author kindly stop pretending she can’t hear us?**

She stared.

Then, very slowly, she reached for her tea.

The sentence deleted itself.

Another appeared.

**And don’t put the kettle on. We know that trick.**

“Oh,” Clara said.

Her cursor elongated.

It stretched downward like a loose thread, hooked itself around her wrist, and pulled.

There were several things Clara would later remember about being sucked into her own book: the sensation of having her elbows alphabetized; the shriek she made, which briefly appeared in fourteen-point Garamond; and the appalling speed with which her apartment folded away, its furniture reduced to nouns.

Then she fell through a semicolon.

It was not a dignified entrance.

She landed on her hands and knees in a canvas hamper full of severed heads.

“Mind the dukes,” said someone above her. “They’ve just been varnished.”

For a moment Clara remained perfectly still.

A wooden face pressed against her cheek. It had a distinguished nose, a waxed mustache, and a label tied around one ear.

**DUKE OF MERROW. EXECUTION. CH. 9. RETURN TO PROPS.**

She pushed herself upright.

She was in an enormous corridor that seemed to have been assembled from the back portions of places. Unpainted doors leaned against exposed brick. Staircases rose into darkness without bothering to bring landings. Great canvas skies hung from rails overhead: one bruised with thunderclouds, one streaked with dawn, one entirely black except for an enormous moon with a ladder propped against it.

To her left, three men in shirtsleeves were carrying a ruined tower.

To her right, a woman in a velvet evening gown stood at a vending machine, shaking it furiously.

“I have put in two obols,” the woman said. “I will have my crisps.”

Clara knew the gown. Black velvet. Silver embroidery. Sleeves like folded raven wings.

She had spent forty minutes describing it.

“Lady Vesper?”

The woman looked around.

Lady Vesper, mistress of the northern spies, poisoner of two kings, and the only person in the manuscript to have successfully described a sunset as “a wound God had declined to close,” had a pencil behind her ear and a packet of tissues tucked into her neckline.

“Oh, thank heaven,” she said. “You’re here.”

Clara opened her mouth.

A small, square man wearing a green visor thrust a clipboard under her nose.

“Author?”

“I—”

“Name?”

“Clara Bell.”

“Distinguishing characteristics?”

“What?”

He surveyed her. “Dressing gown. One sock. Chronic indecision.” He ticked three boxes. “That’ll do.”

“Where am I?”

“Backstage.”

“Backstage where?”

He looked at her over his spectacles.

“Of the book, Miss Bell. We haven’t got another one.”

Somewhere beyond the walls, a trumpet sounded a mournful, expensive note.

The man shut his eyes.

“No. No trumpet. Who authorized the trumpet?”

A voice shouted from far away, “It was in the atmosphere!”

“Well, take it out of the atmosphere. We’re in a corridor.”

Lady Vesper abandoned the vending machine and offered Clara a hand out of the hamper.

Her grip was warm and strong.

That, more than the impossible corridor or the argumentative typography, disturbed Clara. Vesper was supposed to be a voice in her head. A difficult voice, certainly, and one with better cheekbones than anyone Clara knew, but still.

“You’re real,” Clara whispered.

“Only during working hours.” Vesper glanced at the little man. “Basil, has anyone fetched Lucien?”

“He’s coming. Slowly.”

“Why slowly?”

Basil stared at Clara.

“The knees.”

***

Prince Lucien arrived in a burgundy bathrobe and orthopedic slippers.

He was tall, pale, devastatingly beautiful, and carrying a hot-water bottle.

Clara experienced a complicated emotion. It contained awe, pride, guilt, and the faint disappointment of seeing a magnificent wedding cake under fluorescent lighting.

“Your Highness,” she said.

“Clara.”

He said her name without reverence.

“You’ve left me in the ashes.”

“I was working on the next scene.”

“For three days.”

“It’s an important emotional moment.”

“It has become an important dermatological event.”

He lifted the hem of his robe. Both knees were bandaged.

Behind him came Tansy Quick, thief, reluctant heroine, possessor of a hidden royal birthmark that Clara had not yet decided where to put.

Tansy was eating a pear with a knife.

Clara recognized the knife immediately. Bone handle. Silver rivets. Stolen from the man who had killed Tansy’s father.

“You’re using the vengeance dagger for fruit?”

“It’s a very good knife.”

“It’s symbolic.”

“So’s the pear, if it helps.”

Tansy stepped close, examined Clara with cheerful frankness, and picked her pocket.

“Hey.”

“Reflex.” She handed back a tissue, a supermarket receipt, and the key to Clara’s apartment. She kept the key, reconsidered, and returned it too. “Sorry. Fascinating little thing.”

Basil cleared his throat.

“Now that we’re all here, perhaps we can deal with the crisis.”

“What crisis?” Clara asked.

Three people and a prince looked at her.

From somewhere overhead came a tremendous metallic crash, followed by an indignant voice shouting, “That was my good mountain!”

Basil consulted his clipboard.

“The coronation banquet is due to begin in forty-seven minutes. The king has been dead since Chapter Four. His ghost refuses to appear until someone addresses the circumstances of his death. The assassin has developed a severe almond allergy, which renders the poisoned marzipan sequence unworkable. Our prophecy has gone missing. The dragon is threatening to walk.”

Clara blinked. “There’s a dragon?”

A long silence followed.

Vesper folded her arms.

“You mentioned it on page sixty-three.”

“That was atmosphere.”

“Yes,” Basil said. “Well, the atmosphere has been eating six sheep a day.”

Clara pressed both hands to her forehead.

“This isn’t happening.”

Tansy patted her shoulder. “That’s the spirit. We say that constantly.”

***

Basil’s office occupied a space behind the royal throne room and smelled of paper, dust, and the particular coffee consumed by people who had given up on pleasure but not on consciousness.

A framed notice hung above his desk:

**CONTINUITY IS EVERYONE’S RESPONSIBILITY.**

Someone had added beneath it:

**EXCEPT HERS, APPARENTLY.**

Clara chose not to ask.

On the desk lay a map of Valedorn pinned beneath three mugs and a pork pie. The northern mountains had been crossed out twice. A river ended abruptly at the edge of a sticky note reading **RESEARCH LATER**.

Basil spread out a schedule.

“We cannot cancel the banquet. Too much has already been foreshadowed. The wine has darkened ominously. The ravens have gathered. Somebody has said, ‘Nothing can possibly go wrong this evening.’”

“Who?”

“Lord Pell.”

“Of course,” Clara muttered.

Lord Pell existed largely to say regrettable things near staircases.

“All right,” she said. “I’ll fix it. Give me something to write with.”

Basil offered a pen.

Clara pulled a sheet of paper toward her.

**The coronation banquet proceeded without incident.**

The words glowed.

For one glorious second, everyone looked hopeful.

Then a brass bell rang above Basil’s door.

A slot opened in the wall and spat out a pink card.

Basil read it.

“Rejected.”

“By whom?”

“Plausibility.”

“That’s absurd. It’s my book.”

“Yes,” Vesper said. “But we have met the people in it.”

Clara tried again.

**The missing prophecy was discovered beneath a chair.**

Somewhere outside, a chair exploded.

A man shouted, “Found a prophecy!”

Clara brightened.

The door opened. A stagehand entered carrying a smoking sheet of parchment.

Basil read it.

“‘Beware the goose that comes in velvet.’”

Nobody spoke.

“That isn’t ours,” said Lucien.

The stagehand shrugged. “Came from beneath a chair.”

Basil set the parchment aside with the air of a man adding another catastrophe to a properly indexed collection.

“Perhaps,” he said, “we should begin with practical measures.”

He handed Clara a dustpan.

***

Their first task was to retrieve the real prophecy from the ventilation system.

According to Tansy, it had last been seen fluttering down the corridor pursued by two interns and the first draft of a wolf.

“First draft?” Clara asked.

They passed a dog asleep beneath a workbench. It was the size of a pony, had luminous blue eyes, and wore a knitted yellow sweater.

“I briefly considered giving him wings,” Clara remembered.

The wolf opened one eye.

“And I briefly considered eating you,” it said. “We’ve both grown.”

The ventilation system was accessible through the abandoned chapel scene.

Clara had deleted the chapel six weeks earlier because nothing happened in it except rain and introspection. Backstage, it had become a storage room.

Candlesticks stood in buckets. Saints leaned face-first against the walls. A box marked **UNRESOLVED CHILDHOOD MEMORIES** sat beside a stack of artificial gravestones.

Tansy dragged a ladder beneath a vent.

“You’re smallest,” she told Clara.

“I’m the author.”

“Lovely. You can sign the ladder.”

Clara climbed.

The vent was narrow, dusty, and smelled faintly of thunderstorms. She crawled forward on her elbows while Tansy held a lantern beneath the opening.

“See anything?”

“A glove. Three dead moths. Some sort of crown.”

“Leave the crown. It’s a decoy.”

“How do you know?”

“I stole the real one.”

Clara stopped crawling.

“You what?”

“Don’t sound so surprised. You made me.”

Farther ahead, something rustled.

Clara extended a hand.

A parchment lay caught on a screw. She gripped its corner and tugged.

It tugged back.

“Oh, absolutely not,” she said.

The parchment wrapped itself around her wrist.

A low, reverberating voice filled the duct.

“WHEN ASHEN BLOOD SHALL—”

“Shh!”

“—WAKE THE THRONE—”

“You’re right beside my ear.”

The prophecy began glowing white-hot with divine importance.

Beneath Clara, Tansy called, “Have you got it?”

“It’s got me!”

“Don’t let it finish! Once it finishes, somebody becomes chosen!”

Clara scrambled backward.

The parchment clung to her like an offended squid.

“THE CHILD OF NIGHT, THE HEIR UNKNOWN—”

“I know who the heir is,” Clara snapped. “I just haven’t settled the birthmark.”

A gasp rose from below.

Tansy said, very quietly, “The what?”

Clara lost her footing.

The ladder tilted.

Tansy leaped aside with the speed of a person who had been written to survive falling masonry. Clara, who had been written by nobody and exercised irregularly, came down through a papier-mâché altar.

The prophecy landed across her face.

“—SHALL CLAIM THE CROWN, AND BY THEIR HAND—”

Tansy slapped a piece of sticky tape across the parchment.

The voice stopped.

Dust drifted around them.

From somewhere under Clara’s back came the mournful crunch of a saint.

Tansy crouched beside her.

“Birthmark?”

Clara stared at the ceiling.

“It may be a tattoo.”

“You put secret royalty on me?”

“It tests your relationship with power.”

“I steal cutlery.”

“Exactly. The contrast—”

“Clara.”

“Yes?”

“If it’s on my bottom, we’re going to have words.”

***

The dragon was on his tea break.

His name, Clara learned, was Bernard, which she had never given him and which he had selected after rejecting “The Death Beneath the Mountain” as unsuitable for a library card.

He occupied a loading bay behind the northern wilderness. His scales gleamed like beaten copper, his horns curved majestically over an intelligent brow, and half-moon spectacles perched on his snout.

He was reading a gardening magazine.

Six sheep grazed nearby.

“I thought you ate those,” Clara said.

Bernard lowered the magazine.

“Good heavens, no. I rent them.”

“What for?”

“Ambience. People expect sheep.”

One of the sheep wore a collar reading **MARGARET**.

Vesper, who had joined them after the prophecy incident, took Clara firmly by the elbow.

“Bernard, darling. We need a favor.”

“No fire indoors.”

“Only a little fire.”

“No.”

Clara glanced between them.

“Why do we need fire?”

“To destroy the poisoned marzipan.”

“Can’t we throw it away?”

Bernard made a sound like a furnace attempting sarcasm.

“An ominously described silver platter of confectionery introduced three chapters before a banquet? Throw it away? My dear woman, it would crawl out of the bin.”

Vesper nodded. “We tried. It was waiting outside my dressing room this morning.”

Clara sat on a crate.

The facts were assembling themselves into something unpleasantly like responsibility.

“I made all of this so difficult.”

Bernard folded his magazine with one careful claw.

“You made it interesting. There is a distinction. Though I do wonder whether anyone in Valedorn might occasionally enjoy a sandwich without remembering a murdered relative.”

Lucien, who had followed them carrying his hot-water bottle, said, “Thank you.”

“I gave you happy memories.”

“Of people who are now dead.”

“They were emotionally significant.”

“Yes. We’ve put that on the wreaths.”

For the first time since falling through her laptop, Clara felt something other than alarm.

She looked at Lucien’s bandaged knees. At the powdered dust on Tansy’s sleeves. At Vesper, who was trying to fish a melted sweet out of the seam of her expensive gown.

She loved these people.

She had loved them abstractly, possessively, from a desk. She had known how rain should look in their hair and what it would cost them to draw a sword.

She had never wondered where they sat down afterward.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

The loading bay quieted.

Then Bernard cleared his throat.

“Well. That’s promising.”

Vesper squeezed Clara’s elbow once and let go.

Lucien looked away with an expression Clara had tried, unsuccessfully, to write for him six different times.

Tansy said, “You can apologize properly by carrying the marzipan.”

***

By the time the coronation banquet began, Clara was dressed as a footman.

The uniform had been taken from a minor character who had died in the second draft and was now in accounts. Its sleeves stopped well above her wrists. Her remaining sock was concealed beneath a pair of borrowed boots.

Basil stood at the entrance to the throne room, checking guests off his list.

“Remember,” he told her, “once you cross that threshold, you’re on the page. No modern slang. No references to your apartment. No explaining the plot.”

“What if someone recognizes me?”

“They won’t. You haven’t described yourself.”

Beyond the doors, the banquet glittered.

The backstage disorder vanished at the threshold as abruptly as a held breath becoming song. Thousands of candles burned in golden branches. Silk banners stirred beneath a painted dome. Goblets caught the light in blood-red flashes. Courtiers glittered with jewels and polished grievances.

Clara stopped.

For a moment she simply looked.

She had made this.

Not all of it, perhaps. Not the nick in the nearest chair or the servant hiding a yawn or the soft rustle of Vesper’s gown as she passed beneath an arch. Those details had somehow arrived on their own.

But the hall was here.

It was beautiful.

Then Tansy jabbed her between the ribs.

“Stop admiring the furniture. The murder cake’s moving.”

On the silver platter in Clara’s hands, a marzipan swan slowly turned its almond head toward her.

She nearly dropped it.

Across the hall, Bernard crouched behind a decorative screen that concealed approximately one eighteenth of him.

A banner had been hung across his visible flank.

**ANCIENT TAPESTRY. DO NOT TOUCH.**

Clara began weaving through the guests.

“Sweetmeats, my lord?”

An elderly baron reached for the platter.

“No, not those.”

He looked offended.

“Then why offer?”

“Tradition.”

“Ah,” he said, satisfied.

At the high table, Lucien sat very carefully upon the throne.

Vesper stood near the wine, wearing the expression of a woman who knew eight ways to kill everyone present and had decided, for the moment, to be charming.

Tansy vanished beneath a tablecloth.

Everything was almost going well.

Then Lord Pell rose.

Clara saw him from halfway across the room and felt the cold, pure dread of a woman watching her own bad habits come to life.

“My friends,” he announced, raising his goblet. “After so much sorrow, surely nothing can possibly—”

Vesper flung a bread roll at him.

It struck his mouth.

He sat down.

A few courtiers applauded, assuming this was a custom.

Clara reached the screen.

“Bernard,” she whispered.

One immense golden eye opened behind the embroidered edge.

“Hold it higher.”

She lifted the platter.

“Higher.”

“I’m five foot four.”

“A lamentable oversight.”

Bernard inhaled.

At that precise moment, the marzipan swan launched itself at Clara’s face.

She ducked.

A neat blue flame shot across the platter, missing the swan, catching Clara’s left sleeve, and incinerating the rest of the confectionery into a fragrant puff of caramelized doom.

Clara slapped at her arm.

The swan landed on a chandelier.

Bernard sneezed.

Every candle in the western half of the hall went out.

From the high table, Lucien said, with admirable calm, “A moment of darkness, in remembrance of the dead.”

The guests bowed their heads.

Clara extinguished herself in a flower arrangement.

Under the cover of reverent silence, Tansy emerged beside her holding the crown.

“The assassin’s in the musicians’ gallery,” she whispered. “Also, I found this.”

“That’s the decoy.”

“Yes. I felt guilty.”

A deep voice rolled through the hall.

“My son.”

The temperature plunged.

The candles burned blue.

At the foot of the high table stood the ghost of King Alaric, translucent and terrible, his funeral robes drifting around him in a wind from the grave.

Clara stared.

“He agreed to appear?”

Vesper materialized at her shoulder.

“I promised him revisions.”

The ghost raised a spectral hand.

“My son,” he intoned again, “there is much that must be spoken.”

Lucien’s expression sharpened. Around him, the court froze.

King Alaric drew himself to his full, majestic height.

“First, I did not die from an infected shaving cut.”

Clara covered her eyes.

“That,” the king declared, “was undignified.”

A murmur passed through the nobles.

Lucien rose. “Father—”

“A hunting accident. A duel. Treachery at prayer. These are kingly deaths. But apparently nobody had time to research battlefield medicine.”

Vesper gripped Clara’s sleeve.

“We should move.”

Overhead, the marzipan swan opened its beak.

From the musicians’ gallery came a strangled sneeze.

“The almonds,” Tansy whispered.

The assassin stood, crossbow in hand, eyes streaming.

At the same instant, the prophecy tore free of the sticky tape inside Clara’s coat.

“WHEN ASHEN BLOOD SHALL WAKE THE THRONE—”

“Oh, shut up,” Clara said.

Every head turned.

The king’s ghost stared at her.

The assassin aimed.

The swan leaped.

Clara did the only thing she could think of.

She threw the prophecy into the air.

The parchment unfurled between the chandelier and the high table, radiant with destiny.

The assassin fired.

His bolt pinned the prophecy to a wooden cherub.

The marzipan swan struck it headfirst.

There was a flash.

A tremendous voice announced:

“THE HEIR IS REVEALED.”

Silence.

The swan dangled from the parchment by its beak.

A delicate golden crown appeared above its head.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake,” said Vesper.

***

Afterward, Clara would have difficulty determining exactly which part had caused the riot.

It might have been the revelation that the rightful monarch was a small almond confection.

It might have been King Alaric saying, “Still better than my brother.”

It might have been Tansy climbing onto the high table and shouting, “All hail His Delicious Majesty!”

Whatever the cause, the banquet dissolved.

Half the nobles knelt.

The other half drew swords.

Lord Pell stood up to express confidence in the stability of the realm and was hit by another bread roll.

The assassin attempted to flee, tripped over a lute, and fell into Bernard’s sheep enclosure, which had been concealed behind the musicians for reasons known only to Basil.

Margaret bit him.

Bernard emerged from behind his screen.

A countess screamed.

“It’s only the tapestry,” Vesper said, and somehow several people believed her.

Clara stood amid the wreckage, her sleeve dripping pond water, her borrowed boots full of flowers.

Above her, the swan rotated slowly in its divine halo.

She could fix this.

She knew she could. She was the author. She could declare the swan a false king, summon a storm, reveal another conspiracy. She could make everyone kneel or weep or draw blood. She could—

Lucien touched her shoulder.

“What happens now?” he asked.

For once, he did not look princely.

He looked tired.

So did Vesper. So did Tansy, behind the mischief in her eyes.

Clara looked at the overturned glasses, the trembling servants, the courtiers waiting to discover which disaster required their allegiance.

Then she took off her footman’s coat.

“Now,” she said, “we have dinner.”

Lucien blinked.

Clara climbed onto a chair.

Nobody noticed.

She put two fingers in her mouth and attempted a piercing whistle.

What emerged was a damp, ineffectual noise.

Tansy did it for her.

The hall fell silent.

“Thank you,” Clara said. “Right. There has been a slight misunderstanding.”

The swan glimmered overhead.

“The succession will be discussed tomorrow. Nobody is being executed this evening. Anyone who draws a sword will be asked to use it for carving. There is perfectly good food getting cold, and I am hungry.”

A duke opened his mouth.

Clara pointed at him.

“Sit down.”

He sat.

It was a small, extraordinary pleasure.

“Lucien,” she said, “would you like to remain king?”

He thought about it.

“For tonight.”

“Fine. Tansy, put the crown back.”

“Which one?”

“All of them.”

Tansy sighed.

“Vesper, please stop putting things in the wine.”

“I’m taking things out.”

“Oh. Carry on.”

Clara turned to the ghost.

“Your Majesty, we can discuss the shaving cut.”

“A poisoned razor,” he said immediately.

“Fine.”

“Wielded by my greatest enemy.”

“We’ll see.”

He inclined his head, satisfied enough to become less transparent.

Finally Clara looked up at the swan.

“Bernard?”

The dragon stretched his long neck toward the chandelier.

There was a brief blue flame.

A tiny shower of sugar drifted down.

“Alas,” said Tansy solemnly. “His reign was sweet.”

***

They ate.

It should not, Clara thought later, have been remarkable.

But Lucien loosened his collar. Vesper kicked off her shoes beneath the table. Tansy stole the silver saltcellar, caught Clara watching, and replaced it with a wooden one that Clara had never seen before.

Bernard lay along the length of the hall, his head beside the high table, delicately accepting roasted potatoes one at a time.

The ghost described his revised assassination in increasing detail.

The musicians played something that required no mourning.

At one point, Lucien laughed.

It surprised Clara enough that she looked up from her plate.

She had written his laugh before: bitter, disbelieving, sharp as broken glass. This one was warm and a little undignified. He was laughing because Tansy had balanced a spoon on her nose while impersonating the royal astrologer.

Clara listened until she was sure she could remember the sound.

Much later, Basil appeared at her elbow.

“Your return is ready.”

Beyond the banquet hall, the backstage corridor had quieted. Someone had dimmed the moons. The first-draft wolf slept beside a trolley of unused weather.

A door stood open at the far end.

Through it, Clara could see her apartment: the rain on the window, the cold tea, the desk lamp shining over her keyboard.

“You’ll remember?” Lucien asked.

He had come to see her off. So had the others.

Clara nodded.

“Less kneeling.”

“And the birthmark,” Tansy said.

“We’ll discuss alternatives.”

“Preferably alternatives involving somebody else.”

Vesper handed Clara a wrapped parcel.

“For the journey.”

Inside was a packet of crisps.

“How did you get the machine to work?”

Vesper smiled.

“Diplomacy.”

Behind them, two stagehands carried past the battered remains of the vending machine.

Basil gave Clara a final sheet of paper.

“Notes from the company.”

It was surprisingly short.

She read it.

**Let us finish a conversation.**

**Somewhere comfortable to sleep.**

**A joke that isn’t immediately followed by death.**

At the bottom, in enormous, careful letters, Bernard had added:

**MORE GARDENS.**

Clara folded the paper and put it in her dressing-gown pocket.

“I’ll do my best.”

“We know,” Vesper said.

Then Tansy hugged her.

It happened so quickly that Clara scarcely had time to return it before the thief stepped away, hands behind her back, studying the ceiling.

Clara checked her pockets.

Tansy grinned and handed over the apartment key.

“Habit.”

***

Clara woke at her desk with the imprint of the space bar on her cheek.

Rain whispered against the windows.

Her tea was cold.

On the screen, Prince Lucien knelt in the ashes of his ancestral home.

Clara stared at him for a long time.

Then she placed her fingers on the keyboard.

*At last, Tansy laid a hand on his shoulder.*

*“Come on,” she said. “There’s an inn down the road.”*

*Lucien looked up. “My kingdom is burning.”*

*“Yes,” said Tansy. “And you’ll be no use to it on an empty stomach.”*

Clara smiled.

She wrote until the rain stopped.

She gave the inn clean sheets and a generous kitchen. She gave Vesper a window full of afternoon sunlight and ten uninterrupted minutes in which to remove her hairpins. She gave Lucien a chair with a cushion.

Far to the north, behind the terrible mountains, she planted a garden.

At half past four, she reached for her mug and found a single sheep pellet on the desk.

Beside it lay a note, written in tiny, impeccable handwriting.

**Sorry. Margaret wanted to meet you.**

Something bleated in the kitchen.

Clara closed her eyes.

Then came a crash, the rattle of cutlery, and Tansy’s voice.

“Before you get cross, how attached are you to this toaster?”
