answer:
*The medical premise in this story is fictional. In reality, having someone stand or walk on a person’s chest or abdomen can cause serious injury and is not an established way to improve labor outcomes.*

***

By the time I reached my last semester of high school, I thought there was very little left for relationship and childbirth education to tell me.

I was eighteen. I knew how pregnancy worked. I knew babies were expensive, sleep became a distant memory, and prospective fathers were supposed to start taking their health seriously before there was anyone calling them Dad.

And, obviously, I knew about bearing.

Everybody did.

There were advertisements for prenatal support mats between football highlights. My aunt had complained at a family barbecue that my uncle treated every bearing session like an Olympic event. When somebody at the gym said he was “getting ready for family life,” nobody needed him to explain why he was suddenly so interested in strengthening his torso.

It was ordinary adult life, in the same category as joint bank accounts and arguing about whose relatives to visit during the holidays.

Still, seeing **PARTNER SUPPORT DURING PREGNANCY** written across the classroom board made me sit a little straighter.

Beside me, Daniel stopped spinning his pen.

“Here we go,” he muttered.

At the front of the room, Ms. Calder closed the door with her heel. She was carrying a stack of workbooks, a tablet, and the expression of a woman who had heard every possible joke before any of us had thought of it.

“Before we begin,” she said, “yes, you already know what bearing is. No, familiarity is not the same as understanding.”

A few people laughed.

I looked down at my workbook. The cover showed a couple assembling a crib. The man had one of those broad, reassuring builds you saw everywhere in family advertising.

Until that morning, I probably would not have noticed.

***

Our first exercise was to write down three things we associated with being a good partner during pregnancy.

I wrote:

*Patience.*

*Being dependable.*

*Being strong.*

Then I looked around, partly to see whether anybody else had written the same thing.

Ms. Calder walked between the desks.

“Strong comes up every year,” she said, glancing at several pages. “What does it mean?”

“Physically capable,” someone near the windows answered.

“Not complaining,” Daniel said.

There were nods around the room. Mine was probably one of them.

Ms. Calder wrote both answers on the board, then drew a line between them.

“These are not synonyms.”

Daniel leaned back as though he had been personally betrayed by the curriculum.

I smiled, but I kept looking at the words.

My father was not a man who complained much. When my mother talked about her pregnancies, she sometimes mentioned how reliable he had been, how he would put aside whatever he was doing when she needed help settling down. I had always pictured that reliability as something almost structural. Dad was there. Dad could take it. End of explanation.

I had never wondered whether being reliable also meant saying when something was wrong.

***

The presentation began with a diagram of the stress response.

This was the part I had expected to find boring. Instead, it was strangely unsettling to see the familiar custom translated into arrows, hormones, and clinical language.

In our world, the evidence was established: during pregnancy, the customary practice of a woman stepping barefoot across the front of her partner’s torso could produce a distinctive calming response. The resulting release of oxytocin and endorphins reduced prenatal stress and, over time, substantially eased labor.

Nobody in the room reacted to that information as a revelation. We had grown up hearing it.

What caught my attention was the next slide.

**GREATER PARTNER SUPPORT IS ASSOCIATED WITH GREATER REDUCTION IN LABOR PAIN.**

There it was, stripped of the cheerful packaging.

The more a husband could bear, the less painful his wife’s labor would be.

I thought about my third answer.

*Being strong.*

It suddenly looked less like a personality trait and more like an obligation with my name waiting to be written on it.

“Questions?” Ms. Calder asked.

A girl in the front row raised her hand.

“What happens if someone doesn’t have a partner?”

“We’ll cover the full range of prenatal care and support arrangements later this week,” Ms. Calder said. “Today we’re discussing this practice, not claiming it replaces everything else.”

Then she looked around the room.

“And remember: an average benefit is not a promise about one individual birth.”

I underlined that sentence when she put it on the board.

***

We watched an interview with a married couple, both somewhere in their thirties.

The husband looked nothing like the man on our workbook. He wore glasses, had narrow shoulders, and kept pushing his sleeves up while he talked. His wife sat beside him with a sleeping baby against her chest.

“I worried I wasn’t built for it,” he said.

Several boys in the room became very interested in appearing uninterested.

I understood him immediately.

I played some basketball. I went to the gym when homework and laziness allowed it. I was not weak, exactly, but there was a considerable difference between being able to carry two grocery bags in each hand and being the sort of man pictured in prenatal brochures.

His wife glanced at him.

“He thought I was comparing him to the posters at the clinic.”

“Were you?” the interviewer asked.

“No. I was comparing him to himself when he forgot to listen.”

The class laughed.

So did the husband on the screen.

They talked about making time, checking in, and learning not to turn pregnancy into a running argument about who was more tired. Bearing had helped her considerably, she said, but what she remembered most was that he stopped treating every request as a test he might fail.

I wrote that down too, although it was not on any slide.

***

When the lights came back on, Ms. Calder asked us where our ideas about a husband’s role came from.

“Parents,” I said.

“Advertising,” said someone behind me.

“Films.”

“Church.”

“My grandmother,” Daniel added. “Mostly at Christmas.”

Ms. Calder wrote them all down.

Then she projected two advertisements side by side.

One was old enough that the colors looked faded. A muscular man stood behind a pregnant woman beneath the slogan **STRONG FOR HER WHEN IT MATTERS**.

The newer one was more subtle. A man carried a boxed crib up a staircase while his wife smiled from the landing.

“Different presentation,” Ms. Calder said. “Similar message.”

I had seen versions of those pictures all my life. Men in family advertisements were always lifting something, supporting something, holding something steady.

I had never thought much about why.

Of course strength mattered. Pregnancy asked things of a woman that nobody could volunteer to experience for her. Bearing was one of the accepted ways a man took on some physical discomfort in return, and its benefits were real. That was why people called it gentlemanly rather than merely helpful.

But looking at the two advertisements, I could also see how easily useful strength became an entire definition of a person.

The perfect husband did not just help. He looked as though helping could never cost him anything.

***

Our next assignment was a discussion in pairs.

The situation in the workbook was simple: an expectant couple had established a routine. The husband had begun concealing discomfort because he was afraid that reducing what he could bear would make his wife’s labor worse.

“What should they do?”

Daniel read it twice.

“Talk,” he said.

“That’s probably the answer to everything in this book.”

“Expensive book, then.”

I laughed and wrote *talk honestly*.

But when Ms. Calder asked us to explain, the answer became less easy.

“He’s worried about her,” I said. “He doesn’t want her to have a harder time because of him.”

“That’s understandable.”

“So saying something feels selfish.”

“Does concealing a problem give her a fair chance to make decisions with him?”

I looked down at the workbook.

“No.”

“That’s the difficulty,” she said. “A caring motive can still lead to a poor decision.”

A boy across the room objected that surely some discomfort was the whole point. Everybody knew the husband was not doing it for his own comfort.

“Yes,” Ms. Calder said. “The practice involves accepting a burden. That does not eliminate the distinction between discomfort and injury, and it does not eliminate either partner’s right to speak.”

She did not offer us a practical demonstration or instructions. That belonged in individual appointments with qualified prenatal professionals, she said, not in a classroom full of people with different medical histories.

For once, nobody argued that we ought to get out the equipment.

***

I found myself thinking about my parents again.

When I was younger, Mum used to say Dad had been “a proper gentleman” during her pregnancies. I had understood the phrase in the same way I understood holding a door or giving up a seat, only more serious.

Now I remembered something else.

Once, when she was telling the story, Dad had said, “We worked it out.”

Not *I managed it*. Not *I never complained*.

*We worked it out.*

At the time, it had seemed like one of those dull things parents said to avoid telling an interesting story.

Sitting in that classroom, I wondered whether it had actually been the important part.

***

Near the end of the lesson, Ms. Calder invited questions without names attached. We wrote them on slips of paper and passed them forward.

I hesitated for a while before writing mine.

*What if you do everything you can and the labor is still difficult?*

The question looked childish once it was outside my head.

I folded it anyway.

Ms. Calder mixed the slips together. She answered one about family expectations, another about whether marriage preparation courses covered the same material, and a third about partners whose health limited what they could do.

Then she opened mine.

She read it without changing her expression.

“You support your partner through the difficult labor,” she said. “You listen to the clinical team. You remain present. And afterward, you do not turn the birth into a trial where either person has to prove they did enough.”

I stared at a scratch on my desk.

I had always known that without bearing, labor was generally much harder and more painful. Adults spoke about that fact so casually that it had acquired the weight of a moral rule. A considerate man prepared himself. A dependable husband bore what he could. A good father began before the birth.

All of that still made sense to me.

But I could imagine the fear hiding inside it now: that if the woman you loved suffered, every limit you had ever admitted might come back to accuse you.

Ms. Calder let the room stay quiet for a moment.

Then she moved on to the next question.

I was grateful she did.

***

Before the bell, we had to revise our three opening answers.

I left *patience* alone.

Beside *being dependable*, I added: *including when things don’t go as planned*.

I spent longest on *being strong*.

Outside the window, a maintenance worker was trying to coax a wheeled bin over a crack in the pavement. Somewhere down the corridor, another class had already been dismissed.

Finally, I wrote: *physically prepared, but honest about limits*.

It was less impressive than the original. It would never fit beneath a heroic photograph in a clinic.

It was probably more useful.

When the bell rang, Daniel shut his workbook.

“Well,” he said, “I’m definitely going to the gym.”

“Same.”

He glanced at me. “You look worried.”

“Just thinking.”

“Dangerous habit.”

We joined the crowd in the corridor. Someone was complaining about a mathematics test. Two people were arguing over weekend plans. Everything had returned to its normal size.

I still wanted to become strong. If I married someday, if my wife became pregnant, I wanted to offer the support everybody understood a husband should give. I wanted to make that frightening, difficult part of her life easier.

But for the first time, I pictured more than simply enduring.

I pictured asking how she felt. Answering honestly when she asked me. Making room in an ordinary evening. Learning what we needed to learn without pretending I already knew it because I was a man.

At lunch, I took out my phone and opened a message to Dad.

*Was childbirth class this awkward when you were at school?*

His reply came several minutes later.

*Probably worse. Why?*

I started typing *No reason*, then deleted it.

*Can I ask you about it sometime?*

This time the answer arrived almost immediately.

*Of course.*

I put the phone away and opened my lunch.

# 第一章：起哄的人

下午第二节物理课，阳光斜斜地穿过窗框，把黑板上的受力分析图照得有些发白。

胡家熠踩着预备铃走进教室，额前还挂着汗。他把篮球塞到座位底下，刚坐稳，旁边便递过来一张纸巾。

“还有三十秒上课。”马瑞看着手表说。

“够我完成一次绝杀。”

“也够你被周老师叫起来做一道大题。”

胡家熠接过纸巾，笑了一声：“副主席，你就不能盼我点好？”

马瑞没接话，用笔尖点了点他摊开的物理练习册。倒数第二题空着，旁边却画了一张游戏地图，路线标得比受力分析还清楚。

“昨晚又打游戏了？”

“研究团队协作。”

“那你们团队研究出这道题没有？”

胡家熠低头看题，终于老实了。

作为理科联合会主席，他竞赛成绩不错，组织活动也有一套，可一碰上游戏和篮球，时间观念便时好时坏。马瑞当副主席的第一个星期，就给他列过一张工作表，从实验室预约到活动预算，每项后面都有截止日期。

他当时感叹：“你这不是副主席，是我的倒计时器。”

马瑞答：“有用就行。”

此刻，她坐在靠窗的位置，低头翻开课本。她身高一米八，校运会体测时量出的腿长是一百一十六厘米，那张登记表曾在同学间引起过一阵惊叹。教室的课桌对她来说有些低，她坐下时总要把椅子往后挪一点。阳光落在她清秀明艳的侧脸上，前排路过的女生顺手替她拉了半截窗帘。

“谢谢。”她轻声说。

后排，史墨菲把这一幕尽收眼底。

她个子矮小，相貌并不出众，书包和文具却永远是班里最惹眼的。她家境优渥，学校里不少人都知道，她父亲的公司去年赞助过科技节。

理科联合会换届时，她原本很有把握当上副主席。

她准备了一份漂亮的竞选展示，里面有赞助方案，有校外场地，也有印着联合会名字的定制礼品。可投票结果出来，马瑞比她多了整整二十七票。

理由让她尤其不舒服。

同学们说，马瑞做事可靠。

至于胡家熠，他在换届会上公开表示，副主席首先要能负责实验安全和项目审核，拉赞助可以另设岗位。

史墨菲一直记着那句话。

物理老师周老师抱着讲义进来，把保温杯往讲台上一放。

“今天继续讲带电粒子在磁场中的运动。先提醒一句，洛伦兹力不做功，不要看见一个力就急着往动能定理里塞。”

教室安静下来。

周老师画了一道组合场题，粉笔在黑板上敲了两下。

“一个正粒子从这里入射，要从右边这个小孔穿出，磁场方向怎么判断？”

胡家熠盯着图，顺手把篮球往桌底又推了推。

马瑞在草稿纸上画出圆心，接着写下一行关系式。胡家熠侧头看见她的辅助线，压低声音问：“你也取临界轨迹？”

“先定圆心位置。”她把草稿纸往中间挪了一点，“这个条件不能漏。”

就在这时，后排传来一个刻意扬高的声音。

“老师，胡主席和马副主席又开小会呢！”

几排同学下意识回头。

史墨菲托着下巴，笑得很无辜：“理科联合会感情这么好啊，物理课上也舍不得分开。”

教室里响起几声窸窣的笑。

胡家熠直起身，眉头微微皱起。马瑞则停下笔，转头看向她。

周老师拿着粉笔问：“什么事？”

“没什么呀。”史墨菲见大家都在看自己，语气越发轻快，“就是他们天天一起做活动，课间一起去办公室，放学还留在实验室。现在又坐得这么近，我们难免好奇嘛。”

她特意把“好奇”两个字拖长了些。

有人交换了一个眼神，也有人低头憋笑。原本安静的课堂像被投进了一颗小石子，连窗边翻书的声音都停了。

胡家熠正要开口，马瑞先站了起来。

“去办公室是交科技节的安全预案。留实验室，是清点上届活动剩下的器材。座位是上个月班主任调的。”

她声音不高，却说得清清楚楚。

“你如果对联合会工作有疑问，周五可以来公开例会。现在是物理课。”

史墨菲脸上的笑僵了一瞬。

“我又没说什么，你这么认真干吗？”

胡家熠把马瑞的草稿纸拿起来，朝讲台示意。

“周老师，我们刚才在讨论圆心的位置。我说应该先找入射点到小孔的中垂线，马瑞补了一个半径限制。”

周老师点头：“那你上来画。”

胡家熠拿着草稿纸走上讲台，接过粉笔。他平时打球时动作快，做题时却肯停下来，先标了入射点和出射点，再画弦与中垂线。

“圆心必须在这条线上。但粒子入射速度方向确定，所以圆心还得在入射点速度的垂线上，两条线的交点就是圆心。”

周老师问：“磁场方向？”

“垂直纸面向外。”

“很好。马瑞，你补充什么？”

马瑞指了指黑板右侧：“题目要求粒子不能先撞到边界，所以还要检查这段轨迹是否完全在磁场区域内，不能只求出半径就结束。”

“坐下。”

周老师转过身，在图旁边重重画了一道横线。

“这就是容易丢分的地方。”

后排有人小声说：“人家真在研究题。”

另一人没忍住：“史墨菲负责给题目加感情条件。”

笑声一下散开。

史墨菲猛地转头：“有那么好笑吗？”

“安静。”周老师放下粉笔，目光扫过后排，“别拿别人的失误继续起哄。”

教室重新静下来。

随后，他看向史墨菲。

“你刚才打断课堂，不是提问题，也不是提醒纪律，而是在猜测同学的私人关系。这不合适。”

“老师，我只是开个玩笑。”

“玩笑也要看场合，还要看别人愿不愿意。”

周老师语气并不重，反而让她更难堪。

“男女同学一起讨论题目、承担工作，是正常的事。不要让认真做事的人反过来忙着解释这些。下课后，你向两位同学道个歉。”

史墨菲捏着笔帽，没有说话。

“听清楚了吗？”

“听清楚了。”

声音低得几乎被窗外的蝉鸣盖住。

课程继续。周老师擦掉半幅图，换了一个入射角度。前排开始有人抓耳挠腮，胡家熠也顾不上回头，在草稿纸上连着画了三个圆。

马瑞看了眼他的图，把其中一个划掉。

“这个会撞墙。”

胡家熠小声叹气：“我今天的圆怎么都不太自由。”

马瑞唇角动了一下，没让自己笑出声。

后排的史墨菲却再没听进去几句。

她盯着笔记本上的题号，笔尖停了很久，最后把纸戳出了一个小洞。前排偶尔传来的低声讨论，在她听来都像是在议论刚才的事。

下课铃终于响了。

周老师收起讲义，临走前又看了她一眼。史墨菲只好站起来，绕过几张课桌，走到窗边。

“刚才对不起。”她说得很快。

胡家熠正弯腰拿篮球，闻言抬头：“以后别这样就行。”

马瑞合上课本：“你说的那些，容易让别的同学误会。”

“知道了。”

史墨菲转身要走，却瞥见桌角一份文件。

封面写着：《科技节开放实验日项目申报方案》。

负责人一栏，是胡家熠和马瑞的名字。

她停下脚步。

“你们准备做这个？”

“还在修改。”马瑞把文件收进资料夹。

史墨菲看了看她，忽然笑了。

“那挺巧的。我也准备报名。”

胡家熠把篮球夹在胳膊下：“欢迎。周五交方案，评审标准在公告栏。”

“我知道。”

这一次，她没有再开玩笑。

史墨菲回到座位，拿出手机，在桌下发出一条消息：

“爸，上次你说能联系的科技公司，现在还能联系吗？”

窗边，胡家熠正准备去球场，被马瑞叫住了。

“先别走，预算表还差一页。”

他低头看了一眼篮球，又看了一眼资料夹，认命地把球放回桌底。

“十分钟？”

“认真算，五分钟就够。”

走廊里一群男生喊他的名字，胡家熠隔窗摆了摆手，重新拉开椅子。

谁也没有注意到，后排的手机屏幕很快亮了起来。

史墨菲读完回复，慢慢合上了那本被戳破的物理笔记。

## The Rooms That Went Missing

The first thing the dungeon took was the pantry.

“It used to be here,” Mara said.

The Flaaffy stood before a blank wall, holding a bowl of Oran Berries. Above her, a crooked picture showed an Ampharos beside a much smaller Mareep. Someone had drawn a sun in the corner, although both Pokémon were standing in rain.

I checked our map.

According to the map, we were in the pantry.

According to the wall, we weren’t.

From the sitting room, her father called, “Mara? Who’s that in the house?”

“It’s Ash, Dad. My partner.”

A pause.

“Your what?”

“My rescue partner.”

“Oh,” he said. “Good. Good.”

Mara waited until he began humming again before she put the bowl on the floor.

“Last week it was only the cupboard,” she whispered.

***

I had been a Riolu for eight months and a rescue-team member for six.

Before that, I had been human.

Most details of that life were gone, but little things remained: the squeal of brakes on wet roads; a room that smelled sharply clean; someone asking me whether I knew what day it was.

I didn’t tell Mara about those.

She had found me on the beach with seawater in my mouth. She had brought me home. Her father, Orin, had wrapped a blanket around me without asking where I came from.

“Questions after soup,” he’d said.

Back then, the house had seven rooms.

***

Mystery Dungeons weren’t supposed to happen inside houses.

They formed in forests, caves, mountains—places where the world had become unstable. You brought a map, food, Escape Orbs. You didn’t leave anything important behind, because a staircase might not be there when you returned.

The guild called Orin’s house a localized distortion.

They sent a Xatu with a silver measuring rod. He stood in the kitchen, watched the doorway open onto a staircase that belonged upstairs, and wrote for a long time.

“Can you fix it?” Mara asked.

“Sometimes these distortions resolve.”

“And when they don’t?”

Xatu looked toward Orin, who was carefully setting four places at a table for three.

“There are places equipped to keep him safe.”

“He’s safe here.”

A plate slipped from Orin’s hands.

Mara turned at once. “It’s all right, Dad.”

“I know,” he snapped. Then, more quietly, “I know.”

She knelt to gather the pieces.

Xatu left a leaflet on the counter. Mara put it in a drawer.

By morning, the drawer was gone.

***

We learned new rules.

Red string from the front door to the sitting room.

Labels on everything.

**CUPS.**

**BATHROOM.**

**MARA’S ROOM.**

On the back of the front door, Mara pinned a note in her round, careful handwriting:

**You are home.**

Orin read it whenever he passed.

Sometimes he smiled.

Sometimes he asked who had written it.

We stopped taking distant rescue jobs. Then we stopped taking jobs that might keep us out after dark.

Our badges gathered dust beside the kettle.

One afternoon, Mara fell asleep sitting upright while I told her about a lost Budew near Tiny Woods. She woke before I finished, apologized, and asked me to start again.

“It wasn’t important.”

“I want to hear.”

But Orin called from upstairs, and she was already standing.

***

There was a rumor about a seed.

There is always a rumor about a seed.

This one grew beneath the oldest tree in Remembrance Forest. An Audino at the market said it restored what had been lost. She knew a Pokémon whose brother had taken one and recovered his sight.

Mara sold our spare supplies.

I traded away the Power Band we had earned on our first gold-rank mission.

We hired a Chansey to stay with Orin, packed three days of food, and went.

Remembrance Forest had twenty-three floors.

On the ninth, Mara stepped on a trap and lost every move she knew. For a few terrible minutes, she backed away from a wild Scyther with her tail light flashing uselessly.

I got between them.

Afterward, she sat trembling behind a fallen log.

“Is that what it’s like?” she asked.

I checked the corridor rather than answer.

On the seventeenth floor, we found the seed.

It was small and brown and looked like something you might sweep from a doorstep.

Mara held it in both paws all the way home.

***

Orin was sitting beside the window.

“Mara,” he said when she came in.

She stopped so suddenly that I walked into her.

“Dad?”

“You’re muddy.”

She laughed. It came out painfully loud.

“I know.”

“Your mother will have something to say about that carpet.”

Her mother had been dead for six years.

Mara stood still a moment, then crossed the room and kissed his forehead.

We mashed the seed into his supper.

That evening, he told us about the winter the harbor froze. He remembered every boat trapped in the ice, every fisherman who had tried to argue with the weather.

Mara didn’t eat. She kept asking questions.

“And what did Mum say?”

“Who?”

“Mum. When you came home that night.”

Orin glanced at me.

“Is she staying for supper?” he asked.

***

After that, the rooms began going faster.

The bathroom vanished while I was inside it. I spent an hour walking through passages lined with unfamiliar wallpaper before Mara found me.

Her own bedroom became a nursery.

Then a storage room.

Then nothing.

She moved a mattress beside her father’s chair.

At the guild, our team’s name slipped down the rankings.

At home, Orin sometimes mistook Mara for his wife. Sometimes he ordered us out. Once he struck her with his tail when she tried to help him stand.

He stared at the red mark on her arm.

“Who did that?”

“Nobody, Dad.”

She went into the kitchen and stood with her paws braced against the sink.

I waited in the doorway.

“I was angry with him,” she said at last.

“You’re tired.”

“I was angry.”

I came and stood beside her. There wasn’t anything in the sink to wash, but she turned on the water.

***

The last evening was cold.

Orin wanted to go home.

Mara showed him the note on the door.

He read it carefully.

“No,” he said. “My real home.”

She brought him his blanket. He pushed it away.

“My father will be waiting.”

Outside, rain tapped against the windows. Inside, a corridor appeared where the fireplace had been.

Warm yellow light shone at its far end.

Orin stood without help.

“Dad?”

He walked toward the corridor.

Mara caught his paw. “Stay here.”

“I’m late.”

“Please.”

He tried to free himself, bewildered by her grip.

I took an Escape Orb from my bag. Its blue light filled the room. I had brought Pokémon out of collapsed mines with those orbs. I had brought Mara out of a monster house.

I broke it against the floor.

Light rushed around us.

Then I was in the street, on my knees in the rain.

Mara appeared beside me.

Orin didn’t.

She screamed his name and ran back through the door.

I followed.

There was only one room left.

The chair stood beside the window. Orin lay in it with the blanket caught beneath one foot. His tail light had gone out.

Mara climbed into his lap as though she were still the small Mareep in the picture.

She kept rubbing his paws between hers.

They grew cold anyway.

***

By morning, the house had seven rooms.

The pantry was full of things we had bought twice because we couldn’t find them.

Mara’s bed stood beneath her old window. In the kitchen drawer lay the leaflet, a blunt pencil, and three unpaid bills.

Nothing moved when we looked away.

For several weeks, Mara still reached for the red string whenever she entered the hall.

We returned to rescue work in spring.

She was good with frightened Pokémon. She never hurried them. When someone apologized for needing help, she always stayed close until they stopped.

One night, after a long mission, I found her outside the house.

Her paw rested on the latch.

“Forgot your key?” I asked.

She shook her head.

I waited beside her until she could open the door.

The note was still pinned to its back.

**You are home.**

Mara read it, took off her rescue badge, and went inside.

### Dvanáct lekcí pokory

Tomášovi bylo dvacet a byl přesvědčený, že umí skoro všechno lépe než ostatní. Nejčastěji to dával najevo své přítelkyni Katce.

Když něco rozlila, připomínal jí to celý týden. Když se jí nepovedla zkouška, nazval ji před kamarády neschopnou. A když se ohradila, pokaždé se ušklíbl:

„Ty vůbec nerozumíš legraci.“

Jednou po takové poznámce Katka položila hrnek tak prudce, až cinkl o talířek.

„Vsadíme se. Vyberu ti činnost a ty absolvuješ dvanáct lekcí. Nejen že tam přijdeš — budeš se opravdu účastnit.“

„Čehokoliv?“

„Čehokoliv přiměřeného pro začátečníka.“

Tomáš se opřel v židli.

„A když vyhraju, ostříhám ti všechny vlasy.“

Katka si mimoděk sáhla na cop. Pak přikývla, přestože ji okamžitě sevřela lítost nad tím, co právě slíbila.

„A když prohraješ, přede všemi, před kterými jsi mě shazoval, přiznáš, že ses ke mně choval hnusně.“

„Tak to už si kup čepici.“

***

Paní učitelka Váchová vedla malé baletní studio nad knihovnou. Měla rovná záda, šedivé vlasy v drdolu a nepříjemnou schopnost nechat člověka domluvit tak dlouhým tichem, až začal litovat každého slova.

Katku vyslechla bez přerušení.

„Chci, aby to pro něj bylo těžké,“ přiznala Katka. „A trapné. Aspoň jednou.“

„Těžké to být může. A své vlastní neohrabanosti se patrně nevyhne. Ale nikoho tu nezraním ani z něj nebudu dělat atrakci.“

„Myslíte, že to vzdá?“

„To záleží na něm. Dvanáct lekcí baletu není nemožných. Pro člověka, který nesnese být začátečníkem, ovšem mohou být nesnesitelné.“

Domluvily se na individuálním kurzu zakončeném krátkou účastí na otevřené hodině dospělých začátečníků. Učitelka slíbila přísnost, ne nesplnitelné úkoly.

Katce to muselo stačit.

***

Na dveřích první lekce stálo **Baletní studio Váchová**.

Tomáš se zastavil.

„To má být vtip?“

Katka vytáhla papír s podmínkami sázky.

„Dvanáct lekcí.“

„Tohle odskáču po jedné noze.“

V šatně na něj čekaly světlemodré přiléhavé taneční punčocháče, bílý baletní trikot a krátká švestkově fialová tunika s nabíranými rukávy. Na lavičce ležely měkké baletní piškoty s dělenou podrážkou a zkříženými gumičkami přes nárt.

Tomáš zvedl tuniku dvěma prsty.

„Vypadá to jako obleček pro prince z dětského divadla.“

„Je to obleček prince z dětského divadla,“ odpověděla Váchová. „Dnes pracujeme s postavou. Tuniku později odložíte, základní taneční oděv zůstává. Potřebuji vidět postavení kolen a kotníků.“

„Já budu cvičit v džínách.“

„Nebudete. Můžete se převléknout, nebo můžete odejít. V džínách vás do lekce nepustím.“

Tomáš se podíval na Katku. Ta tentokrát neuhnula očima.

Za deset minut vyšel ze šatny s výrazem člověka, kterému osobně ublížila každá gumička na obou botách.

### První lekce: Princ, který neuměl stát

Tomáš čekal skákání. Místo toho měl stát.

Paty u sebe, chodidla jen mírně vytočená podle vlastních možností, kolena volná, pánev neutrálně, ramena dole. Potom pomalá plié u tyče: pokrčit kolena, udržet paty na zemi a zase se vytáhnout vzhůru.

„To je všechno?“ ušklíbl se.

Při čtvrtém opakování vystrčil zadek. Při šestém zvedl ramena. Při osmém se zatvářil, jako by ho tyč urážela.

Následovala princova chůze přes sál. S lehkou pěnovou korunkou na hlavě se měl uklonit, zvednout pomyslný plášť a udělat osm přesných kroků.

Korunka mu spadla při prvním úklonu.

### Druhá lekce: Zákeřně pomalé chodidlo

Váchová nalepila na podlahu papírové paprsky. Tomáš po nich prováděl tendu — vysouval jednu nohu vpřed, stranou a vzad tak, aby špička neztrácela kontakt s podlahou.

Každý pohyb trval osm dob.

„Rychleji by to bylo jednodušší,“ zavrčel.

„Právě.“

Pak přidal paže. Nohy věděly jedno, ruce druhé a Tomáš brzy zjistil, že ani počítání do osmi není samozřejmost.

### Třetí lekce: Ostrovy rovnováhy

Na podlaze ležely ploché barevné značky. Na každé měl zastavit v jiné pozici: výpon na obou chodidlech, krátká rovnováha na jedné noze s rukou u tyče, nízká arabeska s nataženou nohou za tělem.

Žádné vysoké zvedání. Žádné velkolepé pózy.

O to víc ho rozčilovalo, jak často musel došlápnout.

„Ta podlaha je křivá.“

Váchová přešla na stejné místo a bez hnutí vydržela stát.

Tomáš už podlahu nezmínil.

### Čtvrtá lekce: Trest za komentáře

Když učitelce řekl, že její počítání zní jako porouchaná navigace, zastavila hudbu.

„Za každou drzou poznámku se vrátíme k tomu, co právě odbýváte.“

Jeho „trestnými cviky“ nebyly bolestivé výdrže, ale opravné série: čtyři pomalá demi-plié s přesným vedením kolen, čtyři tendu na každou stranu a znovu celá vazba paží před zrcadlem.

S přestávkou, kdykoliv ztrácel techniku.

Tomáš by raději dělal kliky. U kliků mohl zatnout zuby a předstírat hrdinství. Tady mu Váchová klidně říkala:

„Ne. Pravé rameno jste opět zvedl.“

### Pátá lekce: Tanec s peřím

Na hřbety rukou dostal lehká pírka. Měl provádět pomalé port de bras, aniž by rukama škubal a pírka shodil.

Potom měl přejít sálem jako královský posel, který nese důležitou zprávu, ale nesmí probudit spící dvůr.

Připadal si směšně. Ještě horší bylo, že mu úkol vůbec nešel.

„Výraz není škleb,“ upozornila ho učitelka. „Zkuste něco sdělit, ne něco zesměšnit.“

### Šestá lekce: Malé skoky, velké překvapení

Přišly drobné skoky z první pozice, vždy jen několik za sebou: odraz přes chodidlo, natažené nohy ve vzduchu, měkký dopad do plié.

Váchová mezi sériemi nechávala odpočinek a hlídala kolena.

Tomáš dupal.

„Sousedé dole vědí, že jste přistál. Zkuste jim to příště neoznámit.“

Poprvé se zasmál i on. Pak se zarazil, jako by tím porušil vlastní obrannou linii.

### Sedmá lekce: Hudba, která neposlouchala

Stejnou krátkou sestavu musel zatancovat nejprve do pomalého valčíku, pak do svižnějšího klavírního doprovodu.

Nestačilo si pamatovat pořadí. Musel poslouchat.

Když se pokusil hudbu předběhnout, skončil uprostřed sálu s připravenou úklonou, zatímco klavíristka měla před sebou ještě celý takt.

Váchová zdvihla obočí.

Tomáš se mlčky vrátil na začátek.

### Osmá lekce: Zrcadlo bez zrcadla

Učitelka zakryla zrcadla závěsem.

Tomáš opakoval kombinaci podle pocitu, potom podle jejího předvedení z opačné strany. Pravá a levá se mu pletly tak důkladně, že chvíli podezíral Váchovou, že mění zadání.

Nakonec musel nahlas říkat: „Pravá stranou, zavřít, levá vpřed.“

Považoval to za ponižující. Přesto mu to pomohlo.

### Devátá lekce: Dvorní ceremonie

Vrátila se fialová tunika.

Tomáš nacvičoval scénu, v níž princ vstoupí, pozdraví hosty, ustoupí jim z cesty a nabídne rámě taneční partnerce. Partnerkou byla prozatím Váchová.

„Netáhnete vozík,“ řekla, když ji prudce popadl za ruku.

Musel se naučit nabídnout oporu, počkat na její pohyb a přizpůsobit délku kroku.

Právě čekání mu šlo nejhůř.

### Desátá lekce: Minuta, která nechtěla skončit

Váchová spojila dosavadní prvky do minutové sestavy.

Chůze. Úklona. Plié. Dvě tendu. Kroky stranou. Rovnováha. Čtyři malé skoky. Závěrečná póza.

Samostatně už je zvládal. Dohromady zapomínal dýchat, předbíhal hudbu a při soustředění na nohy mu bezvládně klesaly ruce.

Po několika pokusech, proložených odpočinkem, se mu sestava poprvé povedla.

Katka, která čekala u dveří, se přistihla, že mu chce zatleskat.

Tomáš si toho všiml.

„Tak co? Už se bojíš o cop?“

Ruce zase spustila.

### Jedenáctá lekce: Bez výmluv

Na předposlední hodině měla Váchová jediné nové pravidlo: po chybě nesměl hledat viníka. Měl říct, co opraví, a zkusit to znovu.

„Klouže mi bota.“

Učitelka počkala.

Tomáš sevřel čelist.

„Přenáším váhu moc dozadu.“

„Výborně. To se opravit dá.“

Na konci hodiny před něj položila program otevřené lekce.

**Krátký výstup dospělých začátečníků: Dvorní slavnost.**

„Zítra dokončíte kurz.“

„Před lidmi?“

„Před ostatními účastníky a jejich hosty. Věděl jste, že závěr bude společný.“

Tomáš se zadíval na svou roli prince. Najednou už nebylo nejhorší oblečení ani piškoty. Nejhorší bylo, že ho někdo uvidí snažit se o něco, v čem není nejlepší.

### Dvanáctá lekce: Prázdné místo

Přišel včas. Dokonce se převlékl.

V sále stáli ostatní začátečníci: účetní, studentka medicíny, řidič autobusu a dvě kamarádky kolem čtyřicítky. Nikdo se mu neposmíval. Každý měl dost starostí s vlastními kroky.

Pak se otevřely dveře pro hosty.

Tomáš zahlédl Katku.

„Tohle dělat nebudu,“ řekl.

Váchová zůstala stát vedle něj.

„Nemusíte být dokonalý. Stačí dokončit hodinu.“

„V tomhle před ní poskakovat nebudu.“

„Můžete odložit tuniku. Základní sestava zůstává.“

Ani na to nepřistoupil.

Stáhl si korunku, položil ji na klavír a odešel do šatny. Když se vrátil v džínách, hudba už hrála. Na jeho místě zůstala mezera.

Sázku prohrál.

***

Před studiem Katce okamžitě řekl:

„Domluvily jste se proti mně.“

„Ano,“ odpověděla. „Chtěla jsem, aby ses cítil trapně. To ti nebudu zapírat.“

Tomáš čekal výsměch. Nepřišel.

„Ale mohl jsi to dokončit,“ dodala. „Já ti v tom nebránila.“

Chvíli hleděl na dveře.

„Tak sis to užila?“

Katka pomalu zavrtěla hlavou.

„Míň, než jsem čekala.“

O několik dní později se Tomáš před kamarády omluvil. Bez úsměšku a bez dodatku, že to byla jen legrace. Katka ho vyslechla, ale jejich vztah tím zachráněný nebyl.

Když se jí potom zeptal, jestli je teď spokojená, odpověděla:

„Jsem ráda, že jsi to řekl. A už nechci vztah, ve kterém musím vyhrát sázku, abys mě přestal ponižovat.“

Ve studiu zatím Váchová uklidila fialovou tuniku do skříně.

Do Tomášovy karty napsala pouze:

**Jedenáct lekcí dokončeno. Pohybově schopný. Největší obtíž: dovolit si chybu.**

# Mr. Bean and the Overnight Position

## 1. A Reasonable Opportunity

The notice in the newsagent’s window had three qualities Mr. Bean admired in a notice.

It was printed in large letters.

It mentioned money.

And it did not, at first glance, appear to involve much work.

**NIGHT SECURITY ASSISTANT REQUIRED**  
**FREDDY FAZBEAR’S FAMILY PIZZERIA**  
**MIDNIGHT–6 A.M.**  
**£4.20 PER HOUR**  
**NO EXPERIENCE NECESSARY**

Underneath, in considerably smaller print, someone had added:

**Must be reliable.**

Mr. Bean leaned forward.

Below that, in smaller print still:

**Must remain on premises throughout shift.**

He considered this.

Then he took a pencil stub from his jacket, performed a little calculation on the back of a betting slip, and arrived at £25.20.

His eyebrows rose.

For sitting in a chair.

At night.

When he would otherwise be doing nothing useful anyway.

He looked down at Teddy, who was tucked into the crook of his arm.

Teddy appeared equally impressed.

Across the street, in the window of a department store, stood the object that had made employment temporarily attractive: a miniature upholstered armchair, advertised as a *luxury companion chair for dolls and bears*. It had real wooden feet, brass-colored upholstery studs, and a little fabric cushion.

The price was £24.99.

Mr. Bean had inspected it on three separate afternoons. On the second visit, he had pressed one finger into the seat and nodded with professional approval. On the third, an assistant had found him sitting Teddy in it and measuring the distance between Teddy’s feet and the floor with a strip of chewing-gum wrapper.

Now, at last, a sensible financing arrangement had presented itself.

He tore the telephone number from the bottom of the notice.

Unfortunately, the notice had not been designed with detachable strips.

After a moment, he folded the entire lower half of the advertisement into his pocket and walked away.

---

Freddy Fazbear’s occupied a low brick building at the edge of a retail estate, between a carpet warehouse and a shop selling bathroom fixtures. A row of faded flags drooped above the entrance. In the windows, cartoon animals invited the public to celebrate birthdays, win prizes, and “MAKE SOME NOISE!”

The building itself suggested that quite enough noise had already been made.

One of the illuminated letters in **FAZBEAR’S** had failed. A smiling brown bear above the doors held a microphone in one paw and a pizza in the other. Weather had stripped the paint from his front teeth.

Mr. Bean stopped beneath him.

He looked up.

The bear looked down.

Mr. Bean adjusted his tie.

Inside, the restaurant smelled of warm dough, floor cleaner, overheated electrical equipment, and the faintly sweet residue of hundreds of spilled drinks.

A woman in a purple polo shirt stood behind the front counter, trying to persuade a receipt printer to perform its single function.

“You here about the night position?”

Mr. Bean straightened.

“Ah. Yes.”

“Name?”

“Bean.”

She waited.

“Mr. Bean.”

The printer gave a strangled mechanical whine and issued nine inches of blank paper.

The woman tore it off.

“I’m Mrs. Pritchard. Acting manager.”

She said *acting* in the tone of someone who had expected the arrangement to last a fortnight and was now approaching her second Christmas.

“Have you done security before?”

Mr. Bean thought of his flat. He thought of the numerous locks he had fitted to it. He thought, with some satisfaction, of the time he had prevented a man from entering the wrong changing cubicle.

He nodded.

“What sort?”

“Private.”

Mrs. Pritchard looked at his tweed jacket, his narrow tie, and the small bear under his arm.

“Right.”

From somewhere beyond the counter came a burst of tinny music, followed by a mechanical voice announcing that birthdays were better with friends.

Mr. Bean turned.

On a low stage at the far end of the dining room stood three enormous figures.

The bear was in the middle. He wore a black bow tie and a little top hat. To his left stood a purple rabbit holding a guitar. To his right was a yellow bird with a white bib that read **LET’S EAT!**

They were substantially less reassuring at full size.

The rabbit’s head turned with a soft electric whirr.

Mr. Bean immediately looked elsewhere.

Mrs. Pritchard slid a form across the counter.

“Address. Emergency contact. National Insurance number if you know it.”

He began writing.

“We’ve had trouble keeping people,” she said.

Mr. Bean stopped.

“Transport, mostly.”

He glanced through the window at his little green Mini, parked diagonally across the end of a space.

Transport, he indicated with a modest lifting of the chin, would not be a problem.

“Excellent. You can start tonight.”

He had not expected employment to progress this quickly.

Mrs. Pritchard put a key on the counter, along with a plastic badge.

The badge said **NIGHT SECURITY**.

Underneath, a piece of white tape had been stuck over another name.

Mr. Bean picked it up.

Then he smiled.

It was a proper badge.

## 2. The Induction

Mrs. Pritchard’s induction took twelve minutes, four of which were spent looking for a pen that was already clipped to her collar.

She showed him the dining room, the toilets, the kitchen, the prize counter, the maintenance cupboard, and the office.

The office was at the back of the building, approached by two narrow service corridors. It contained a desk, a swivel chair, a little electric fan, a telephone, and a bank of black-and-white security monitors. Heavy sliding security doors had been fitted across the two corridor entrances.

Mr. Bean immediately approved of the doors.

They were thick.

They had large buttons.

They made a satisfactory sound.

He pressed the left-hand button.

The door descended with a hydraulic clunk.

“Don’t play with those,” said Mrs. Pritchard.

He took his finger away.

“The building switches to its old standby system after midnight. Long story. The new supply’s connected to the front half, the back half isn’t, and the electrician says he needs approval from the landlord.”

Mr. Bean nodded with the grave understanding of a man who had once changed a plug.

“The doors draw power while they’re held shut. So do the corridor lights. Cameras, too, but less. You’ve got a meter there.”

She tapped a little display.

**AVAILABLE POWER: 100%**

“If you leave everything on, you’ll run the night system flat.”

Mr. Bean looked at the fan.

Then at the fluorescent light.

Then back at her.

“The emergency exits aren’t on that system,” she added. “Push bars, ordinary mechanical locks. If there’s a fire, go outside and call the brigade.”

He nodded again.

“Your main job is to keep an eye on things, log anything unusual, and be here when the morning supervisor arrives at six. Don’t let anybody in. Don’t use the kitchen equipment. Don’t touch the stage controls.”

Mr. Bean’s expression suggested that it had not occurred to him to do any of these things.

Mrs. Pritchard had managed family restaurants for eighteen years. She did not believe the expression.

“The performers go through an overnight maintenance cycle,” she said. “So you may notice them moving.”

He looked up.

“Moving?”

“A little.”

She looked down at her clipboard.

“Repositioning. Joint circulation. Something like that. There’s a recording by the phone that explains it. Press play after midnight.”

From the dining room came a heavy, distant thump.

Mrs. Pritchard continued speaking more briskly.

“They’ve been here longer than I have. Don’t stand right next to them while they’re active, don’t put your hands near the joints, and don’t try to remove any of the costumes. Any problems, write them in the book.”

She pointed to a thick ledger.

Mr. Bean opened it.

The last completed entry read:

**01:40 — Rabbit in west corridor.**

Below it:

**02:15 — Rabbit still in west corridor.**

Below that, in much larger handwriting:

**I HAVE LEFT.**

He slowly turned the page.

It was blank.

“Previous chap wasn’t a good fit,” Mrs. Pritchard said.

She led him back into the dining room.

A cleaner was dragging a mop between the tables. An employee in an oversized baseball cap was emptying the last bin. The stage figures stood beneath colored lights, motionless now.

Mr. Bean took a few cautious steps toward them.

Up close, their costumes were covered in short, dense fabric, worn smooth on the hands and elbows. Dust gathered along the seams. The rabbit’s guitar had chips around its edges. The bird’s bib bore a faint brown stain.

Freddy’s microphone was bolted into his paw.

Mr. Bean examined the top hat.

Very small, for such a large head.

He glanced over his shoulder.

No one was watching.

He lifted Teddy up beside Freddy’s face.

A family resemblance, perhaps, but not a flattering one.

Freddy’s eyes shifted.

It was a tiny movement. Just a click and a turn beneath the brow.

Mr. Bean lowered Teddy.

He took one step backward.

Then another.

“Good,” said Mrs. Pritchard, appearing beside him. “You’ve met the team.”

Mr. Bean looked at her.

She was already walking toward the entrance.

“Midnight. Don’t be late.”

---

At eleven forty-three, he returned carrying a shopping bag, a thermos flask, a cushion, a folded newspaper, and Teddy.

He had brought his own dinner.

A cheese sandwich.

An apple.

Three individually wrapped sweets.

He had also brought an alarm clock, because six o’clock in the morning was an awkward time to remember by oneself.

The last employee let him in and seemed unusually relieved to see him.

“Office is back there.”

Mr. Bean held up his badge.

The employee did not examine it.

“Brilliant. Cheers.”

He was outside before Mr. Bean had finished clipping it to his lapel.

The front door closed.

The sound of the employee’s car faded away.

For the first time, Mr. Bean heard the restaurant without people in it.

Refrigeration compressors hummed behind the kitchen walls. Something dripped into a metal sink. The prize machines made occasional small clicking noises, as if remembering children.

Far away, the stage curtains rustled.

Mr. Bean stood very still.

Then he cleared his throat, quite loudly, to establish that the premises were occupied by a person in authority.

## 3. Sensible Economies

By midnight, he had improved the office considerably.

The cushion was on the chair.

The thermos was on the desk.

The newspaper had been folded to the crossword.

Teddy sat on top of the monitor console, where he could supervise.

Mr. Bean had turned off the fan.

He had also removed the fluorescent tube above the desk, after discovering that the light switch controlled something else.

The room was now lit by the monitors and a small desk lamp he had brought from home.

The lamp, unfortunately, had a much brighter bulb than the fluorescent tube.

Mr. Bean regarded this as irrelevant. His lamp was smaller.

At precisely twelve, a relay clicked somewhere in the wall. The overhead emergency strip glowed faintly, and the power display dropped from 100 to 99.

Mr. Bean frowned at it.

He had hardly started.

He pressed the button beside the telephone.

A cassette mechanism engaged.

There was a hiss, a cough, and then a tired man’s voice.

“Right, hello. If you’re hearing this, you’re covering the night shift. I’ll keep it short.”

Mr. Bean unscrewed his thermos.

“The characters don’t stay onstage all night. That’s normal for this site. Their movement program runs between closing and opening.”

Mr. Bean paused with the cup halfway to his mouth.

“You’re safest staying in the office and keeping track through the cameras. If one comes right up to an entrance, use that side’s security door until it moves off.”

He put down the cup.

“Try not to keep both doors down longer than necessary. The backup system isn’t what it used to be.”

Mr. Bean looked at the power display.

Ninety-eight.

“The recognition equipment’s old. Out of hours, the units don’t always identify staff correctly. So, for your own safety, do not approach them, attempt repairs, or—”

The cassette began to warble.

“—allow yourself to be—”

The voice slowed into a deep, watery groan.

Mr. Bean leaned toward the machine.

A loop of brown tape emerged from beneath the cassette lid.

He stopped it.

For a moment, he regarded the tangled ribbon with annoyance.

Then he removed the cassette, inserted his pencil into one spool, and began winding.

On the monitor directly in front of him, the purple rabbit turned its head toward the camera.

Mr. Bean was busy restoring the tape.

The rabbit stepped off the stage.

Its large foot came down on the dining-room floor.

The image broke into white static.

Mr. Bean looked up.

The picture settled.

There were two figures onstage.

He glanced at Teddy.

Then back at the screen.

He leaned forward and counted with his finger.

One.

Two.

He selected another camera.

Dining room.

Empty tables.

Another.

Prize corner.

A glass cabinet full of plastic whistles.

Another.

West corridor.

The rabbit stood six feet from the camera.

Mr. Bean jerked backward so violently that the swivel chair rolled into the wall.

The rabbit’s face filled most of the screen. One ear leaned sideways. Its black nose caught the infrared light.

Mr. Bean’s mouth opened.

Nothing came out.

He looked toward the left-hand doorway.

Darkness.

He reached for the light button with one very extended finger.

The corridor illuminated.

The rabbit stood at the far end.

It had not looked nearly so tall on television.

Mr. Bean pressed the door button.

The steel shutter slammed down.

He pressed the right-hand door button as well.

Then, after some consideration, he pushed the chair against the left door.

He stood back.

The office was secure.

The power display fell to 96.

Then 95.

Mr. Bean watched it.

His expression changed from fear to indignation.

He looked at the doors.

At the lamp.

At the display.

This was clearly a design fault.

He switched off the lamp.

Ninety-four.

He pulled the fan’s plug out of the socket, although the fan was already off.

Ninety-three.

He narrowed his eyes.

On the desk sat the security ledger.

He opened it and wrote:

**12.14. Rabbit loose. Doors expensive.**

## 4. The Rabbit Problem

For several minutes, Mr. Bean conducted a careful experiment.

He switched on the left corridor light.

The light could not be seen through the closed door.

He switched it off.

He pressed the door button.

The shutter rose.

The rabbit was standing immediately outside.

Mr. Bean pressed the button again.

The shutter came down.

Something struck it from the other side with a deep metallic knock.

Mr. Bean withdrew his hand and tucked it under his opposite arm.

He stared at the door.

Another knock.

Not loud.

Patient.

He shook his head at it.

“No.”

Silence.

He pointed at the door.

“No.”

The rabbit did not reply.

Mr. Bean took this as the beginning of an understanding.

He returned to the monitors.

On the west-corridor camera, the rabbit was too close to the office to be visible. He changed to the dining room.

Empty.

Then the stage.

The yellow bird was gone.

Mr. Bean shut his eyes.

When he opened them, the bird was still gone.

He checked the right-hand corridor camera.

Nothing.

The kitchen camera showed only a black screen labeled **AUDIO ONLY**.

Through the little monitor speaker came a clatter of pans.

Mr. Bean listened.

A tray fell.

Then another.

Something scraped across a work surface.

His face settled into a disapproving scowl.

He had been specifically told not to use the kitchen equipment. It seemed unfair that the restriction did not apply to everyone.

The power display reached 87.

It was twelve thirty-one.

Mr. Bean examined the right door.

No bird there, as far as he knew.

He opened it.

The power-use indicator dropped by one bar.

Better.

He moved the chair away from the left door, sat down, and tried to think.

Machines, he understood, generally required a firm hand. Parking meters, washing machines, ticket barriers—each had its own little weaknesses, but all could eventually be brought to reason.

He looked at the monitor image of the rabbit’s empty corridor.

Then at the plastic badge on his jacket.

He unpinned it.

On a sheet torn from the ledger, he wrote in large capitals:

**STAFF ONLY**

He held the paper in front of himself, took a breath, and opened the left door.

The rabbit was there.

Mr. Bean thrust out the sign.

The rabbit’s head tilted.

Mr. Bean pointed at the words.

Then at his badge.

Then at the rabbit.

He made a small shooing movement with his fingers.

The rabbit leaned forward.

Mr. Bean dropped the sign and shut the door.

The bottom edge caught the paper, leaving **ONLY** visible on his side.

He stood in the middle of the office with his arms pressed against his ribs.

After a while, he retrieved the ledger.

**12.36. Rabbit cannot read.**

---

The solution, when it came, was simple.

There was a maintenance cupboard twenty feet down the right corridor.

He had seen its contents during the induction.

Broom.

Bucket.

Mop.

A long-handled window squeegee.

And a stack of yellow folding signs.

Mr. Bean checked the right corridor light.

Empty.

He checked the kitchen camera.

The crashing continued.

He looked at Teddy.

“Stay.”

He slipped out of the office.

The restaurant’s nighttime scale was different from its daytime scale. The corridors seemed longer, the ceiling lower. Pipes clicked overhead. His shoes made embarrassingly clear sounds on the floor.

He reached the cupboard, opened it, and pulled out two yellow signs.

**CAUTION — WET FLOOR**

He smiled.

Back at the office, he placed one sign just inside the left entrance, facing outward.

Then he took the second sign, opened the right security door, and positioned it in the corridor.

He checked the west camera.

The rabbit had moved back several feet.

Now.

He opened the left door and immediately slid the sign forward with the squeegee.

The rabbit stopped.

Mr. Bean held his breath.

The rabbit’s head lowered a fraction.

He pushed the sign another inch.

The rabbit remained still.

Slowly, carefully, Mr. Bean pulled the squeegee back.

He waited.

The rabbit did not advance.

Mr. Bean’s expression brightened.

Of course.

Safety regulations.

He sat down, folded his hands over his stomach, and gave Teddy a modest little nod.

At twelve fifty-two, the rabbit stepped over the sign.

## 5. Supper Service

The door came down just in time.

The yellow sign did not.

There was a sharp crack as the shutter folded it flat.

Mr. Bean looked at the broken plastic protruding beneath the door.

Then at the squeegee.

Then at the power meter.

Seventy-six.

He rubbed his forehead.

From the right corridor came a faint squeak.

He turned.

A large yellow hand curled around the edge of the open doorway.

Mr. Bean made a noise resembling the beginning of a sneeze and slapped the right-hand button.

The door struck the fingers.

Stopped.

Rose six inches.

Descended again.

The hand withdrew.

The shutter closed.

For a few seconds, Mr. Bean stood with both palms pressed flat against the desk.

Then he slowly turned toward Teddy.

Teddy, in Mr. Bean’s opinion, was being remarkably little help.

He picked him up and placed him facing the right door.

If there were two corridors, the work ought to be divided.

---

The bird lingered outside for eleven minutes.

Mr. Bean knew this because he checked his watch every forty seconds.

On the east-corridor camera, she stood with her bib turned toward the lens.

**LET’S EAT!**

He looked at the words.

Then at the shopping bag beneath his chair.

A possibility occurred to him.

He removed his cheese sandwich.

It was wrapped in greaseproof paper and secured with an elastic band. He undid the band, peeled back the paper, and inspected the bread.

A respectable sandwich.

He had been looking forward to it.

He glanced at the bird.

At the power meter.

Sixty-nine.

With great reluctance, he removed one small triangle.

He laid it on the end of the squeegee.

Then he opened the right door just enough to reveal the bird’s enormous feet, pushed the sandwich into the corridor, and closed the door again.

He watched the monitor.

The bird looked down.

Mr. Bean leaned forward.

The bird bent.

Her arm moved.

The sandwich disappeared beneath her hand.

Mr. Bean smiled.

At last, a reasonable person.

The bird lifted the sandwich to her beak.

There was a grinding sound.

A fragment of bread fell to the floor.

Another fragment lodged at the corner of her mouth.

Her jaw opened.

Closed.

Opened.

Closed.

A thin strand of cheese stretched between the upper and lower beak.

Mr. Bean’s smile faded.

The bird’s head twitched.

Somewhere inside her chest, a motor changed pitch.

She turned away from the office and walked heavily toward the kitchen, scattering crumbs.

Mr. Bean watched her go.

Then he looked at the remaining sandwich.

He folded the paper over it.

It no longer seemed quite as appetizing.

He opened the right door.

The power-use indicator dropped.

From the kitchen came a tremendous crash.

Mr. Bean winced.

A second crash followed.

He picked up his pencil.

**1.18. Bird fed. Untidy eater.**

---

At one thirty, he tried the telephone.

There was a sticker on the base with an out-of-hours number.

He dialed it.

A recorded voice thanked him for calling Fazbear Entertainment’s regional support service.

Mr. Bean nodded impatiently.

If his inquiry concerned a booking, he was invited to call during normal office hours.

If his inquiry concerned an invoice, he was invited to call during normal office hours.

If his inquiry concerned equipment—

Mr. Bean straightened.

—he was invited to leave a message after the tone.

The tone sounded.

He leaned into the receiver.

“Hello.”

He glanced at the left door.

“There is a rabbit.”

He waited, as if this ought to be sufficient.

The recording offered no assistance.

“A large one.”

From behind the shutter came a slow scraping sound.

Mr. Bean lowered his voice.

“He won’t go.”

He listened.

Then he replaced the receiver with unnecessary firmness.

## 6. Pirate Cove

At one forty-seven, the rabbit finally left.

Mr. Bean confirmed its departure three times before raising the left door.

The power meter showed 61.

Four hours and thirteen minutes remained.

He performed another calculation.

It did not produce the encouraging result he wanted.

He turned the paper over and tried again.

That was no better.

He decided arithmetic was not helpful under the circumstances.

For the next ten minutes, he worked with great concentration.

Corridor light.

Off.

Camera.

Different camera.

Other corridor light.

Off.

He used the buttons delicately now, pressing them with the speed of a man trying not to be charged for a telephone call.

It was during one of these economical checks that he noticed the curtain.

On camera 4, a small stage stood beneath a sign reading **PIRATE COVE**.

He remembered seeing it during the induction. The striped curtains had been closed. A wooden notice had stood in front.

**SORRY! OUT OF ORDER**

Now the curtains were open by several inches.

Something narrow and reddish stood behind them.

Mr. Bean leaned toward the screen.

An ear.

A long muzzle.

A glint of metal.

He changed cameras.

Then immediately changed back.

The curtain was wider.

Mr. Bean’s face went blank.

He reached for the ledger.

After a moment, he decided not to write anything. Recording additional problems seemed to encourage them.

On the screen, a hooked hand appeared around the curtain.

Mr. Bean put the pencil down very carefully.

He looked around the office.

There were only two doors.

Three moving animals had already been quite enough.

He peered at the monitor again.

The fox was still there.

Watching.

Mr. Bean, who had considerable experience with people who stared, stared back.

He leaned closer.

The fox’s jaw hung open, revealing narrow teeth and a dark mechanical framework beneath the costume.

Mr. Bean slowly raised one eyebrow.

The fox did not respond.

He raised the other.

Nothing.

He pulled a face.

The fox remained behind the curtain.

Mr. Bean sat back.

Apparently, this one could be managed.

He left Pirate Cove on the main monitor and took a small sip of tea.

Then the telephone rang.

He jumped, spilling tea onto his trousers.

The ringing came again.

He snatched up the receiver.

“Yes?”

Silence.

A faint electrical crackle.

Then a low, distant sound, almost like music played through a wall.

“Hello?”

The line clicked dead.

Mr. Bean stared at the receiver.

On the monitor, Pirate Cove was empty.

He put the telephone down.

Slowly, he selected the west corridor.

At first, the image showed nothing but the long stretch of floor, the posters, and the corner by the dining room.

Then a shape came around that corner.

Fast.

The fox’s movements were nothing like the rabbit’s. It lurched forward on long articulated legs, hook swinging, its torn costume fluttering around the exposed metal of its thighs.

Mr. Bean slapped the left button.

The shutter fell.

A fraction of a second later, something hit it hard enough to shake dust out of the ceiling vent.

The thermos cup bounced.

Teddy fell off the monitor.

Mr. Bean’s chair rolled backward.

There was another impact.

Then a dragging noise.

Then silence.

Mr. Bean remained where he was.

His legs were rigid.

His hands gripped the arms of the chair.

Very slowly, he turned his head toward the power display.

Fifty-four.

He looked at the door.

Then at the squeegee.

He picked it up and struck the shutter once.

Not very hard.

A reprimand.

## 7. A Temporary Withdrawal

At two nineteen, Mr. Bean decided that £25.20 was not, after all, an enormous sum of money.

It had seemed substantial in the newsagent’s.

It seemed rather less substantial while sitting in a cupboard between two reinforced doors with a fox attempting to dent one of them.

He packed his thermos.

He wrapped his sandwich.

He put the apple in his pocket.

He took his cushion off the chair.

Then he remembered Teddy.

Teddy was no longer on the monitor.

Mr. Bean looked beneath the desk.

Nothing.

Under the chair.

Nothing.

Behind the wastepaper basket.

Nothing.

He crouched down and peered along the floor.

A small brown ear protruded from beneath the desk’s rear support.

He smiled with relief and reached for it.

His fingers came within an inch.

Not close enough.

He lay flat on his stomach.

Still not close enough.

He reached for the squeegee, hooked Teddy gently by the arm, and drew him out.

Unfortunately, the squeegee caught the telephone cable.

The telephone slid off the desk.

Mr. Bean flinched.

The squeegee jerked sideways.

Teddy skidded through the open right doorway.

Mr. Bean froze.

Teddy lay on his back in the corridor, six feet away.

Entirely recoverable.

Mr. Bean got to his knees.

A yellow foot stepped into view.

He stopped breathing.

The bird stood over Teddy.

Her beak still had a small patch of bread caught beside one hinge.

She looked down.

Her hand lowered.

Mr. Bean reached out.

“Ah—”

The bird picked Teddy up.

Not by the arm or the leg.

Around the middle.

Firmly.

Mr. Bean rose halfway.

The bird’s head turned toward him.

He dropped below the desk.

A moment later, her heavy footsteps began moving away.

Mr. Bean remained crouched until they had faded.

Then he peered around the doorway.

The corridor was empty.

So was the floor.

He looked at his shopping bag.

At his cushion.

At the green **FIRE EXIT** sign above the far door.

Leaving would have been straightforward. Twenty paces, a push bar, fresh air.

He took one step toward it.

Then stopped.

He pictured Teddy in the bird’s hand.

He pictured Teddy in the kitchen.

He pictured Teddy on a pizza.

His expression hardened.

He set down the cushion.

Removed his jacket.

Folded it.

Put it back on.

There was no need to be reckless.

Then he picked up the squeegee and went after them.

---

The kitchen was lit by two fluorescent strips, one of which flickered at irregular intervals.

On a stainless-steel preparation table lay a flour scoop, several empty topping tubs, and a pizza crust in a state of violent disassembly.

Mr. Bean watched from behind the door.

He appeared calm.

The crash made Mr. Bean squeeze his eyes shut.

He opened them again.

There had to be a way.

He surveyed the kitchen.

A wheeled wire rack.

A bin.

A roll of cling film.

A large cardboard box marked **PARTY SUPPLIES**.

Mr. Bean considered the photograph.

Then the bird.

Then Teddy.

He took the apple from his pocket.

Held it up.

No.

Too small.

Instead, he quietly opened the party-supplies box.

Paper plates.

Napkins.

Hats.

A collapsible cardboard birthday cake for the stage presentation.

Mr. Bean lifted the cake.

It was nearly two feet across, decorated with painted icing and wooden candles.

Promising.

He placed it on a wheeled serving trolley.

Then, with the elaborate care of someone returning a dangerous animal to the wild, he rolled the trolley into the kitchen.

One wheel squealed.

The bird’s head snapped toward him.

Mr. Bean smiled.

It was not a convincing smile.

He pointed to the cake.

Then pressed both palms together beside his cheek and made a delighted expression.

Birthday.

Lovely birthday.

Cake.

The bird stared.

Mr. Bean gave the trolley another push.

It struck the leg of the preparation table and stopped.

The cardboard cake tilted.

He caught it.

The bird took one step toward him.

Mr. Bean released the cake and retreated behind the door.

He waited.

Metal wheels rattled.

Something knocked against the table.

He peered around the frame.

Chica had put Teddy down.

She was lifting the cake.

Mr. Bean’s eyes widened.

Teddy sat on the preparation table, directly beside the flour scoop.

Mr. Bean crouched.

Extended the squeegee.

Hooked Teddy’s leg.

Pulled.

Teddy tipped over.

The bird turned slightly.

Mr. Bean stopped.

The cardboard cake creaked in her grip.

He pulled again.

Teddy slid through a thin drift of flour.

Another inch.

Another.

Then the bird’s fingers punched through the cardboard icing.

She looked down.

Mr. Bean snatched Teddy off the table and ran.

Behind him came a noise like a cupboard being thrown down stairs.

## 8. The Birthday Emergency

He did not return directly to the office.

The rabbit was standing in the junction ahead.

Mr. Bean stopped so abruptly that one shoe squeaked.

Bonnie’s guitar hung against his chest.

His ears nearly touched the overhead pipework.

Mr. Bean clutched Teddy beneath his jacket.

The rabbit’s head turned.

Mr. Bean looked left.

Storage alcove.

Right.

Dining room.

He chose the dining room.

Behind him, the rabbit began to move.

Mr. Bean passed between the nearest tables, ducked under a paper streamer, and slid behind the prize counter.

He crouched among boxes of plastic rings and finger traps.

Heavy footsteps entered the room.

Stopped.

A faint servo whine rose and fell.

Mr. Bean held Teddy against his chest.

Flour had whitened the bear’s nose.

With the corner of his tie, he carefully wiped it clean.

Across the room, something moved behind the Pirate Cove curtain.

Mr. Bean lowered his tie.

This was becoming unnecessarily crowded.

He peered over the counter.

The rabbit stood beside a table laid with paper placemats.

The bird had emerged from the kitchen carrying half the cardboard cake.

Onstage, Freddy remained motionless beneath a single dim bulb.

For a moment, all three were visible.

Mr. Bean looked at the stage.

At the party tables.

At the sign behind the counter:

**BIRTHDAY HOST STATION**

Beneath the sign was a little control panel.

Four large buttons.

**MUSIC**

**ANNOUNCEMENT**

**STAGE**

**ALL STOP**

Mr. Bean looked at **ALL STOP**.

His whole face brightened.

He pressed it.

The dining-room background music ceased.

A small mirror ball stopped turning.

The rabbit continued forward.

Mr. Bean stared at the button.

He pressed it several more times.

The button remained entirely satisfied with its performance.

Mr. Bean ducked back down.

The rabbit’s foot scraped the floor on the other side of the counter.

He could see its shadow beneath the gap.

His hand groped upward.

Found another button.

Pressed.

A fanfare exploded from the ceiling speakers.

Mr. Bean nearly swallowed his tongue.

Colored bulbs flashed above the stage.

A recorded voice boomed:

“WHO’S READY FOR A FAZ-TASTIC CELEBRATION?”

The rabbit stopped.

The bird stopped.

A relay clacked.

Then Freddy’s head rose.

Mr. Bean stayed very low.

Music began: bright, repetitive, and much too loud for three o’clock in the morning.

The rabbit turned away from the counter.

He walked toward the stage.

The bird followed.

Mr. Bean slowly lifted his head.

Bonnie stepped up onto the performance platform.

Chica took her place on Freddy’s right, still carrying the ruined cake.

Freddy raised his microphone.

All three began to sing.

Their jaws opened and closed with cheerful mechanical precision. The rabbit’s fingers moved across the guitar. The bird swayed. Colored spots traveled across their faces.

Mr. Bean watched in astonishment.

Then he looked down at the control panel.

**STAGE**

He had found it.

A proper control.

For the first time since midnight, the place was behaving like an ordinary badly designed establishment.

Mr. Bean rose carefully.

The performers continued singing.

He stepped out from behind the counter.

No reaction.

He took another step.

Still nothing.

He began moving toward the service corridor.

The song reached its chorus.

Freddy’s eyes followed him.

Mr. Bean stopped.

Freddy’s head remained turned toward the audience.

His eyes did not.

Mr. Bean resumed walking.

Faster.

Then faster still.

He reached the office just as the song ended.

## 9. Power Management

The clock on the wall read 3:08.

The power display read 34%.

Mr. Bean sat down.

Very slowly.

He put Teddy on his lap.

He looked at the meter for a long time.

Then he reached across the desk and unplugged his lamp.

The room darkened.

Thirty-three.

He looked personally betrayed.

---

For the next half hour, the birthday routine gave him peace.

The characters remained onstage, executing little idle movements.

Mr. Bean discovered that the birthday-host panel could be seen from the dining-room camera. He also discovered, through the zoom function, a red light that flashed when the performance cycle ended.

He could not operate it from the office.

This was inconvenient.

He thought about tying string to the button.

Then thought about the distance.

Then about the rabbit.

He abandoned the idea.

Instead, he made a schedule.

He drew six small boxes on a page and labeled them with times.

Check rabbit.

Check bird.

Check fox.

Check bear.

Repeat.

This was proper security work, and he performed it with growing competence.

When the bird left the stage, he tracked her through the east hall and shut the right door only when she reached the corner.

When the rabbit appeared in the west hall, he waited until it came close, then lowered the left shutter.

When the fox’s curtain opened, he kept returning to that camera, watching until the shape withdrew.

There were no sandwiches.

No signs.

No negotiations.

Mr. Bean leaned forward in the blue-gray light, lips pursed, one hand on the controls, the other resting protectively on Teddy.

At three forty-six, the meter showed 26%.

At four twelve, it showed 21%.

He allowed himself a small nod.

Perhaps.

Perhaps this could still be done.

Then he sneezed.

Not an alarming sneeze.

A modest sneeze, caused by flour on Teddy’s fur.

But it startled him enough that he knocked his thermos off the desk.

The flask struck the floor.

The lid sprang open.

Tea spread beneath the chair.

Mr. Bean looked down.

The puddle moved toward the electrical sockets.

He lifted both feet.

For several seconds, he considered the matter from this position.

Then he took off his jacket and laid it on the floor to absorb the tea.

He bent to retrieve the flask.

Teddy slipped from his lap.

Mr. Bean caught him.

His elbow struck the telephone.

The telephone fell again.

He lunged for it.

His shoulder hit the monitor selector.

Every screen went black.

Mr. Bean froze.

He slowly straightened.

The power meter still glowed.

Nineteen.

So that was something.

He examined the console.

A large toggle beneath a plastic guard had been knocked to **OFF**.

He flipped it back.

The monitors returned one at a time, accompanied by a rising electronic whine.

Stage.

Empty.

Dining room.

Empty.

East corridor.

Bird.

West corridor.

Rabbit.

Pirate Cove.

Curtains wide open.

Mr. Bean pressed the left door button.

The fox struck it before it had quite reached the floor.

The shutter bucked in its frame.

The safety mechanism began to lift it.

Mr. Bean stabbed the button again.

Down.

Impact.

Up an inch.

Down.

The third time, it closed.

On the right, the bird’s face appeared in the doorway.

Mr. Bean turned.

Her beak opened.

A piece of dried cheese fell onto the threshold.

He hit the right button.

The second shutter descended.

The room shook.

The power meter dropped to 14%.

Mr. Bean sat with his back against the desk.

His jacket lay in a puddle.

His thermos was empty.

Teddy had one damp foot.

He looked at the wall clock.

4:27.

An hour and thirty-three minutes.

He began, very quietly, to reconsider the luxury armchair.

Perhaps Teddy did not need one.

Perhaps the chair would have encouraged poor posture.

Perhaps the entire thing had been a foolish extravagance.

On the other side of the left door, the fox dragged its hook slowly across the steel.

Mr. Bean covered Teddy’s ears.

## 10. Freddy

At four fifty-one, Freddy left the stage.

Mr. Bean did not see the movement.

He saw the absence.

The bear’s place beneath the colored lights was empty.

He checked the dining room.

Nothing.

Prize corner.

Nothing.

East corridor.

The bird had gone.

He raised the right door.

The power-use indicator dropped.

Nine percent.

Mr. Bean sat absolutely still between camera checks.

He had developed the belief that moving his own body might somehow use electricity.

A low sound came through the speaker.

Not speech.

A chuckle.

He turned up the volume by a fraction.

The chuckle came again.

Then the image on camera 2 changed.

Freddy stood at the back of the dining room, half concealed by a support column.

Only one eye reflected the camera’s infrared light.

Mr. Bean leaned closer.

Freddy’s head was turned toward the office corridor.

His microphone hung at his side.

There was something different about the bear when he was not onstage.

The others moved with an obvious, clattering awkwardness. Even when frightening, they were busy mechanisms: feet landing, gears turning, joints struggling beneath heavy costumes.

Freddy stood with a stillness that did not seem mechanical at all.

Mr. Bean selected the east hall.

Empty.

Back to dining room.

Freddy was closer.

Mr. Bean’s hand hovered over the right door control.

He looked at the meter.

Eight.

At the clock.

5:07.

He could shut the door.

He could keep the bear outside.

For a while.

He looked down at Teddy.

Then toward the emergency exit sign at the end of the right corridor.

There was still a way out.

No one had locked it.

No one was forcing him to sit there.

He picked up Teddy.

Rose.

Took two careful steps into the corridor.

Freddy stood at the far end.

Mr. Bean stopped.

The bear’s silhouette blocked most of the available width.

His eyes caught the faint green exit light.

Very slowly, Mr. Bean stepped backward into the office.

He lowered the door.

Seven percent.

He stood listening.

There were no footsteps.

That was worse.

He wrote in the ledger:

**5.09. Bear.**

He considered adding more.

There did not seem to be much point.

At five sixteen, the telephone rang again.

Mr. Bean stared at it.

It rang a second time.

He answered.

“Yes?”

This time, there was a real voice.

Mr. Bean nearly sagged with relief.

“Yes. Yes!”

He nodded violently.

Then remembered.

Six.

“No.”

A pause.

“What do you mean, no?”

“Six.”

Another pause.

Mrs. Pritchard inhaled.

At the flour on Teddy.

The kitchen trolley.

The cardboard cake.
