He reached for his newspaper.

Not to read it.

To fan himself.

## 11. The Last Twenty Minutes

By five thirty-four, the left corridor was clear.

Mr. Bean raised the shutter.

Four percent.

The right door remained closed.

Freddy stood outside it.

Mr. Bean knew this because every time he briefly checked the corridor camera, the bear’s face occupied the same patch of darkness.

Sometimes closer.

Never farther away.

He tried not to look directly at the eyes.

At five thirty-nine, the fox emerged again.

Mr. Bean had been watching Pirate Cove every few seconds, but watching did not seem to discourage it anymore.

The curtain drew back.

A narrow head leaned out.

Mr. Bean shook his head at the screen.

“No.”

The fox’s leg appeared.

Mr. Bean leaned closer.

“No.”

The fox stepped into the dining room.

Mr. Bean pressed the left door button before it began running.

The impact came moments later.

The power display flashed.

**2%**

Both doors were down.

The office fan, which he had unplugged hours earlier, stood silent on the desk.

His lamp was off.

The fluorescent tube leaned against the wall.

Everything he could economize upon had already been economized upon.

Mr. Bean looked around the room with mounting outrage.

There ought to have been something else to turn off.

He pulled the clock’s plug from the wall.

The clock stopped.

The power meter remained at two.

He looked at the plug.

Then at the clock face.

He had only made it harder to know how long remained.

He put the plug back.

The hands stayed at five forty-two.

Mr. Bean stared at them.

Then he took his own alarm clock from the shopping bag.

It read five forty-three.

He placed it on the desk.

The second hand went around with unbearable cheerfulness.

**1%**

He sat.

He placed Teddy on his knee.

Straightened Teddy’s legs.

Adjusted his little arms.

Then Mr. Bean took the apple from his pocket.

He polished it on the dry part of his sleeve.

He considered taking a bite.

From the right door came a faint metallic click.

He put the apple down.

At five forty-seven, the power failed.

The monitors folded into bright points.

The desk display went dark.

The security doors rose with a long, falling mechanical sigh.

The small green exit signs remained lit on their independent batteries.

Everything else disappeared.

Mr. Bean sat rigid in the chair.

The restaurant settled around him.

Without the office electronics, he could hear sounds from far across the building: a compressor starting, a loose vent ticking, water dripping in the kitchen.

And somewhere near the right entrance, a soft click.

Two pale eyes appeared.

Then a mouth.

Not illuminated from outside.

Lit from within.

Freddy stood in the doorway.

A little tune began to play.

It came from the bear’s chest, thin and wavering, like an old music box heard through a closed tin.

Mr. Bean did not move.

His fingers tightened around Teddy.

The tune played on.

Freddy’s jaw shifted.

The lights inside his face flickered.

Mr. Bean’s gaze moved very slowly across the desk.

Telephone.

Dead monitor.

Empty cup.

Apple.

Alarm clock.

Shopping bag.

Nothing useful.

The music stopped.

Freddy’s face went dark.

Mr. Bean’s breathing grew shallow.

A floorboard creaked.

Not a floorboard, he realized.

The floor was concrete.

Something heavy had shifted its weight.

He raised Teddy slightly.

Then lowered him again.

No.

Absolutely not.

He tucked Teddy inside his shirt and buttoned his jacket over him.

The jacket was wet and cold.

Teddy was safe.

Mr. Bean closed his eyes.

And then the alarm clock rang.

It had not been set for six.

He had intended to set it for six. But in the comfort of his flat, while preparing for an easy night of paid sitting, he had decided he would want ten minutes to tidy the office before the morning supervisor arrived.

The alarm rang at five fifty.

A fierce, metallic, spring-driven clatter.

Mr. Bean jumped.

Freddy’s head snapped toward the desk.

The clock continued ringing.

Mr. Bean stared at it.

Freddy took a step.

Toward the clock.

Mr. Bean looked from the bear to the alarm.

Then, with sudden inspiration, he picked it up.

Freddy’s head followed.

Mr. Bean moved it slowly to the left.

The bear’s eyes shifted.

To the right.

The head turned.

Mr. Bean’s eyebrows rose.

He stood cautiously.

Held the ringing clock at arm’s length.

Freddy moved toward it.

Mr. Bean moved away.

The bear followed.

Not quickly.

But deliberately.

Mr. Bean backed through the open left doorway.

The clock rattled in his hand.

Freddy turned to follow.

Mr. Bean glanced over his shoulder.

The west corridor was empty.

At the far end, the dining room opened into darkness.

He walked backward.

One step.

Then another.

The bear advanced.

Mr. Bean swallowed.

The alarm mechanism began to slow.

He shook the clock.

It rang harder for a moment.

Freddy continued forward.

Mr. Bean reached the dining room.

A green emergency light washed the nearest tables in a sickly glow.

He looked left.

Pirate Cove.

The curtain was open.

Empty.

He looked right.

The birthday station.

And behind it, the stage.

Mr. Bean’s face changed.

He had a plan.

It was not an especially good plan.

But it had the considerable advantage of being the only one currently available.

## 12. One More Show

The clock stopped ringing halfway to the birthday station.

Mr. Bean gave it an encouraging shake.

One feeble rattle.

Nothing.

Freddy stopped.

His head lowered toward Mr. Bean.

Mr. Bean smiled weakly.

Then he reached over the counter and pressed **STAGE**.

Nothing happened.

Of course.

No power.

He pressed it again.

Harder.

The button remained dark.

Freddy took a step.

Mr. Bean backed into the counter.

Behind him, among the party supplies, something crackled beneath his hand.

He looked down.

A paper crown.

A handful of balloons.

A plastic party blower.

He picked up the blower.

Looked at it.

Looked at Freddy.

Then he put it between his lips and blew.

A thin, rude squeal filled the dining room.

The paper tube unrolled and tapped Freddy on the nose.

There was a pause.

Mr. Bean slowly let the tube curl back.

Freddy stared at him.

Mr. Bean removed the blower from his mouth.

For a moment, neither moved.

Then, somewhere to his left, the rabbit stepped out between two tables.

To his right came the bird.

The fox stood at the edge of the service corridor, head angled forward, hook hanging low.

All four.

Mr. Bean looked at them.

At the dead control panel.

At the stage.

Then his gaze settled on the party crown in his hand.

He opened it.

Placed it on his head.

Smiled.

The four figures remained still.

Mr. Bean raised both hands, palms outward.

A host’s gesture.

Welcome.

Lovely to see you.

He pointed toward the stage.

No one moved.

He tried a broader gesture.

This way.

Please.

Bonnie’s head tilted.

Chica’s jaw clicked.

Mr. Bean swallowed.

Then, in a small, unsteady voice, he began to hum the birthday tune.

He had heard it only once.

That was enough. It was not a complicated tune.

He hummed and clapped.

Once.

Twice.

He took a little sideways step.

Then another.

The rabbit’s guitar arm twitched.

Mr. Bean stopped.

The rabbit stopped.

Mr. Bean clapped again.

The guitar arm moved.

He stared.

Then he resumed with greater determination.

“Hm-hm-hm, hm-hm-hm…”

He pointed toward the stage.

Stepped in that direction.

Clapped.

The rabbit turned.

One heavy foot lifted.

Mr. Bean’s eyes widened.

Whether some fragment of a performance routine remained active in the old control system, whether the noise and gestures were being classified as a birthday cue, or whether the figures simply wanted him to go where he was going, he could not have said.

He did not pause to investigate.

He walked toward the stage, humming louder.

Bonnie followed.

Chica followed Bonnie.

Freddy followed Mr. Bean.

The fox came last, uneven footsteps scraping between the tables.

At the foot of the stage, Mr. Bean stopped and swept out one arm.

After you.

The rabbit climbed up.

The bird mounted the step beside him.

Mr. Bean almost laughed.

It was working.

Freddy stood in front of him.

Waiting.

Mr. Bean gestured toward the center position.

Freddy did not move.

Mr. Bean made the gesture larger.

The bear’s head turned.

Not toward the stage.

Toward the slight bulge inside Mr. Bean’s jacket.

Mr. Bean’s smile vanished.

Teddy’s head protruded above the top button.

Freddy looked at Teddy.

His large paw lifted.

Mr. Bean clapped both hands over his chest.

“No.”

The word was quiet.

Firm.

Freddy’s paw continued forward.

Mr. Bean took one step back.

Then another.

His heel struck the stage.

Behind the bear, Foxy moved closer.

Mr. Bean’s expression, for the first time that night, was not frightened or offended or calculating.

It was furious.

He seized the party blower.

Blew it directly into Freddy’s face.

The paper tube struck the bear between the eyes.

Freddy’s head jerked back.

Mr. Bean ducked beneath the raised paw, scrambled onto the stage, and squeezed between Bonnie and Chica.

There was a smell of old fabric, hot wiring, and pizza grease.

He could feel Teddy against his ribs.

Freddy turned below him.

The fox reached the foot of the stage.

Mr. Bean looked left.

Rabbit.

Right.

Bird.

Behind him, a painted backdrop.

Nowhere sensible to go.

So he did the only thing that remained.

He pretended to be part of the show.

He stood straight.

Raised one arm.

Opened his mouth in a fixed, foolish grin.

Freddy stared.

Mr. Bean moved his head to the left in three stiff increments.

Click.

Click.

Click.

He supplied the clicks himself.

Bonnie’s head turned toward him.

Mr. Bean turned his own head back.

Click.

Click.

He lifted one knee.

Lowered it.

Raised his hand to his mouth as though holding a microphone.

“Hm-hm-hm.”

Chica’s jaw opened.

Mr. Bean opened his.

Chica’s jaw closed.

Mr. Bean closed his.

The fox stopped.

For an extraordinary few seconds, the five figures stood together beneath the dead stage lights: four enormous restaurant mascots and one damp man in tweed wearing a paper crown.

Mr. Bean held his smile so hard that his cheeks began to tremble.

Freddy leaned closer.

One dark eye examined him.

Mr. Bean’s left eyelid twitched.

He forced it still.

The bear’s hand rose toward his face.

Then a car door slammed outside.

All four heads turned.

Mr. Bean did not.

He had committed to the performance.

Keys rattled at the front entrance.

A lock turned.

Footsteps entered the lobby.

“All right in there?”

Mr. Bean’s eyes moved toward the sound.

He did not otherwise react.

A man in a brown work coat walked into the dining room, carrying a ring of keys and a paper bag.

He looked at the stage.

At Mr. Bean.

At the animatronics gathered around him.

“Blimey.”

The man crossed to a locked panel beside the prize counter, opened it, and turned a large selector switch.

Somewhere behind the walls, a contactor slammed home.

The ceiling lights came on.

The stage bulbs lit.

Freddy straightened abruptly.

Bonnie’s arms returned to his guitar.

Chica pivoted into position.

Foxy’s shoulders sagged, and his head drooped forward.

A recorded chime sounded.

The wall clock above the kitchen clicked to six.

Mr. Bean remained frozen.

Mr. Hargreaves looked up at him.

“You the new night chap?”

Mr. Bean’s smile trembled.

“You can come down.”

Slowly, Mr. Bean lowered his arm.

His face relaxed.

His knees buckled.

He sat down heavily on the edge of the stage.

Mr. Hargreaves set the paper bag on a table.

“Rough first one?”

Mr. Bean turned toward him.

For a long time, he said nothing.

Then he took off the paper crown.

Folded it very carefully.

And dropped it into the nearest bin.

## 13. The Morning Report

Mrs. Pritchard arrived at six twenty-three.

Mr. Bean was in the office, wearing his damp jacket and holding Teddy.

Mr. Hargreaves had given him tea.

Mr. Bean had not drunk it.

He did not trust tea anymore.

Mrs. Pritchard stood in the doorway.

“I’ve had a look round.”

Mr. Bean stared at her.

“There’s a broken caution sign.”

He looked away.

“A birthday cake display in the kitchen.”

He rubbed Teddy’s ear.

“Cheese in Chica.”

He glanced at the ceiling.

“And someone’s taken the fluorescent tube out of here.”

Mr. Bean looked directly at the empty fitting, as though discovering this for the first time.

Mrs. Pritchard sighed.

“On the other hand, nothing’s missing, nobody got in, and you did stay until six.”

Mr. Bean sat slightly straighter.

Mr. Hargreaves appeared behind her, holding the night ledger.

“You want to read this.”

Mrs. Pritchard took it.

Her eyes moved down the page.

**Rabbit loose. Doors expensive.**

She turned a page.

**Rabbit cannot read.**

Another.

**Bird fed. Untidy eater.**

She reached the final entry.

**Bear.**

Mrs. Pritchard closed the book.

There was a brief silence.

“Perhaps,” she said, “this isn’t quite the position for you.”

Mr. Bean nodded.

Quite strongly.

“We do have a vacancy for a weekend party assistant.”

He stopped nodding.

Mrs. Pritchard gestured toward the dining room.

“Hargreaves says you got them all back to the stage.”

Mr. Bean stood.

He picked up his thermos.

His newspaper.

His cushion.

He put the squeegee in Mrs. Pritchard’s hands.

Then he removed his badge and placed it on top of the ledger.

“Oh,” she said.

He held out his hand.

She looked at it.

After a moment, understanding dawned.

“Your wages.”

Mr. Bean nodded.

“We normally pay Friday.”

He continued holding out his hand.

Mrs. Pritchard regarded him.

He regarded her.

Teddy regarded neither of them.

Finally, she opened the desk drawer, took out the petty-cash tin, and counted out twenty-five pounds and twenty pence.

Mr. Bean checked the amount.

Twice.

Then he tucked it into his wallet.

Mrs. Pritchard pushed a receipt toward him.

He signed it.

Under **Reason for Payment**, she had written:

**One overnight shift.**

Mr. Bean added a firm underline beneath **One**.

---

As he crossed the dining room, the stage system began its morning test.

The lights flashed.

Bonnie strummed.

Chica’s jaw opened and closed.

A small piece of cheese fell onto the stage.

Mr. Bean stopped.

He looked at her.

She stared over his head with a fixed, cheerful expression.

He raised one finger.

A final warning.

Then Freddy’s head turned.

The bear lifted his microphone.

Mr. Bean did not wait to hear what happened next.

He walked out of the restaurant at a speed that became, during the last six feet, a run.

## 14. The Companion Chair

The department store opened at nine.

Mr. Bean was outside at eight fifty-seven.

He had changed into a dry jacket.

Teddy had been brushed.

The flour was gone.

Except, on close inspection, from one ear.

At nine precisely, an assistant unlocked the doors.

Mr. Bean entered.

Walked directly to the display.

Lifted the little upholstered chair.

Examined it once more.

Real wooden feet.

Brass-colored studs.

A proper cushion.

He smiled.

At the till, he counted out £24.99.

The assistant put the chair in a large carrier bag.

“Someone’s in for a treat.”

Mr. Bean glanced down at Teddy.

“Yes.”

He carried the bag to a bench outside.

Removed the chair.

Placed it carefully beside him.

Then he sat Teddy in it.

The fit was excellent.

Teddy’s feet rested just above the pavement. His arms lay neatly along the upholstered sides. He looked comfortable, prosperous, and completely unaware of the labor that had supported his new circumstances.

Mr. Bean adjusted the cushion.

Sat back.

Folded his hands.

At last.

A satisfactory conclusion.

From inside the department store came a burst of electronic music.

Mr. Bean turned.

Near the entrance, an employee had activated a display of battery-operated toys.

A rabbit danced.

A yellow duck flapped its wings.

A fox in a little waistcoat waved one paw.

And in the middle of them stood a brown bear holding a microphone.

Mr. Bean’s face slowly emptied.

The bear began to sing.

He rose.

Picked up Teddy.

Picked up the chair.

And hurried toward the car.

---

That evening, after a restorative bath and an extremely early supper, Mr. Bean placed Teddy’s new armchair beside his bed.

He sat Teddy in it.

Straightened him.

Pulled the curtains.

Checked the window latch.

Checked it again.

Then he went to the bedroom door.

He examined the lock.

There was only one.

This now seemed inadequate.

He fetched a dining chair and wedged it beneath the handle.

Better.

He got into bed.

Turned off the lamp.

Lay still.

For several minutes, the flat was quiet.

Then, from beside the bed, came a soft mechanical click.

Mr. Bean’s eyes opened.

He turned his head.

In the darkness, Teddy sat in his new chair.

Motionless.

Mr. Bean stared.

Another click.

He reached very slowly toward the bedside lamp.

Switched it on.

Nothing had changed.

Teddy sat where he had been placed.

His new armchair leaned very slightly to the left.

Mr. Bean examined it.

One wooden foot had not been screwed in all the way.

He exhaled.

A long, relieved breath.

He tightened the foot.

Tested the chair.

Solid.

He gave Teddy an embarrassed little smile.

Then he switched off the lamp again.

A pause.

The lamp came back on.

Mr. Bean lifted Teddy out of the chair and brought him into bed.

He tucked the blanket beneath Teddy’s chin.

Considered the empty armchair.

Got up.

Carried it into the sitting room.

Shut the bedroom door.

Replaced the chair beneath the handle.

Then, finally, he returned to bed.

Just before turning out the light, he looked down at Teddy and gave him a stern, meaningful glance.

“Stay.”

Teddy did.

answer:
# **Whitney’s Last Badge**
*A Pokémon fan script*

**Characters**
- **Whitney** — Goldenrod City’s Gym Leader
- **Alex** — A visiting Pokémon Trainer
- **Mara** — A Goldenrod Gym attendant
- **Nurse Joy**
- **Clefairy**
- **Miltank**

---

## **Scene One: One Last Rollout**

*Goldenrod Gym shakes with the sound of a heavy impact.*

*Miltank skids across the battlefield, her hooves scraping against the floor. Across from her, Alex’s Heracross struggles to remain upright.*

*Whitney grips the railing of her platform.*

**WHITNEY:** Come on, Miltank! They’re barely standing! One more hit and we’ve got this!

**ALEX:** Heracross, keep your eyes on her!

*Miltank snorts. She lowers her head, trying to steady herself.*

**WHITNEY:** Rollout! Let’s finish it!

*Miltank curls into a ball and barrels forward.*

**ALEX:** Wait for it…

*The rolling Pokémon thunders closer.*

**WHITNEY:** There’s nowhere left to dodge!

**ALEX:** Now! Brace yourself and use Brick Break!

*Heracross plants its feet. Its arm glows, then swings down.*

*A sharp crack echoes through the Gym.*

*Miltank tumbles out of her roll and lands on her side.*

**WHITNEY:** Miltank?

*Heracross drops to one knee.*

*Miltank tries to rise. One hoof slips. After another exhausted effort, she settles back onto the floor.*

*Mara raises a flag.*

**MARA:** Miltank is unable to battle! Heracross wins! The victory goes to challenger Alex!

*There is a little applause from the waiting trainers.*

*Whitney doesn’t move.*

**ALEX:** You did it, Heracross.

*Alex kneels beside Heracross, resting a hand on its shoulder.*

**ALEX:** That was close. Really close.

**WHITNEY:** No.

*The applause stops.*

**MARA:** Whitney—

**WHITNEY:** No, hang on. She can still—

*Miltank looks up at her.*

*Whitney’s mouth remains open, but the command never comes.*

*She steps off her platform and runs onto the field.*

**WHITNEY:** Hey. Hey, don’t get up.

*She kneels beside Miltank, gently brushing dust off her face.*

**WHITNEY:** You’re okay. I’ve got you.

**MILTANK:** Mil…

**WHITNEY:** I know.

*Whitney recalls Miltank. She stares at the Poké Ball.*

**ALEX:** Whitney? That was an amazing battle.

**WHITNEY:** Please don’t.

**ALEX:** I just meant—

**WHITNEY:** I know what you meant.

*Her voice is sharper than she intended. Alex falls quiet.*

*Whitney wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist, angry that she has to.*

**WHITNEY:** Congratulations. You won.

*She turns toward the side door.*

**MARA:** Whitney. The badge.

*Whitney stops.*

*For several seconds, all anyone can hear is the Gym’s ventilation system.*

**WHITNEY:** Right.

*She reaches into her pocket and takes out a Plain Badge. Her fingers shake.*

**WHITNEY:** Almost forgot the important part.

---

## **Scene Two: The Badge**

*Alex stands a few steps away, uncertain whether to approach.*

*Whitney holds out the badge without looking at them.*

**WHITNEY:** Here.

**ALEX:** Thank you.

*Alex takes it.*

**WHITNEY:** There. Official.

**MARA:** And the registration, Whitney.

**WHITNEY:** Can you do it?

**MARA:** Of course.

*Whitney gives a short, humorless laugh.*

**WHITNEY:** Great. Wonderful. Then we’re done.

**ALEX:** Did I do something wrong?

*Whitney looks up.*

**WHITNEY:** What?

**ALEX:** If I said something—

**WHITNEY:** No! You didn’t do anything wrong!

*Her voice echoes. Clefairy peeks around the side door.*

*Whitney sees several waiting trainers watching her. One quickly looks down at his shoes.*

**WHITNEY:** You trained your Pokémon. You came here. You beat me. That’s what you’re supposed to do.

**ALEX:** Okay.

**WHITNEY:** So don’t stand there looking guilty. I don’t need that too.

**MARA:** Whitney, let’s go into the office.

**WHITNEY:** Why? So I can cry in there instead?

*Mara says nothing.*

*Whitney’s face reddens.*

**WHITNEY:** I know how this goes. Everybody gives me a few minutes, someone says I did my best, and then I come back out smiling for the next challenger.

**MARA:** We can cancel the next match.

**WHITNEY:** And tomorrow?

**MARA:** We don’t have to decide that right now.

**WHITNEY:** There’s always another match!

*Clefairy walks onto the battlefield.*

**CLEFAIRY:** Clefairy?

*Whitney glances down. Her expression falters.*

**WHITNEY:** Not now, sweetie.

*Clefairy stops.*

*Whitney immediately crouches and reaches for her.*

**WHITNEY:** No, I didn’t mean—come here.

*Clefairy presses against her. Whitney holds her tightly.*

**WHITNEY:** I didn’t mean you.

*After a moment, Whitney stands.*

**WHITNEY:** Cancel them.

**MARA:** Today’s challengers?

**WHITNEY:** All of them.

**MARA:** Whitney—

**WHITNEY:** I’m quitting.

*Alex looks toward Mara.*

**MARA:** You’re upset.

**WHITNEY:** Yes, Mara. I’m very upset. I think everybody noticed.

**MARA:** I mean you don’t have to make a permanent decision five minutes after a loss.

**WHITNEY:** Maybe I should’ve made it before the loss, then.

*Whitney picks up Clefairy.*

**WHITNEY:** Close the Gym. Tell the League. Tell whoever needs telling.

*She looks briefly at Alex.*

**WHITNEY:** Your badge still counts.

*Then she disappears through the side door.*

---

## **Scene Three: Behind the Pink Door**

*The Gym office is cheerful in a way Whitney suddenly finds unbearable.*

*There are framed tournament photographs, pink curtains, a shelf of Pokémon figurines, and a hand-lettered poster reading: KEEP ROLLING!*

*Whitney shuts the door with her heel.*

*She sets Clefairy on the couch, then pulls the poster off the wall.*

*One corner tears.*

**WHITNEY:** Of course.

*She tries to peel away the remaining scrap. It refuses to come loose.*

**WHITNEY:** Come on.

*She picks at it harder.*

**WHITNEY:** Come on!

*The paper tears again.*

*Whitney throws what remains onto her desk.*

**WHITNEY:** Fine! Stay there!

*Clefairy watches her.*

*Whitney sinks into her chair.*

**WHITNEY:** I’m yelling at paper.

*A knock.*

**WHITNEY:** I don’t want a pep talk.

**MARA, outside:** Good. I didn’t prepare one.

*Whitney rubs her eyes.*

**WHITNEY:** Come in.

*Mara enters carrying a glass of water.*

**MARA:** Nurse Joy’s expecting Miltank. I can take her over.

*Whitney takes Miltank’s Poké Ball from her pocket. She hesitates before handing it over.*

**WHITNEY:** Tell her the last hit was to the shoulder.

**MARA:** I will.

**WHITNEY:** And she’d already used Milk Drink, but she was still tired. I thought—

*She stops.*

**MARA:** I’ll tell her.

*Mara sets the water on the desk.*

**MARA:** The waiting trainers have gone. Alex’s paperwork is finished.

**WHITNEY:** Are they angry?

**MARA:** Disappointed. Mostly worried about you.

**WHITNEY:** That’s worse.

*Mara sits in the chair across from her.*

**MARA:** Do you want me to call the League?

*Whitney looks surprised.*

**WHITNEY:** You’re not going to tell me I’m being ridiculous?

**MARA:** I think you had a bad afternoon. I also think you’ve been having quite a few bad afternoons.

*Whitney looks away.*

**MARA:** Last week, you stayed in here for forty minutes before the first challenge.

**WHITNEY:** I had a headache.

**MARA:** I know. And on Tuesday you asked me whether the reservation system could accidentally lose an entire day.

*Whitney almost smiles.*

**WHITNEY:** You said no very quickly.

**MARA:** I’ve learned to recognize that tone.

*Whitney turns the glass between her hands.*

**WHITNEY:** I hate losing.

**MARA:** I know.

**WHITNEY:** No, I really hate it. I know all the things I’m supposed to say. “You learn from every battle.” “A loss helps you grow.” I’ve said them to challengers.

**MARA:** Sometimes they’re true.

**WHITNEY:** Sometimes I just lose and feel rotten.

*She takes a drink.*

**WHITNEY:** And then I feel stupid for feeling rotten, because it’s one match. Nobody stole my Pokémon. The roof didn’t fall in. Some trainer was better than me today.

**MARA:** That doesn’t make the disappointment imaginary.

**WHITNEY:** It makes running out of my own Gym pretty embarrassing.

**MARA:** Yes.

*Whitney looks at her.*

**MARA:** You said you didn’t want a pep talk.

*Whitney lets out a startled laugh, then presses both hands over her face.*

**WHITNEY:** Oh, I was awful to them.

**MARA:** A little.

**WHITNEY:** They said it was a good battle.

**MARA:** It was.

**WHITNEY:** I know.

*She lowers her hands.*

**WHITNEY:** That’s what’s making me so angry. Miltank did everything I asked. Clefairy worked hard. Alex wasn’t showing off. There’s nobody to blame, and I’m still furious.

*Clefairy climbs onto Whitney’s lap.*

*Whitney strokes one of her ears.*

**WHITNEY:** I keep bringing it home now. I replay matches while I’m eating. I wake up remembering moves I should’ve called. When someone asks for a picture, I wonder if they’re going to make a joke about making me cry.

**MARA:** Have people done that?

**WHITNEY:** A few.

*She shrugs, trying to make it smaller.*

**WHITNEY:** Enough that I think about it.

*Mara sits back.*

**MARA:** You could take leave.

**WHITNEY:** And spend the whole leave counting down until I have to come back?

**MARA:** Maybe. Or discover you miss it.

**WHITNEY:** I don’t want to miss it. Not right now.

*Whitney looks around the room.*

**WHITNEY:** I want one day where nobody wants me to prove anything.

---

## **Scene Four: Pokémon Center**

*By evening, Goldenrod’s streets glow with shop signs and streetlights.*

*Whitney sits beside Miltank’s recovery bed. Clefairy is asleep against her hip.*

*Nurse Joy checks a monitor, then removes a small sensor from Miltank’s shoulder.*

**NURSE JOY:** She’ll be fine. Rest tonight, nothing strenuous tomorrow.

**WHITNEY:** No battling?

**NURSE JOY:** Not tomorrow.

**WHITNEY:** That won’t be a problem.

*Nurse Joy notices her tone but doesn’t press.*

**NURSE JOY:** I’ll get her discharge notes.

*She leaves.*

*Miltank nudges Whitney’s hand.*

**WHITNEY:** Hey, you.

**MILTANK:** Miltank.

**WHITNEY:** I’m sorry about all the shouting.

*Miltank tilts her head.*

**WHITNEY:** You didn’t do anything wrong.

*Whitney leans forward, resting her forehead against Miltank’s.*

**WHITNEY:** I need you to know that part.

*There is a hesitant voice from behind her.*

**ALEX:** Whitney?

*Whitney straightens. Alex stands near the doorway with Heracross.*

**ALEX:** Sorry. Nurse Joy said Miltank was doing okay. I wanted to check before we left.

**WHITNEY:** She’s fine.

**ALEX:** Good.

*A pause.*

**WHITNEY:** Wait.

*Alex stops turning away.*

**WHITNEY:** I owe you an apology.

**ALEX:** You don’t have to—

**WHITNEY:** Yes, I do. I snapped at you because I lost. You shouldn’t have had to stand there wondering if you’d done something bad.

**ALEX:** I wasn’t sure what to say.

**WHITNEY:** You said the normal, nice thing. I just didn’t want to hear it.

*Alex nods.*

**WHITNEY:** And that Brick Break? Good timing.

**ALEX:** We practiced that a lot.

**WHITNEY:** It showed.

*Heracross gives a pleased little sound.*

**ALEX:** Are you really quitting?

*Whitney glances at Miltank.*

**WHITNEY:** Yeah.

**ALEX:** Because of our battle?

*Whitney takes a moment.*

**WHITNEY:** Today pushed me into saying it. But I’ve been miserable about this for a while.

**ALEX:** I’m sorry.

**WHITNEY:** Don’t apologize for winning. Please.

*Her voice softens.*

**WHITNEY:** Go enjoy your badge.

*Alex touches the badge case clipped to their bag.*

**ALEX:** I will.

**WHITNEY:** Good.

**ALEX:** Take care, Whitney.

**WHITNEY:** You too. Both of you.

*Alex and Heracross leave.*

*Whitney watches them go, then looks back at Miltank.*

**WHITNEY:** That went better than the first conversation.

*Miltank nudges her again.*

---

## **Scene Five: The Call**

*The next morning, Whitney sits at her office desk in ordinary clothes.*

*Her Gym uniform hangs on the back of the door.*

*Mara stands beside a box containing Whitney’s photographs and figurines.*

*A League administrator’s voice comes through the speakerphone.*

**LEAGUE ADMINISTRATOR:** We can process this as an immediate leave of absence while you consider your position.

**WHITNEY:** I’ve considered it.

**LEAGUE ADMINISTRATOR:** A resignation requires a written notice, a badge inventory, and arrangements for the Gym’s temporary management.

**WHITNEY:** Mara has the inventory. I’m writing the notice.

**LEAGUE ADMINISTRATOR:** Understood. May I ask your reason for stepping down?

*Whitney looks at the unfinished letter.*

**WHITNEY:** I’m frustrated all the time. Yesterday I lost a match and took it out on the challenger.

*She swallows.*

**WHITNEY:** I don’t want to keep doing that. And I don’t want to keep battling.

**LEAGUE ADMINISTRATOR:** All right. I’ll send the necessary forms.

**WHITNEY:** Thank you.

*The call ends.*

*Whitney stares at the phone.*

**MARA:** How do you feel?

**WHITNEY:** Like I’m going to be sick.

**MARA:** There’s a bin under the desk.

*Whitney laughs weakly.*

**WHITNEY:** Also relieved.

**MARA:** That’s easier to clean up.

*Whitney turns back to the letter and begins writing.*

*Mara resumes packing.*

**WHITNEY:** Leave the tournament photo.

**MARA:** This one?

*She holds up a photograph of Whitney with Clefairy and Miltank, all three crowded around a trophy.*

**WHITNEY:** Yeah.

**MARA:** You don’t want it?

**WHITNEY:** I do. Just… not in the box.

*Mara places it on the desk beside her.*

*Whitney studies her younger, beaming face.*

**WHITNEY:** I really liked that day.

**MARA:** You talked about it for months.

**WHITNEY:** I know. You hid the trophy once.

**MARA:** You brought it to lunch six times.

*Whitney smiles, briefly.*

*Then she signs the letter.*

---

## **Scene Six: No Match Scheduled**

*Late afternoon. Whitney stands at the Gym entrance with a box balanced against her hip.*

*A temporary closure notice is taped to the glass.*

*Inside, the battlefield lights are off.*

*Whitney looks toward the far platform.*

**WHITNEY:** I thought I’d be angrier when I left.

**MARA:** You’ve had a busy couple of days.

**WHITNEY:** Give me ten minutes. I might get started again.

*Mara holds out her hand.*

*Whitney places the Gym keys in it, then immediately closes her fingers around them again.*

**WHITNEY:** Sorry.

**MARA:** Take your time.

*Whitney takes one last look.*

*Then she lets go.*

**WHITNEY:** There.

*Mara pockets the keys.*

**MARA:** Call me tomorrow?

**WHITNEY:** About the paperwork?

**MARA:** About lunch.

**WHITNEY:** Oh.

*Whitney nods.*

**WHITNEY:** Yeah. Lunch sounds good.

---

*At home, Whitney sets the box by the couch.*

*Miltank walks straight to her favorite cushion. Clefairy follows Whitney into the kitchen.*

*The apartment is quiet.*

*Whitney opens the refrigerator, stares inside, and closes it again.*

**WHITNEY:** I forgot to buy groceries.

**CLEFAIRY:** Clefairy.

**WHITNEY:** Yes, that is usually part of making dinner.

*She finds a takeaway menu in a drawer.*

*Her phone buzzes.*

*A reminder fills the screen:*

**TOMORROW — 9:00 A.M. — GYM TRAINING**

*Whitney stands still.*

*She taps the reminder.*

*Then she deletes the recurring event.*

*Miltank lifts her head from the cushion.*

**WHITNEY:** Nothing tomorrow.

*Whitney sits beside her. Clefairy climbs up on the other side.*

**WHITNEY:** No drills. No challengers. No practicing Rollout until I’m sick of hearing my own voice.

*Miltank settles her head in Whitney’s lap.*

*Whitney rests a hand between her horns.*

**WHITNEY:** I’m still mad, you know.

*Clefairy leans against her arm.*

**WHITNEY:** I still think we could’ve won.

*She exhales, slowly.*

**WHITNEY:** But we’re not having a rematch.

*Outside, a train pulls into Goldenrod Station. Its distant brakes squeal, then fade.*

*Whitney picks up the menu.*

**WHITNEY:** All right. Who wants dinner?

*Clefairy raises both arms.*

*Miltank gives an eager rumble.*

*For the first time all day, Whitney’s smile comes easily.*

**FADE OUT.**

# Yakko, Wakko & Dot vs. Discord
## *The Last Laugh*

**Research note:** I can’t perform live web searches in this chat, so I can’t honestly claim to have searched Fandom. The analysis below uses established portrayals of the characters, and I’ve included relevant Fandom reference links at the end. The battle is an original crossover interpretation—not an official result.

**Battle conditions:** A deserted studio backlot, with no preparation, outside help, or prior knowledge of the opposition. Victory requires incapacitating the entire opposing side. The Warners count as one team.

---

# Character Analysis

## Yakko Warner

### Abilities and arsenal

Yakko’s greatest weapon is his intelligence expressed through comedy. He typically assumes the leadership role among the Warner siblings, interpreting a situation quickly and directing a coordinated response.

His cartoon abilities include:

- **Hammerspace:** Producing props far larger than anything he could reasonably carry.
- **Cartoon resilience:** Recovering from impacts and deformations that would incapacitate a conventional opponent.
- **Disguises and theatrical deception:** Turning a confrontation into a staged routine and maneuvering another character into playing along.
- **Fourth-wall awareness:** Addressing the audience and treating aspects of the presentation as part of the joke.
- **Improvised equipment:** Mallets, explosives, signs, costumes, and other gag-dependent objects.
- **Verbal misdirection:** Distracting and frustrating opponents with rapid jokes, misunderstandings, and deliberate literalism.

### Fighting approach

Yakko is most dangerous when an opponent tries to argue with him. Every response gives him material, and every interruption gives his siblings another opening.

However, fourth-wall jokes do **not** automatically establish unlimited control over a crossover’s story. He can exploit cartoon conventions without necessarily possessing unrestricted authority over another character’s powers.

---

## Wakko Warner

### Abilities and arsenal

Wakko is the trio’s most straightforward source of physical chaos.

His usual resources include:

- **A seemingly bottomless gag bag**, containing improbable tools and weapons.
- **Large mallets and other oversized props.**
- **Explosives and slapstick traps.**
- **An enormous appetite**, including the ability to eat things that would not ordinarily qualify as food.
- **Cartoon bodily flexibility and resilience.**
- **Unpredictable improvisation**, making his attacks difficult to anticipate conventionally.

### Fighting approach

Wakko overwhelms opponents with successive physical gags: a blow becomes an explosion, the explosion becomes a prop change, and the prop change produces another blow.

His limitation here is that hitting Discord harder is not necessarily meaningful. A being who can rearrange his own body and transform incoming objects may not need to absorb a blow in the first place.

---

## Dot Warner

### Abilities and arsenal

Dot combines the same broad cartoon resilience as her brothers with a more pointed ability to manipulate attention.

Her arsenal includes:

- **Hammerspace and improvised cartoon weapons.**
- **Disguises and performance-based trickery.**
- **Explosive shifts between apparent sweetness and aggression.**
- **Psychological manipulation**, especially against arrogant opponents.
- **Strong coordination with Yakko and Wakko.**

### Fighting approach

Dot is likely to recognize the emotional weak point in an otherwise overwhelming adversary. Against Discord, that means his vanity, theatricality, and desire to prove that he is the most entertaining presence in the room.

Her cuteness is a useful distraction, not an irresistible supernatural power. Against an opponent who stops indulging her performance, she needs her siblings’ support.

---

## Discord

### Abilities and arsenal

Discord is a draconequus whose magic can reshape his surroundings on a massive scale. His powers are not merely visual jokes; they repeatedly produce physical and psychological changes within his setting.

Relevant abilities include:

- **Reality alteration:** Changing the behavior, appearance, and arrangement of his environment.
- **Transmutation:** Transforming objects and creatures.
- **Teleportation and unusual spatial movement.**
- **Conjuration:** Producing objects, structures, and other manifestations.
- **Shapeshifting and bodily rearrangement.**
- **Levitation and telekinetic manipulation.**
- **Environmental control**, including weather and gravity-related absurdities.
- **Mental and personality manipulation:** Most notably demonstrated when he corrupts the dispositions of Twilight Sparkle’s friends.
- **Large-scale illusion and perceptual deception.**

### Fighting approach

Discord prefers to humiliate opponents before defeating them. He creates situations in which their expectations work against them, often allowing resistance because resistance entertains him.

That is also his major weakness: **he can be careless, vain, and distractible**. His magic is immense, but he is neither omniscient nor incapable of being caught off guard.

### Important matchup distinction

Both sides use absurdity, but not in exactly the same way:

- The Warners excel at **surviving, interrupting, and reversing cartoon situations**.
- Discord can **deliberately rewrite the situation itself**, including an opponent’s perceptions and disposition.

The Warners have excellent resistance to ordinary physical punishment. They do not have comparably clear, consistent protection against direct magical personality alteration.

**Likely advantage:** Discord, provided he stops trying to win a comedy contest and starts using his more decisive abilities.

# The Battle

## Part 1: An Unscheduled Cancellation

The deserted studio backlot lay beneath a pale afternoon sky. Painted storefronts faced one another across an empty street, and the Warner water tower stood above them like a watchful metal giant.

Then the sky folded.

It bent along a sharp crease, revealing a checkerboard underside. Purple rain fell upward. A streetlamp twisted into a flamingo and stalked away.

Yakko stopped walking.

“Either the effects department got a raise, or somebody put something in the coffee.”

Wakko held up his cup, looked inside, and swallowed it whole.

Dot watched a familiar studio building stretch into a long, crooked staircase.

“That’s our dressing room.”

Suspended above the street was a creature none of them recognized: serpentine body, mismatched limbs, antlers, horn, and a grin too comfortable for the circumstances.

Discord examined the backlot with open distaste.

“Painted scenery. Repeated architecture. Predictable weather. Honestly, who approved this place?”

He snapped his fingers.

The water tower became a porcelain teapot.

The three siblings went still.

Yakko’s smile narrowed. “You’ve redecorated our house.”

“You’re welcome.”

Dot stepped forward. “Change it back.”

Discord lowered his head toward her.

“No.”

A laugh track sounded from nowhere.

None of the Warners laughed.

Yakko rolled up his sleeves (despite not having any).

“All right, tall, dark, and taxidermied.”

Wakko opened his gag bag.

“Let’s redecorate *him*.”

---

## Part 2: First Contact

Wakko struck first.

His mallet emerged from the bag headfirst, followed by a handle that seemed to keep arriving. He swung with both hands.

**WHAM!**

Discord flattened against the street in a bright, serpentine silhouette.

Dot immediately dragged a printing press over him. Yakko cranked its handle.

A newspaper rolled out.

[LOCAL NUISANCE PRESSED FOR COMMENT]

Yakko lifted it toward the invisible audience.

“Finally, something worth reading.”

The photograph on the front page turned its head.

Discord’s printed eyes narrowed.

“Derivative.”

He stepped out of the newspaper, unfolding himself into three dimensions. The press sprouted hooves and kicked Yakko through a false storefront.

Wakko charged again.

Discord caught the mallet’s descending head between two fingers. It became a bouquet of daisies.

Wakko ate them.

For the first time, Discord hesitated.

Wakko spat the stems into his face.

Dot’s anvil arrived a heartbeat later.

**CLANG!**

Discord’s head sank into his shoulders. His antlers vibrated like tuning forks.

Yakko emerged from the broken storefront wearing a shopkeeper’s apron.

“Can I interest you in a headache remedy?”

He hurled the entire shop counter.

Discord vanished before it hit.

The counter smashed into Wakko, who briefly became an accordion.

Discord reappeared on the teapot’s spout.

“Oh,” he said softly. “You’re *those* kinds of creatures.”

He still did not know what they were.

But he had learned that ordinary injury would not settle the matter.

---

## Part 3: The Wrong Kind of Playground

Discord snapped both hands.

The street rose into a vertical wall.

Yakko and Dot slid upward. Wakko fell sideways through a window, emerged from a chimney, and landed on the underside of a floating taxi.

Gravity changed again.

The taxi dropped toward the other two.

Yakko produced a traffic sign.

[NO FALLING BETWEEN 2 AND 5 P.M.]

The taxi stopped inches above his head.

Discord stared.

Dot checked an imaginary wristwatch.

“You’ll have to come back later.”

With a flick of his claw, Discord turned the sign into a venomously hissing ribbon. Dot struck it with a tennis racket, sending it back around his snout.

Wakko pulled a portable hole from his bag and slapped it against the airborne pavement.

All three Warners jumped through.

They emerged directly above Discord.

Yakko held a piano.

Dot held the stool.

Wakko held a second, considerably larger piano.

The resulting crash demolished the teapot’s spout.

Porcelain rained across the backlot.

Discord reassembled himself out of falling musical notes, his smile now showing teeth.

He had expected fear, confusion, perhaps begging.

Instead, these intruders into his new playground were using it as freely as he was.

“Do you have any respect,” he demanded, “for the artistry involved?”

Yakko dusted off his hands.

“We’ll let you know when we see some.”

---

## Part 4: Stage Fright

Dot noticed the reaction first.

Not the snapping fingers. Not the floating debris.

The pause before his reply.

She leaned toward Yakko.

“He hates being upstaged.”

Yakko’s grin returned.

“Then let’s give him a show.”

He blew a whistle.

Curtains descended across the street. Footlights burst through the pavement. Wakko appeared behind a drum kit, and Dot stepped into a spotlight wearing a glittering gown.

Discord found himself seated in the front row.

He had not agreed to sit.

That alone made his expression dangerous.

Yakko strode onto the stage.

“Ladies, gentlemen, and whatever’s happening in seat one: welcome!”

Dot pointed at Discord.

“Our special guest appears to have been assembled from the leftovers.”

Wakko punctuated the line with a drumroll.

Discord rose.

His chair clamped around his waist.

Yakko continued, faster.

“He’s got a lion’s paw, an eagle’s claw, and apparently nobody’s permission.”

Dot flicked a lever behind the curtain.

The spotlight above Discord dropped.

He teleported away—

—and emerged inside a glass cabinet onstage.

Yakko slapped a sign against it.

[PLEASE DO NOT FEED THE EGO]

For one sharp moment, Discord saw the trick: the cabinet had simply been placed where he chose to reappear. No cosmic superiority, no cancellation of his magic.

Just excellent timing.

Then Wakko detonated the charges beneath the stage.

The explosion tore through the street and sent scenery spinning into the sky.

When the smoke cleared, Discord hovered over a crater.

His eyes had lost their playfulness.

“You’re finished.”

Dot discarded her gown.

“Now he’s getting the premise.”

---

## Part 5: No More Audience

Discord did not attack the siblings.

He attacked their coordination.

Three doors appeared beneath their feet.

Yakko fell through the first.

Wakko dropped through the second.

Dot caught the third doorframe with both hands, but the frame softened like wax. Her fingers slipped.

The doors slammed.

Silence replaced the shattered backlot.

Yakko landed in a corridor of mirrors. Every reflection spoke a fraction of a second before he did.

Wakko found himself in an endless kitchen. His gag bag sat on a countertop, visible behind a transparent wall.

Dot stood in an empty theater.

Discord’s voice came from every seat.

“There. Much better. You were beginning to interrupt one another.”

Yakko pulled a saw from behind his back and cut a doorway into a mirror.

Behind it was another corridor.

He cut again.

Another corridor.

Wakko bit the transparent barrier.

His teeth squeaked. He frowned, took out a napkin, and tied it around his neck.

Dot ignored the phantom audience.

“You separated us because three against one was embarrassing.”

Discord appeared in the royal box.

“I separated you because I can.”

She studied him.

That answer was less theatrical.

More troubling.

---

## Part 6: Breaking the Rooms

Yakko stopped cutting.

He examined his reflections.

They anticipated his jokes, gestures, and movements—but not perfectly. They were distractions constructed around his own behavior.

So he did nothing.

The reflections kept talking.

Yakko smiled without looking at them and reached into his pocket.

He pulled out a paintbrush.

A few strokes covered the nearest mirror in black paint. More strokes added a frame, a handle, and the words:

[EMERGENCY EXIT]

He opened it.

Beyond lay not freedom, but the outer edge of Discord’s conjured corridor: a twisting service space full of impossible angles.

“Good enough.”

Elsewhere, Wakko had eaten the kitchen wall.

Not the transparent barrier.

The wall beside it.

He crawled around the obstruction, retrieved his bag, and produced a jackhammer.

Dot, meanwhile, had climbed onto the theater stage.

“If you’re going to threaten me,” she called, “come down here and do it without the balcony.”

Discord vanished from the royal box and appeared before her.

She smiled.

“There you are.”

Wakko’s jackhammer broke through the floor between them.

Yakko fell from a painted doorway overhead.

All three collided with Discord at once.

They tumbled out of the collapsing illusion and into the wrecked backlot.

Yakko caught Dot’s hand. Dot seized Wakko’s sleeve.

The siblings landed together.

For the first time, Discord looked genuinely angry.

The Warners had escaped his traps.

But they had also revealed something important:

They worked hard to reunite.

He decided to use that.

---

## Part 7: The Vanishing Act

Discord raised his paw.

Wakko’s bag disappeared.

Wakko immediately reached behind his back and produced another mallet.

Discord turned it into dust.

Dot drew an oversized hammer.

It became a flock of moths.

Yakko pulled out a cannon.

Discord transformed its barrel into a long rubber neck, which bent around and swallowed its own wheels.

The Warners scattered.

Discord followed without moving. His head appeared in windows, puddles, scraps of glass—watching from every reflective surface.

Yakko hurled a lit bomb into a puddle.

The reflection opened its mouth.

The bomb vanished.

A distant explosion flashed behind Discord’s teeth.

He shut his mouth, smoke curling from his ears.

It hurt—or at least inconvenienced him enough to make him snarl.

Wakko used that instant to strike with a sledgehammer pulled from beneath his hat.

Discord’s torso separated around it.

His eagle claw closed around Wakko’s wrist.

A sharp pulse of magic ran across the contact.

Wakko’s colors flickered.

His expression went strangely blank.

Then Dot hit Discord’s claw with both feet, breaking the grip.

Wakko stumbled backward.

Yakko caught him.

“You all right?”

Wakko blinked.

For a moment, he looked at the mallet as though he had forgotten what it was for.

Then his usual grin returned.

“Think so.”

Yakko’s own grin disappeared.

That attack had been different.

---

## Part 8: The Last Big Gag

“Don’t let him touch you,” Yakko said.

Discord heard.

His anger softened into something colder.

“So you *can* learn.”

Yakko ignored him and whispered to his siblings.

They split in three directions.

Dot ran directly toward Discord, shouting insults fast enough to keep his eyes on her. Wakko dragged a fuse through the wreckage, leaving it conspicuously visible.

Yakko disappeared behind the remains of the studio entrance.

Discord watched Dot approach.

“No more little performances.”

He snapped.

The ground beneath her became a steep glass slope.

She slid toward him—

—then lifted a small sign.

[STUNT DOUBLE]

The Dot-shaped bundle burst open, releasing a swarm of mousetraps.

They snapped across Discord’s face.

Wakko lit the fuse.

Discord reflexively teleported above the street, clear of the apparent blast zone.

Exactly where Yakko wanted him.

A giant iron weight dropped from a crane.

Discord looked up.

Printed across its underside were the words:

[SUBTLE FORESHADOWING]

It struck him squarely.

The weight drove him through the pavement and into the buried explosive rig Wakko had assembled.

The backlot vanished inside a rolling fireball.

Windows burst across the false buildings. The crane folded. The remaining teapot fragments disintegrated.

Yakko, Wakko, and Dot sheltered behind an absurdly small umbrella while debris thundered around them.

Then silence.

Wakko peered around the umbrella.

“Did we get him?”

A single finger tapped Yakko’s shoulder.

“No,” Discord said.

He stood behind them.

His outline was ragged, his eyes furious, and his usual theatrical posture was gone.

The attack had caught him.

It had not removed his ability to reshape the fight.

---

## Part 9: Silence Between the Jokes

Yakko shoved his siblings away and swung a boxing glove on a spring.

Discord let it strike his face.

His head bent backward.

His body remained still.

Before Yakko could retract the spring, Discord’s claw caught his forehead.

The magic arrived without an explosion.

Yakko saw the backlot become a quiet office.

Neat desks. Straight lines. No audience. No interruptions.

He tried to make a joke.

For one moment, he could not remember why he wanted to.

His colors began to fade.

Dot screamed his name and attacked from Discord’s left.

Discord split his upper body around her hammer. A lion’s paw emerged from the displaced mass and touched her brow.

She recoiled.

The studio seemed to become an empty dressing room. No applause. No rivals. No one whose opinion mattered.

Her fury dulled into heavy indifference.

Wakko struck Discord from behind with everything he could produce: mallet, frying pan, cannonball, anchor.

The blows drove Discord forward.

His spell on Dot broke before it was complete.

She staggered, fighting to regain focus.

Yakko remained standing beside Discord, gray and motionless.

“Yakko!” Wakko shouted.

His brother looked at him.

There was recognition.

But no impulse to help.

That instant of hesitation was enough.

Discord turned and caught Wakko beneath the chin.

The second pulse of mental magic took hold faster than the first.

Wakko’s raised mallet lowered.

Dot forced herself upright.

For the first time in the fight, she was alone.

---

## Part 10: The End of the Show

Dot did not run.

She reached behind her back and drew a detonator.

Discord looked at it, then at the long cable disappearing beneath his feet.

“You really are persistent.”

Dot’s hand tightened.

“And you talk too much.”

She pushed the plunger.

Nothing happened.

Discord opened his other hand.

Inside it sat the disconnected end of the cable.

Dot threw the detonator at his face and lunged past him toward her brothers.

She nearly reached them.

Yakko stood with his hands at his sides. Wakko stared silently at the ruined street.

“Come on,” Dot hissed, grabbing their arms. “Snap out of it.”

Neither moved.

Behind her, Discord’s shadow stretched across the pavement.

Dot turned and produced one final mallet.

He caught its handle.

She kicked his paw, released the weapon, and tried to duck beneath his arm.

A small flash of magic exchanged the space ahead of her with the space directly in front of him.

His claw touched her forehead.

Dot fought it.

Her expression twisted with anger. One hand reached toward Yakko. The other curled into a fist.

“You don’t get,” she whispered, “the last—”

Her colors faded.

Her hand fell.

Discord held the contact a moment longer, ensuring the altered disposition settled. Then he withdrew.

All three Warners remained upright and conscious.

All three had lost the will to continue fighting.

No hidden hammer followed. No sudden drumroll broke the silence. Discord had not battered them into submission; he had used a kind of attack their physical resilience could not answer.

“Sit,” he said.

They sat on the broken curb.

He conjured three transparent enclosures around them, keeping the incapacitated siblings separated while he regarded the devastation.

The backlot was a cratered ruin. His elaborate playground had been demolished. His opponents had repeatedly outmaneuvered and humiliated him.

His victory had cost him the pleasure of pretending it was effortless.

Discord straightened his bow tie.

Above the street, a final sign appeared:

[SHOW CANCELLED]

He stared at it for a moment.

Then, without a smile, he snapped it out of existence.

**Winner: Discord.**

---

# Why Discord Wins This Version

The Warners make the fight competitive because their teamwork, improvisation, and cartoon resilience undermine Discord’s preferred style. Trying to frighten them, crush them, or trap them in an elaborate gag gives them opportunities to retaliate.

Their strongest route to victory is exploiting his ego long enough to land a decisive surprise. They successfully create those openings here—but their conventional gag weapons do not reliably neutralize his magic.

Discord’s winning adjustment is **targeting their minds rather than their bodies**.

His demonstrated personality-altering magic provides a stronger basis for incapacitation than assuming that sufficiently large explosions will defeat him. The exact crossover interaction is necessarily speculative, but the Warners do not have a firmly established blanket immunity to this kind of attack.

This does **not** mean Discord is omnipotent, nor that cartoon characters always lose to reality warpers. It means that, under these conditions, he has the more clearly supported nonphysical finishing option.

## THE GREAT BUREAUCRATIC MACHINE
### An episode of *Pending Approval*

**INT. MUNICIPAL ADMINISTRATION BUILDING — BASEMENT — MONDAY, 8:57 A.M.**

The basement of the Municipal Administration Building had been designed in 1963 by someone who believed natural light encouraged appeals.

Its walls were the color of wet envelopes. Its carpet had surrendered so completely that certain patches were now legally considered floor. A fluorescent tube above the stairwell flickered with the exhausted determination of a man trying to remember why he’d come into a room.

In the center of the basement stood **THE GREAT BUREAUCRATIC MACHINE**.

It was enormous.

Brass pipes climbed its flanks like ivy that had joined the civil service. Flywheels sat behind wire cages. Glass tubes contained bubbling liquids in three official colors: red, amber, and “awaiting clarification.” Across its vast iron face were hundreds of dials, switches, slots, little wooden drawers, and a single brass bell beneath a sign that read:

**DO NOT RING BELL.  
BELL WILL RING WHEN RINGING IS APPROPRIATE.**

Near the base, a velvet rope protected a smaller velvet rope.

Someone had polished the machine’s brass nameplate for the occasion. Someone else had taped a note beneath it:

**PLEASE DO NOT LEAVE YOGURT IN DOCUMENT INTAKE.**

**MARTIN PELL**, deputy assistant director of Civic Processes, stood beside the machine wearing a hard hat over hair that already resembled a hard hat. He held a clipboard firmly enough to suggest it might attempt escape.

Beside him, **PRIYA SHAH**, the department’s newest analyst, studied the machine’s control panel.

**DORIS VALE**, who had worked in Municipal Administration since the building was merely controversial, sat at a folding table knitting something narrow and gray.

**LEN**, the facilities manager, had his head inside an open maintenance hatch.

From within the machine came a clank, a muttered insult, and the sound of something small being dropped a very long distance.

**MARTIN:** Is that normal?

**LEN, from inside:** Depends what it hits.

They listened.

A distant gong sounded.

Doris ticked something on a sheet of paper.

**PRIYA:** What was that?

**DORIS:** Housing.

Martin checked his watch.

**MARTIN:** Right. Three minutes until the mayor arrives. Everyone remember: today marks the end of delays, duplication, and needless administrative complexity.

Priya looked up at a lever labeled **PRELIMINARY DUPLICATION**.

**PRIYA:** Then why does it have—

**MARTIN:** Heritage feature.

Len crawled out of the hatch. He was a broad, cheerful man with the expression of someone who knew where the bodies were buried because he’d been asked to check for pipes first.

He wiped his hands on a rag.

**LEN:** Mechanically, she’s beautiful. Bearings lubricated, belts tensioned, emergency tea reservoir topped up.

**PRIYA:** Tea reservoir?

Len pointed to a pressure gauge.

Its markings read:

**WEAK — ACCEPTABLE — STRONG — MEETING OVERRUN**

**LEN:** You don’t want that needle going into Meeting Overrun. Last time, Planning annexed the kitchen.

Martin straightened his tie.

**MARTIN:** There will be no “last time” stories in front of the mayor.

**DORIS:** Shall I hide the memorial plaque?

Martin glanced sharply toward the far wall.

Doris continued knitting.

**DORIS:** Joke.

A beat.

**DORIS:** It’s behind the coat rack.

Footsteps sounded on the stairs.

**MAYOR VIVIENNE CRISP** entered with a photographer, a ribbon-cutting smile, and the purposeful stride of someone who had never personally needed a parking permit.

Behind her came **GARY**, a local resident in paint-stained overalls, holding a single sheet of paper.

Martin intercepted him.

**MARTIN:** Sorry, sir. This is a closed event.

**GARY:** Woman upstairs said come down here.

**MARTIN:** Which woman?

**GARY:** The one under the sign saying “All Inquiries.”

Martin absorbed this betrayal.

**GARY:** I just need permission to put a little shed in my garden.

**MARTIN:** Today is not—

The mayor turned.

**MAYOR CRISP:** A resident! Wonderful. An authentic service user.

She took Gary gently by the elbow and moved him two feet to the left, into better light.

**MAYOR CRISP:** You haven’t already complained publicly, have you?

**GARY:** Not yet.

**MAYOR CRISP:** Excellent. Get one of us together.

The photographer lifted his camera.

Martin’s smile became tight and managerial.

**MARTIN:** Madam Mayor, welcome to the launch of a new era in civic efficiency.

He swept an arm toward the machine.

A little metal flap opened behind him.

A paper emerged.

Doris tore it off and read it.

**DORIS:** Unauthorized sweeping gesture.

Martin lowered his arm.

**MAYOR CRISP:** It’s magnificent. What exactly does it do?

**MARTIN:** It integrates every municipal process into a single seamless system.

**PRIYA:** It receives an application, checks relevant regulations, consults departmental records, resolves conflicts, and issues a decision.

**GARY:** So it says yes or no.

Everyone looked at him.

**DORIS:** We’re hoping to work up to that.
